text: Who euer my priuate opinion condemneth as faultie, Master Gascoigne is not to bee abridged of his deserued esteeme, who first beate the path to that perfection which our best Poets haue aspired too since his departure; whereto he did ascend by comparing the Italian with the English, as Tullie did Graecacum Latinis.
author: Greene, Robert, 1558?-1592.
title: Menaphon Camillas alarum to slumbering Euphues, in his melancholie cell at Silexedra. VVherein are deciphered the variable effects of fortune, the wonders of loue, the triumphes of inconstant time. Di

text: Was this the prophecie of thy souereigntie, to yeeld vp thy life to death so vntimely? wretched was I of al women to bring thee foorth to this infancie.
author: Greene, Robert, 1558?-1592.
title: Menaphon Camillas alarum to slumbering Euphues, in his melancholie cell at Silexedra. VVherein are deciphered the variable effects of fortune, the wonders of loue, the triumphes of inconstant time. Di

text: Tune on my pipe the praises of my Loue, And midst thy eaten harmonie recount How faire she is that makes thy musicke mount, And euerie string of thy hearts harpe to moue.
author: Greene, Robert, 1558?-1592.
title: Menaphon Camillas alarum to slumbering Euphues, in his melancholie cell at Silexedra. VVherein are deciphered the variable effects of fortune, the wonders of loue, the triumphes of inconstant time. Di

text: Thus Fates and Fortune dallying a dolefull Catastrophe, to make a more pleasing Epitazis, it fell out amongst them thus.
author: Greene, Robert, 1558?-1592.
title: Menaphon Camillas alarum to slumbering Euphues, in his melancholie cell at Silexedra. VVherein are deciphered the variable effects of fortune, the wonders of loue, the triumphes of inconstant time. Di

text: She did demaunde what was the cauſe of her great griefe and piteous mone Wherat this Ladie yet did pauſe at laſt ſhe ſaide, I am vndone, ALCIONE is caſt awaye with CEYX his death: For he hath yelded vp I ſaye his vitall breath.
author: Hubbard, William.
title: The tragicall and lamentable historie of two faythfull mates Ceyx kynge of Thrachine, and Alcione his wife: dravven into English meeter. By W. Hubbard. 1569

text: All this ſhe did yet being a ſleape, and by and by ſhe did awake, And rewfully began to wéepe, and heauely the matter take: Shee rent her Clothes, and fare her heere, with extreme woe: Her Nurce then roſe with rewfull feare and ranne her to.
author: Hubbard, William.
title: The tragicall and lamentable historie of two faythfull mates Ceyx kynge of Thrachine, and Alcione his wife: dravven into English meeter. By W. Hubbard. 1569

text: The Sea doth make mee ſore afraide to thinke on it, my Corps doth quake, My minde with muſing is diſmaide, for verie woe my Ioinctes do ſhake: For broken late vpon the ſhoare the Ribbes of Ships I ſawe, whoſe Maſters long before the waues in whips.
author: Hubbard, William.
title: The tragicall and lamentable historie of two faythfull mates Ceyx kynge of Thrachine, and Alcione his wife: dravven into English meeter. By W. Hubbard. 1569

text: When CEYX the matter did perceiue, miſdoubting what was beſt to doo: He did deuiſe where he might haue, a remedie to ſlake his woo: For counſell he to ſéeke with ſpéede at Sacred SPELS, Deuiſeth thus, as I do reade, where this God dwels.
author: Hubbard, William.
title: The tragicall and lamentable historie of two faythfull mates Ceyx kynge of Thrachine, and Alcione his wife: dravven into English meeter. By W. Hubbard. 1569

text: Now dead and drowned in the Sea, yet ſhe the dayes doth compt and tell, She thinkes poore wretch ALCIONE, her huſbandes home returne from SPELL To be but ſlowe: and ſhe doth thinke, eche hower a day, No ioyes into her hart can ſink, for his delay.
author: Hubbard, William.
title: The tragicall and lamentable historie of two faythfull mates Ceyx kynge of Thrachine, and Alcione his wife: dravven into English meeter. By W. Hubbard. 1569

text: Whilſte CEYX doth lye thus in the Sea: quite drownde with ouer gulfing waues On rufull Bed ALCIONE with weeping eies, ſhe reſtles craues For ſafe and ſpeedie comming home of CEYX her Mate: Who lieth toſt on ſalt Sea fome, vnfortunate.
author: Hubbard, William.
title: The tragicall and lamentable historie of two faythfull mates Ceyx kynge of Thrachine, and Alcione his wife: dravven into English meeter. By W. Hubbard. 1569

text: Their ſhip and they with fearefull ſpeede do cut down Sailes, & Clothes down rend Eche man is buſie nowe at neede, Yet all in vaine thei do contend: For now the Tempeſt hath by force the vpper hande: King CEYX doth oftimes wiſh his Corſe to be on lande.
author: Hubbard, William.
title: The tragicall and lamentable historie of two faythfull mates Ceyx kynge of Thrachine, and Alcione his wife: dravven into English meeter. By W. Hubbard. 1569

text: He was ſomtime of Thracine King, And CEYX I reade he had to name: Dame Fortune his miſchaunce ſeeking ſhe tolde him ſtreight by flickering Fame How Peleus his brother was by ruinous chaunce, With Death diſtroyed, as cam to paſſe, by Fortunes Launce.
author: Hubbard, William.
title: The tragicall and lamentable historie of two faythfull mates Ceyx kynge of Thrachine, and Alcione his wife: dravven into English meeter. By W. Hubbard. 1569

text: King CEYX did of his Loue ſtill ſpeake, he alwaies cried (ALCIONE,) Nothing would make his tonge of breake but wicked waues of watrie Sea When thus with Death he conquered was and diynge in Sea: He ſeemde to ſpeake halfe dead (alas) ALCIONE.
author: Hubbard, William.
title: The tragicall and lamentable historie of two faythfull mates Ceyx kynge of Thrachine, and Alcione his wife: dravven into English meeter. By W. Hubbard. 1569

text: FOr the Lord is not ſo vnkinde, that he can hate his owne fleſh, his owne members, his owne bowels.
author: Augustine, Saint, Bishop of Hippo.
title: S. Augustines manuel Conteining special, and piked meditations, and godlie praiers: drawne out of the Word of God, and writings of the holie Fathers, for the exercise of the soule. Corrected, translat

text: Through loue, firſt honeſt things are wel handled in the world; ſecondlie, honeſt things of the world are deſpiſed, and laſt of al, the ſecrets of God are ſeene and beholden.
author: Augustine, Saint, Bishop of Hippo.
title: S. Augustines manuel Conteining special, and piked meditations, and godlie praiers: drawne out of the Word of God, and writings of the holie Fathers, for the exercise of the soule. Corrected, translat

text: And although I am yet à ſinner, yet I doubt no whit of this participation of grace; although my ſinnes do hinder me, yet my ſubſtance doth require it; and although mine owne offences doe exclude me, yet the communion of nature doth not repel me.
author: Augustine, Saint, Bishop of Hippo.
title: S. Augustines manuel Conteining special, and piked meditations, and godlie praiers: drawne out of the Word of God, and writings of the holie Fathers, for the exercise of the soule. Corrected, translat

text: For thou art the bread, and the wel of life; thou art the light of euerlaſting cleerenes; to conclude thou art al things, whereof the righteous do liue, which loue thee.
author: Augustine, Saint, Bishop of Hippo.
title: S. Augustines manuel Conteining special, and piked meditations, and godlie praiers: drawne out of the Word of God, and writings of the holie Fathers, for the exercise of the soule. Corrected, translat

text: FOR our Sauiour came into ye world and was crucified, and put vnto death for our ſakes, that he might through his death, deſtroie him that had the power of death, that is the Diuel.
author: Augustine, Saint, Bishop of Hippo.
title: S. Augustines manuel Conteining special, and piked meditations, and godlie praiers: drawne out of the Word of God, and writings of the holie Fathers, for the exercise of the soule. Corrected, translat

text: Heerevpon let vs earneſtlie muſe; theſe things let vs hartelie deſire, the ſooner to come vnto their happie ſtate.
author: Augustine, Saint, Bishop of Hippo.
title: S. Augustines manuel Conteining special, and piked meditations, and godlie praiers: drawne out of the Word of God, and writings of the holie Fathers, for the exercise of the soule. Corrected, translat

text: There the pleaſant organes do ſounde-out moſt heauenlie hymnes; the bleſſed Angels moſt ſweetelie do ſing; & ſongs of rare excellencie are vttered out by the ſupernal Citizens, vnto the praiſe and glorie of thy Name.
author: Augustine, Saint, Bishop of Hippo.
title: S. Augustines manuel Conteining special, and piked meditations, and godlie praiers: drawne out of the Word of God, and writings of the holie Fathers, for the exercise of the soule. Corrected, translat

text: And after theſe ſo manie, and ſo great euils, ſucceedeth raging death, which bringeth vaine delights vnto ſuch an ende, that when they are once gone, they are as quite forgotten, as if they had neuer bin at al!
author: Augustine, Saint, Bishop of Hippo.
title: S. Augustines manuel Conteining special, and piked meditations, and godlie praiers: drawne out of the Word of God, and writings of the holie Fathers, for the exercise of the soule. Corrected, translat

text: Doubtles there ſhal be ſtore of happines, when the Lord ſhal bring his ſancts to the contemplation of his fathers glorie, and make them to ſit together in heauenlie places, that God may be al in al.
author: Augustine, Saint, Bishop of Hippo.
title: S. Augustines manuel Conteining special, and piked meditations, and godlie praiers: drawne out of the Word of God, and writings of the holie Fathers, for the exercise of the soule. Corrected, translat

text: Therefore seing the wise man hath counselled me otherwise, namely, not to go to Law with the Iudge forasmuch as he will giue sentence according to his owne honor, it were but Foly then to subiect my Faith to the iudgement of these counseles whereof Antichristes haue bene hea des and Iudges.
author: Fergusson, David, d. 1598.
title: Ane answer to ane epistle written by Renat Benedict the Frenche doctor, profesor of Gods worde (as the translator of this epistle calleth him) to Iohn Knox, and the rest of his brethren ministers of t

text: To the lord our god be praise for euer more, that thus hath Illuminat our eyes to se and espye the enimie to all ryghteousnes, to the end we may auoyde him, and so the plagues that God hath prepared to poure out vpon that beastlie kingdome, and the pertakers therewith.
author: Fergusson, David, d. 1598.
title: Ane answer to ane epistle written by Renat Benedict the Frenche doctor, profesor of Gods worde (as the translator of this epistle calleth him) to Iohn Knox, and the rest of his brethren ministers of t

text: The Angel of the Lorde is sent vnto him, to otter vnto him the yeares determinat of their captiuitie, their returninge home, the reedifying of the citie, the cōming of Christ, his slaughter, and destruction of the citie Ierusalem.
author: Fergusson, David, d. 1598.
title: Ane answer to ane epistle written by Renat Benedict the Frenche doctor, profesor of Gods worde (as the translator of this epistle calleth him) to Iohn Knox, and the rest of his brethren ministers of t

text: Let vs stere vp the negligēce and sluggishnes of Pastors, not tollarable, and let vs plainely argew their abuses with the vehemēcie of Gods word.
author: Fergusson, David, d. 1598.
title: Ane answer to ane epistle written by Renat Benedict the Frenche doctor, profesor of Gods worde (as the translator of this epistle calleth him) to Iohn Knox, and the rest of his brethren ministers of t

text: Ye affirme that your masse wes authorised in the Primatiue Church, and alwayes vsed of Gods chosen, and yet ye infer none of their excersices for your exemple, but the bare names of two men, whose autoritie and strenth is to weak to withstand Gods worde.
author: Fergusson, David, d. 1598.
title: Ane answer to ane epistle written by Renat Benedict the Frenche doctor, profesor of Gods worde (as the translator of this epistle calleth him) to Iohn Knox, and the rest of his brethren ministers of t

text: First the Lorde our God expresly forbiddeth in the Second cōmandement of the Decaloge, that we shall make any ymages, similitudes or lycknesses of any kynde of thing in the heauē aboue, the earth beneth, or in the water vnder the earth.
author: Fergusson, David, d. 1598.
title: Ane answer to ane epistle written by Renat Benedict the Frenche doctor, profesor of Gods worde (as the translator of this epistle calleth him) to Iohn Knox, and the rest of his brethren ministers of t

text: Because (sayeth he) that we were deliuered by the death of the Lord, we in eating and drinking of this thing (he meaneth the Sacrament) do signifie the fleshe and blood whiche were offered for vs. &c.
author: Fergusson, David, d. 1598.
title: Ane answer to ane epistle written by Renat Benedict the Frenche doctor, profesor of Gods worde (as the translator of this epistle calleth him) to Iohn Knox, and the rest of his brethren ministers of t

text: Hereby plainely witnessing that they are ashamed of the name of Christ before men that he may deny them before his Father in any wise to apertean to him, but to be of the nomber of those filthy locustes that S. Iohn remembreth in his Reuelation, to haue come out of the bottomles pit.
author: Fergusson, David, d. 1598.
title: Ane answer to ane epistle written by Renat Benedict the Frenche doctor, profesor of Gods worde (as the translator of this epistle calleth him) to Iohn Knox, and the rest of his brethren ministers of t

text: But this can no man do, but Christ alone, for of him and to him, alone were these wordes spoken out of the heauen, by the mouth of his Father.
author: Fergusson, David, d. 1598.
title: Ane answer to ane epistle written by Renat Benedict the Frenche doctor, profesor of Gods worde (as the translator of this epistle calleth him) to Iohn Knox, and the rest of his brethren ministers of t

text: He also made such deuision of his victuals amongs the Souldiers, that euery man had as great portion as him selfe, or rather a greater, so that he still wanne their good wills and fauour.
author: Diodorus, Siculus.
title: A righte noble and pleasant history of the successors of Alexander surnamed the Great, taken out of Diodorus Siculus: and some of their lives written by the wise Plutarch. Translated out of French int

text: At the foure corners were foure great pillers of wood, armed and bound with yron, eche of them an hundred cubits hie, so leaning and bending one to an other, that the whole building, hauing in it.ix. stories or sellers, the lowermost had.lx. beddes, and the vppermost but.ix.
author: Diodorus, Siculus.
title: A righte noble and pleasant history of the successors of Alexander surnamed the Great, taken out of Diodorus Siculus: and some of their lives written by the wise Plutarch. Translated out of French int

text: He found likewise among the hurte men, Ierome Cardian, a wise and politike man, whome Eumenes greatly honoured and familiarly vsed: and therefore Antigone in like sorte, after Eumenes hys death, honoured and well entreated him.
author: Diodorus, Siculus.
title: A righte noble and pleasant history of the successors of Alexander surnamed the Great, taken out of Diodorus Siculus: and some of their lives written by the wise Plutarch. Translated out of French int

text: When Ptolome vnderstood of his comming, he aduised with hys counsaile what should be best to doe, whether to attend the enimie in Syrie and there to fight, or to returne into Egipt, and from thence make warre as he hadde before done against Perdicas.
author: Diodorus, Siculus.
title: A righte noble and pleasant history of the successors of Alexander surnamed the Great, taken out of Diodorus Siculus: and some of their lives written by the wise Plutarch. Translated out of French int

text: For the right wing or vowarde wherein lay all his hope, he caused to marche against the ennimie, meanyng they should charge all alongest the flanke of the enimie.
author: Diodorus, Siculus.
title: A righte noble and pleasant history of the successors of Alexander surnamed the Great, taken out of Diodorus Siculus: and some of their lives written by the wise Plutarch. Translated out of French int

text: Antigone gaue a fierce and sterne aunswer, and therewith sent Demetre his Sonne with a great armie, store of engines and artillery to besiege and beat downe the citie.
author: Diodorus, Siculus.
title: A righte noble and pleasant history of the successors of Alexander surnamed the Great, taken out of Diodorus Siculus: and some of their lives written by the wise Plutarch. Translated out of French int

text: Whereupon he began to reproue him of manie false and slaunderous imputacions, whereby might easely be perceiued, that he went about to bring him to his finall end and destruction.
author: Diodorus, Siculus.
title: A righte noble and pleasant history of the successors of Alexander surnamed the Great, taken out of Diodorus Siculus: and some of their lives written by the wise Plutarch. Translated out of French int

text: Wherefore quod he) I thinke it good that of the kings treasure a Throne imperiall be forged & made of golde, and thereupon to be placed and set the statue or image of Alexander crouned, holding a Scepter as he did in his life time.
author: Diodorus, Siculus.
title: A righte noble and pleasant history of the successors of Alexander surnamed the Great, taken out of Diodorus Siculus: and some of their lives written by the wise Plutarch. Translated out of French int

text: On the other side, the Samnites séeing the Romaine armies farre from their countrey, burnt, wasted, and pilled the landes and countrey of the Iapides, confederats with the Romaines.
author: Diodorus, Siculus.
title: A righte noble and pleasant history of the successors of Alexander surnamed the Great, taken out of Diodorus Siculus: and some of their lives written by the wise Plutarch. Translated out of French int

text: Thys place is notable, declarynge the dignitie of hym that eateth Christ, and the effecte of that eatynge to be euerlastynge lyfe and sanctification, bothe of bodye and soule.
author: Watson, Thomas, 1513-1584.
title: Twoo notable sermons made the thirde and fyfte Fridayes in Lent last past, before the Quenes highnes, concernynge the reall presence of Christes body and bloude in the blessed Sacrament: also the Mass

text: But Christe is a sacrifyce aboue the aultare, who suffred for all men, these two vnder ye aultare, that were redemed by his passion.
author: Watson, Thomas, 1513-1584.
title: Twoo notable sermons made the thirde and fyfte Fridayes in Lent last past, before the Quenes highnes, concernynge the reall presence of Christes body and bloude in the blessed Sacrament: also the Mass

text: It was no newe thing, worthy the newe Testamente, to eate & drynke Christe in a fygure: and therfore it is certayne, that Christ in hys mysticall supper dydde not eate and drynke his body and bloude onlye fyguratiuely.
author: Watson, Thomas, 1513-1584.
title: Twoo notable sermons made the thirde and fyfte Fridayes in Lent last past, before the Quenes highnes, concernynge the reall presence of Christes body and bloude in the blessed Sacrament: also the Mass

text: The breade whyche we breake, is it not the communion of Christes body (that is to say) doth it not ioyne & knitte vs in the vnitye of one body of Christ?
author: Watson, Thomas, 1513-1584.
title: Twoo notable sermons made the thirde and fyfte Fridayes in Lent last past, before the Quenes highnes, concernynge the reall presence of Christes body and bloude in the blessed Sacrament: also the Mass

text: If a man make hys excuse, that he is not worthye the sacrifice, nor to communicate, then is he not worthy to be present there at the prayer.
author: Watson, Thomas, 1513-1584.
title: Twoo notable sermons made the thirde and fyfte Fridayes in Lent last past, before the Quenes highnes, concernynge the reall presence of Christes body and bloude in the blessed Sacrament: also the Mass

text: Eusebius also in his story of the churche, wryteth of one Attalus a martyr, who beynge roasted in an yron cradell wyth fyre put vnderneath, when the sauour of hys burnte flesh came to the smellynge of the people that looked on: he cryed wyth a loude voyce to the people.
author: Watson, Thomas, 1513-1584.
title: Twoo notable sermons made the thirde and fyfte Fridayes in Lent last past, before the Quenes highnes, concernynge the reall presence of Christes body and bloude in the blessed Sacrament: also the Mass

text: What is more credible we shuld thinke he ment by those woordes, then that perteyneth to the participation of this table, whych Christ him selfe a prieste and mediatour of the newe Testamente dothe exhibite after the ordre of Melchisedech of his body & bloude?
author: Watson, Thomas, 1513-1584.
title: Twoo notable sermons made the thirde and fyfte Fridayes in Lent last past, before the Quenes highnes, concernynge the reall presence of Christes body and bloude in the blessed Sacrament: also the Mass

text: And that thys is not my priuate collectiō, but the mind of all the aunciente fathers, I shall wyth youre patience recite their sentences.
author: Watson, Thomas, 1513-1584.
title: Twoo notable sermons made the thirde and fyfte Fridayes in Lent last past, before the Quenes highnes, concernynge the reall presence of Christes body and bloude in the blessed Sacrament: also the Mass

text: Why shuld anye man doubte of that, that in the beginnyng of ye churche the holye martirs dydde, and taught wythout al doubte.
author: Watson, Thomas, 1513-1584.
title: Twoo notable sermons made the thirde and fyfte Fridayes in Lent last past, before the Quenes highnes, concernynge the reall presence of Christes body and bloude in the blessed Sacrament: also the Mass

text: And after that last purification, the Athenyās dedycated in the honnour of god Apollo, one solempne feaste frome fyue yeares into fyue yeares.
author: Thucydides.
title: The hystory writtone by Thucidides the Athenyan of the warre, whiche was betwene the Peloponesians and the Athenyans, translated oute of Frenche into the Englysh language by Thomas Nicolls citezeine a

text: And neuerthels Alcibiades wēt about to get auctoritie towardes Tissaphernes, in manner that he shuld geue faith vnto him.
author: Thucydides.
title: The hystory writtone by Thucidides the Athenyan of the warre, whiche was betwene the Peloponesians and the Athenyans, translated oute of Frenche into the Englysh language by Thomas Nicolls citezeine a

text: And in despite of them that helde them assieged: they passed by the sea coaste, and the more parte came through the campe of the Athenyans so that they entredde into Scyone.
author: Thucydides.
title: The hystory writtone by Thucidides the Athenyan of the warre, whiche was betwene the Peloponesians and the Athenyans, translated oute of Frenche into the Englysh language by Thomas Nicolls citezeine a

text: To wit in breakyng your promes and apoynctement, afterwardes in kyllynge them with whom you had made it, & thirdly by promising vs deceitefully not to slay them: seinge yt we did no dammage in your land.
author: Thucydides.
title: The hystory writtone by Thucidides the Athenyan of the warre, whiche was betwene the Peloponesians and the Athenyans, translated oute of Frenche into the Englysh language by Thomas Nicolls citezeine a

text: And after that Aristonymus hadde reaported that same at Athens, al the Athenians were of opiniō to begyn warre against the sayd Scyonians and dyd prepare themself, for to make it.
author: Thucydides.
title: The hystory writtone by Thucidides the Athenyan of the warre, whiche was betwene the Peloponesians and the Athenyans, translated oute of Frenche into the Englysh language by Thomas Nicolls citezeine a

text: Also in lyke manner, men founde no remedy by vowes, by diuinations nor by any suche meanes, as they vsed.
author: Thucydides.
title: The hystory writtone by Thucidides the Athenyan of the warre, whiche was betwene the Peloponesians and the Athenyans, translated oute of Frenche into the Englysh language by Thomas Nicolls citezeine a

text: For the thynges, for the whyche, I am renommed and estemed amongeste men, besydes thys, that they redounde to the glory of my ancesters and to myne: brynge also honnour and welthe vnto the commmon welth.
author: Thucydides.
title: The hystory writtone by Thucidides the Athenyan of the warre, whiche was betwene the Peloponesians and the Athenyans, translated oute of Frenche into the Englysh language by Thomas Nicolls citezeine a

text: And also it cannot be sayd, that, that our puyssance sheweth not itself but by tokens and signes, for there be sene so greate experiences, that bothe those that be present, & also those that shall come after, shal hold them for myracles.
author: Thucydides.
title: The hystory writtone by Thucidides the Athenyan of the warre, whiche was betwene the Peloponesians and the Athenyans, translated oute of Frenche into the Englysh language by Thomas Nicolls citezeine a

text: And if any of the sayd allyes did the contrary, the other shulde prohybitt & resist them: and the king lykewise, if any of his subiectes did it in the lādes of the sayd confederates.
author: Thucydides.
title: The hystory writtone by Thucidides the Athenyan of the warre, whiche was betwene the Peloponesians and the Athenyans, translated oute of Frenche into the Englysh language by Thomas Nicolls citezeine a

text: And thorow this vyle auarice / a mā doth lose ye pytie, he shuld haue of his own soule.
author: Mardeley, John.
title: Here beginneth a necessarie instruction for all couetous ryche men to beholde [and] learne what perel [and] daunger they be brought into, yf they haue theyr consolacion in theyr daungerous and myserab

text: Thou arte not so discharged of thy dutie & reconīg, which yu must rēder of thy bayliwike, as in this lytle treatis shalbe declared.
author: Mardeley, John.
title: Here beginneth a necessarie instruction for all couetous ryche men to beholde [and] learne what perel [and] daunger they be brought into, yf they haue theyr consolacion in theyr daungerous and myserab

text: And prouideth for his own, he is a wyse man which can by his wit and pollicie get & heap ryches to gether & moch in estimaciō with the wycked.
author: Mardeley, John.

text: TAke Dwall or Nightshade, and stampe it well, and putte it in the potte with meate, and the meate will cleane together.
author: Hill, Thomas, b. ca. 1528.
title: A briefe and pleasaunt treatise, intituled, Naturall and artificiall conclusions: written first by sundrie scholers of the Vniuersitie of Padua in Italie, at the instant request of one Barthelmewe a T

text: AND to do this take vnfleke Lime, and quench the same with wine, and beate the same into fine powder, mixing therewith both Figges and Swines greace, and after labour them well together, for this as Plinie writeth passeth the hardnesse of a Stone.
author: Hill, Thomas, b. ca. 1528.
title: A briefe and pleasaunt treatise, intituled, Naturall and artificiall conclusions: written first by sundrie scholers of the Vniuersitie of Padua in Italie, at the instant request of one Barthelmewe a T

text: Also take an Apple of Coliquintida, and infuse the same in water, and in that water boyle Wormewood, whiche cast aboute the Chamber, killeth all the Fleas.
author: Hill, Thomas, b. ca. 1528.
title: A briefe and pleasaunt treatise, intituled, Naturall and artificiall conclusions: written first by sundrie scholers of the Vniuersitie of Padua in Italie, at the instant request of one Barthelmewe a T

text: Also take Lupines or flat Beanes, & boyle them in water with Wormwood, and that water sprinkle well aboute the Chamber, and al the Fleas shall auoyde that Chamber.
author: Hill, Thomas, b. ca. 1528.
title: A briefe and pleasaunt treatise, intituled, Naturall and artificiall conclusions: written first by sundrie scholers of the Vniuersitie of Padua in Italie, at the instant request of one Barthelmewe a T

text: TAke the bloud of a Wat or of a Kid, and drye it and keepe it from the ayre, then cast it on fishe or fleshe that is hot, and it will seeme rawe.
author: Hill, Thomas, b. ca. 1528.
title: A briefe and pleasaunt treatise, intituled, Naturall and artificiall conclusions: written first by sundrie scholers of the Vniuersitie of Padua in Italie, at the instant request of one Barthelmewe a T

text: And the same candle so lighted, will not goe out vntill the whole sustaunce bee spent, thus Cardanus writeth.
author: Hill, Thomas, b. ca. 1528.
title: A briefe and pleasaunt treatise, intituled, Naturall and artificiall conclusions: written first by sundrie scholers of the Vniuersitie of Padua in Italie, at the instant request of one Barthelmewe a T

text: Also take the fat of a Goate, and anoint what you list therewith, and set the same vnder your bed, and all the Fleas will gather vnto the same.
author: Hill, Thomas, b. ca. 1528.
title: A briefe and pleasaunt treatise, intituled, Naturall and artificiall conclusions: written first by sundrie scholers of the Vniuersitie of Padua in Italie, at the instant request of one Barthelmewe a T

text: Also if any annointeth this Stone with Garlicke, it doeth then hinder the Stone from drawyng any Iron or Needle vnto it, although the Needle should bee laied on the Stone.
author: Hill, Thomas, b. ca. 1528.
title: A briefe and pleasaunt treatise, intituled, Naturall and artificiall conclusions: written first by sundrie scholers of the Vniuersitie of Padua in Italie, at the instant request of one Barthelmewe a T

text: Also Cardane writeth, that if you take oile, puttyng into it mosten Leave seuen times together, and after quenche your Iron redde hotte into that Oile, for fower or fiue tymes together, and it will so make the same soft to woorke.
author: Hill, Thomas, b. ca. 1528.
title: A briefe and pleasaunt treatise, intituled, Naturall and artificiall conclusions: written first by sundrie scholers of the Vniuersitie of Padua in Italie, at the instant request of one Barthelmewe a T

text: They haue publiſhed in Print that the miniſterie of England is out of ſquare / & he hath publiſhed at Paules croſſe / that the biſhops of England haue bene vncircumſpect in making of miniſters / and that hathe he publyſhed before any councell in England had determined it.
author: Cartwright, Thomas, 1535-1603, attributed name.
title: A second admonition to the parliament

text: Lorde haue mercye vpon vs / Chriſte haue mercy vpon vs / is it not kyrie eleeſon / Chriſte eleeſon? their many Pater noſters / why vſe they them?
author: Cartwright, Thomas, 1535-1603, attributed name.
title: A second admonition to the parliament

text: But it is to be vſed continually / for the exerciſe of the miniſters / and others / as it ſhoulde ſeeme by the Apoſtle in the place to the Corinthes / to exerciſe their gates in the interpretation of ye ſcriptures.
author: Cartwright, Thomas, 1535-1603, attributed name.
title: A second admonition to the parliament

text: This conſiſtorie is for that onely congregation / and muſt doe that which they we / wyntly in any common cauſe of the churche.
author: Cartwright, Thomas, 1535-1603, attributed name.
title: A second admonition to the parliament

text: And further / I wyll not excuſe all thoſe that eyther reſygne / or ſuffer them ſelues to be depryued to auoyde further trouble / wythout conſyderation of theyr flocke / if the ſame conſpire not generally againſt them / ſeeing they oughte to giue theyr lyues for their flocke.
author: Cartwright, Thomas, 1535-1603, attributed name.
title: A second admonition to the parliament

text: Neuertheleſſe / what they do wel / the congregation cannot alter / neither ſhall the congregation put them / or any of them out / but vpō iuſt cauſe proued / either in that conſiſtorie / or in ſome one of the counſels / and the cauſe accepted for ſufficient.
author: Cartwright, Thomas, 1535-1603, attributed name.
title: A second admonition to the parliament

text: Shortly to ſay: Excommunication is a fearfull thing / as it is preſcribed by the ſcriptures / and vſed by the Churches of Chriſt reformed accordingly.
author: Cartwright, Thomas, 1535-1603, attributed name.
title: A second admonition to the parliament

text: For good orders / lette vs heare any one they make / but euen as the lawe directeth them / which any other temporall officers myght / and woulde doe as well as they / if the lawes dyd not prohibite it.
author: Cartwright, Thomas, 1535-1603, attributed name.
title: A second admonition to the parliament

text: Yea ſome of them haue ſayde / that cōformable Papiſtes were more tollerable then theſe preciſians and godlye men that ſeeke for reformation?
author: Cartwright, Thomas, 1535-1603, attributed name.
title: A second admonition to the parliament

text: For whoſoeuer ſuffreth aduerſitie, him do men call patient, but let vs with all marke that to be patient, it behooueth vs to moderate our ſorrowe.
author: Frewen, John, 1558-1628.
title: Certaine fruitfull instructions and necessary doctrines meete to edify in the feare of God faithfully gathered together by Iohn Frewen ... ; whereunto is added a table, wherein the reader may easily f

text: For where the cōmandement cōmeth either by mā or angel: and alſo where freewill is moued, prouoked, & enformed either by the motion of man or of angell: yet vnleſſe Gods grace goe withall preuenting and following the ſame, what is it able to do?
author: Frewen, John, 1558-1628.
title: Certaine fruitfull instructions and necessary doctrines meete to edify in the feare of God faithfully gathered together by Iohn Frewen ... ; whereunto is added a table, wherein the reader may easily f

text: He excepteth none, & therefore the grace of God, & benefits of his church, are not tyed to any one place: as to Rome, to Hieruſalem, to Conſtantinople, or to any other place.
author: Frewen, John, 1558-1628.
title: Certaine fruitfull instructions and necessary doctrines meete to edify in the feare of God faithfully gathered together by Iohn Frewen ... ; whereunto is added a table, wherein the reader may easily f

text: Lift vp your handes (ſaith the authour to the Hebrues) that hange downe, and your weake knees.
author: Frewen, John, 1558-1628.
title: Certaine fruitfull instructions and necessary doctrines meete to edify in the feare of God faithfully gathered together by Iohn Frewen ... ; whereunto is added a table, wherein the reader may easily f

text: For the Lord ſayth in his goſpell, he that loueth father or mother more then mee, is not worthy of me.
author: Frewen, John, 1558-1628.
title: Certaine fruitfull instructions and necessary doctrines meete to edify in the feare of God faithfully gathered together by Iohn Frewen ... ; whereunto is added a table, wherein the reader may easily f

text: When wee care for nothing that is godly, when we ſaye peace and reſt: then will the ſonne of man come to iudgement, then ſhall deſtruction ſodainely fall vppon vs. Therefore let vs be readie for in the houre that wee thinke not, will the Sonne of man come.
author: Frewen, John, 1558-1628.
title: Certaine fruitfull instructions and necessary doctrines meete to edify in the feare of God faithfully gathered together by Iohn Frewen ... ; whereunto is added a table, wherein the reader may easily f

text: And thus it is euident yt god by no means may be coūted ye author of euil, which he hath not created, made, or wrought, but ordeined yt it ſhould proceede from the freewill of his reaſonable creatures for the illuſtration of his glory.
author: Frewen, John, 1558-1628.
title: Certaine fruitfull instructions and necessary doctrines meete to edify in the feare of God faithfully gathered together by Iohn Frewen ... ; whereunto is added a table, wherein the reader may easily f

text: Concerning the firſt, the papiſtes ſpeake blaſphemie againſt God, in ſaying that the Shepheardes of the Church of Chriſt, are called to ſacrifice Ieſus Chriſt.
author: Frewen, John, 1558-1628.
title: Certaine fruitfull instructions and necessary doctrines meete to edify in the feare of God faithfully gathered together by Iohn Frewen ... ; whereunto is added a table, wherein the reader may easily f

text: For as the name of God is holie, ſo it behoueth vs to take diligent heede, that we doe not in ſuch ſorte name it that either we may ſeme to paſſe lightly of it our ſelues, or geue to other occaſion to haue it in ſmall reuerence.
author: Frewen, John, 1558-1628.
title: Certaine fruitfull instructions and necessary doctrines meete to edify in the feare of God faithfully gathered together by Iohn Frewen ... ; whereunto is added a table, wherein the reader may easily f

text: And I can suffer colde and hete, and that that god sendeth withouten grudge, that is to saye bycause I am a wretche.
author: Lucian, of Samosata.
title: A dialogue betwene Lucian and Diogenes of the life harde and sharpe, and of the lyfe tendre and delicate

text: And yet afore ye fall ye know not that ye shall falle, but this olde clooke / that ye mocke / and my here / and my facion, is of such power, that it gyueth me a quiete lyfe / that I may do what I woll, and company with whome I woll.
author: Lucian, of Samosata.
title: A dialogue betwene Lucian and Diogenes of the life harde and sharpe, and of the lyfe tendre and delicate

text: Nor yet those beddes of golde, and of yuery, gyueth not a sweter slepe / ye thou shalt se oft tymes, in an yuery bed & vnder a costly coueringe, those blessed folke can take no slepe at all.
author: Lucian, of Samosata.
title: A dialogue betwene Lucian and Diogenes of the life harde and sharpe, and of the lyfe tendre and delicate

text: Than is not that inough for euery man / that satisfieth his nede? or wolt thou say any other thyng?
author: Lucian, of Samosata.
title: A dialogue betwene Lucian and Diogenes of the life harde and sharpe, and of the lyfe tendre and delicate

text: But this diuerse, precious, and fortunate prouisyons, wherin ye tryumphe, bringe vnto you great wretchednes and mischieffe.
author: Lucian, of Samosata.
title: A dialogue betwene Lucian and Diogenes of the life harde and sharpe, and of the lyfe tendre and delicate

text: And it is lyke with you as with hym, that had lepte vppon a wilde horsis backe, the horse ranne carienge the manne awaye: And he might not nowe a lyght / the horse runninge / one met with hym, and asked hym whider he wente?
author: Lucian, of Samosata.
title: A dialogue betwene Lucian and Diogenes of the life harde and sharpe, and of the lyfe tendre and delicate

text: Wolte thou then (sins we ar gone so ferre) that we see what thyng skarsite is, and what plentie is?

text: But to lyue wantynge all these goodes, truely were wretchednes, ye if thou sholdest want any of them.

text: And we do knowe that the falſe Prophetes haue euer had thys good Lucke, that they haue had Kynges and Princes to be theyr Defedors and protectors.

text: SO the people, being charged to kepe all the commaundementes of god and his ordinances, and more ſtraitlie commaunded to kepe mo ordinances of men then goddis commaundemē tes, muſt nedes coldlye kepe ſome of the commandementes of God.
title: The Exposition of certain partes of Scripture, according to the mindes of the chieffe doctors ...

text: But as theſe arguments ar full of Pride, and ſwelling: So ar they moſt ful of vanitie, for firſt to begin withal.

text: Neyther againe haue we here to feare any tumult, if mens preceptes & rules eſpeciallye being ſuperſtitious be remoued out of the chirch, wher bye we kyndle and prouoke the wrath of God.
title: The Exposition of certain partes of Scripture, according to the mindes of the chieffe doctors ...

text: Becauſe thapoſtel is about to entreate diligently, and largly of this matter, that we may vnderſtand the better what his meaning is, we will define, what is a Magiſtrate?
title: The Exposition of certain partes of Scripture, according to the mindes of the chieffe doctors ...

text: The Prophetes & Apoſtells following this coū cel, ouercame the whole world, and did purge and ſkoure the chirch from vngodlines and Idolatry.
title: The Exposition of certain partes of Scripture, according to the mindes of the chieffe doctors ...

text: And afterward the Apoſtell Peter in the 5. chapiter of his former epiſtell, and god him ſelfe in the old teſtament reproued in falſe ſhepherdes whyche playd the Lordes, to cruelly ouer his ſlocke.
title: The Exposition of certain partes of Scripture, according to the mindes of the chieffe doctors ...

text: For the apparell affecting and occupiēg mennes eies, do ſtay and hynder theyr myndes from the conſideration of ſuch ſpirituall thynges as are don in the ſacramētes, and drawe thē to delyghtes and pleaſures of the Senſes.
title: The Exposition of certain partes of Scripture, according to the mindes of the chieffe doctors ...

text: And with this kind of foliſhnes ar the Religious men nowe a dayes ſicke, which will haue there garmentes, there manners, and the owtward cō dition of there liffe newe, in ſo much, as they muſt chaunge there old names alſo, where with they were named before.
title: The Exposition of certain partes of Scripture, according to the mindes of the chieffe doctors ...

text: Now Venus and the craftie fidler goes, into a close faire arbour for to walke: Adornd with darnecks of the Damask Rose, whilest Venus enters into this same talke, And proudly in her statelinesse doth stalke: And toong-ripe in her rhetorick doth run, And to Musaeus thus her tale begun.
author: Dymoke, Tailboys, attributed name.
title: Caltha poetarum: or The bumble bee. Composed by T. Cutvvode Esquyre

text: To this her Cupid answered pretely, how often (mother) haue I seene you shake The beawtie and the splendor of this tree, and of the Marygoulds, gay garlands make: Yea you your self to weare them for their sake.
author: Dymoke, Tailboys, attributed name.
title: Caltha poetarum: or The bumble bee. Composed by T. Cutvvode Esquyre

text: Alas, if the woods, the poore brooks, and the dales of the countrey, sound not sometime in our eares, as well as the Prince of Riuers, let the lasses giue ouer laaking in the greene, and dauncing about the Maypole.
author: Dymoke, Tailboys, attributed name.
title: Caltha poetarum: or The bumble bee. Composed by T. Cutvvode Esquyre

text: In like maner, as we please our selues, so some are pleased with vs. For as these are admired & deified almost by the wisest, the lernedst, & the deepest sighted into great matters, the ignorant not being able to attaine vnto thē.
author: Dymoke, Tailboys, attributed name.
title: Caltha poetarum: or The bumble bee. Composed by T. Cutvvode Esquyre

text: So, for this Bee, the best and chiefest thing, Is his owne hony, for to kill his sting.

title: Caltha poetarum: or The bumble bee. Composed by T. Cutvvode Esquyre

text: One doth his boots vnbutton from his shins, an other helps for to vntie his hose: An other wipeth hony from his wings, that came from Lady Caltha and the rose, The which he gets when he his prograce goes.

title: Caltha poetarum: or The bumble bee. Composed by T. Cutvvode Esquyre

text: Now is she made Dianas hunting dame, and to Eurotas banks, and Cynthias hill, And vnto Gargaphy must seeke her game, where she the Roes with Bucks & does must kill: With pleasure, sport, and pastime at her will.
author: Dymoke, Tailboys, attributed name.
title: Caltha poetarum: or The bumble bee. Composed by T. Cutvvode Esquyre

text: And in a Cage that he must learne to sing, But soft and faire, not till the next year spring.

text: Heere could I set you downe the Honysuckle the pretie Pinke and purple Pianet, The Bugles, Boradge, and the blew Bottle, the bonny Belamour and Violet, And thriuing Thrift if men would gather it With louely Lillies and the faire Narcis, And Venus sleepe at noone with Adonis.

text: For as I rede prayer peaseth almyghty god & maketh hym torne to mercy. but whan deuoute teeres come wt prayer than of his grete pyte he may no lenger suffre / but anone as he were ꝯstrayned he graūteth what we aske.

text: Fyrst for the trauaylous werkynge of his body that he suffred whan the flesshe stryued soo sore ayenst the goodnes of the spyryte.

text: He is blessyd that is perseueraūt vnto his lyues ende Here of thou hast ensamples of holy martyrs & cōfessours whiche neuer wolde be departed fro the loue of god for all the persecucyon that myght be do to them Also to suche men of feble herte & vnlust speketh saȳt Bernarde and sayth thus.

text: Of this desyre there ben many men and women whiche haue full grete lykynge to speke of the loue of god / and all daye askynge how they sholde loue god & in what maner they sholde loue to his pleasaunce for his endeles goodnes.

text: For whan he trauayleth a man with temptacyons and he be withstande / than be his paynes moche the more encreased in hell / withstande than his temptacyons with the vertue of pacyence & so thou shalt ouercome hym.

text: Therfore (as sayeth holy Basile) if we be bidde of any man to do that is contrarye to the commaundementes of Christe: there is hye tyme for vs to say, we be bounde more to obeye god thanne men.

text: For as I perceyue & here, some of them folowe more affections and respectes: than goddes worde onely and truthe.

text: In the dayes of Nehemias, Socrates (the ornament of ſchooling) kept a great ſchoole of Phiſoſophers; for order and diſcipline very excellent, and a moſt perfect looking glaſſe, wherein wee may beholde the image and ſtate of a good ſchoole.

text: In the firſt ſchoole therefore, though Adam be conteyned, who no doubt did his duetie in teaching his children: yet for that we finde no euidence thereof in writing, wee will paſſe by him and come to his ſonne Seth, a very godly and learned ſchoolemaiſter, as I may terme him.
author: Kempe, William.
title: The education of children in learning declared by the dignitie, vtilitie, and method thereof. Meete to be knowne, and practised aswell of parents as schoolmaisters.

text: In the tyme ye moost blessyd Domynyck the noble fader and leder moost famouse of ye ordre of prechers / preched throughout the worlde in many regyons and exhorted incessaūtly ye people to the laude: and prayse of ye blessyd marye vyrgyn vndefyled / & to her angelyke cōfraternyte.
author: Rolle, Richard, of Hampole, 1290?-1349, attributed name. aut
title: [The remedy against the troubles of temptations]

text: The thyrde remedye is this / that for as moche as the fende laboureth to make a man dredefull and sorye / a man agayne ought to the honour of god and confusyon of the fende to strength hymselfe and be mery though it be ayenst his herte / and drede noo thynge the fendes malyce.
author: Rolle, Richard, of Hampole, 1290?-1349, attributed name. aut
title: [The remedy against the troubles of temptations]

text: Thus I shewe vnto you that ye shall haue in experyence the spyryte of god bothe in sayenge and in forgyuynge.
author: Rolle, Richard, of Hampole, 1290?-1349, attributed name. aut
title: [The remedy against the troubles of temptations]

text: It was also vnfayned / for the woman afterwarde felte in her handes and fete the sorowe of crystes passyon / and in other partes of her body.
author: Rolle, Richard, of Hampole, 1290?-1349, attributed name. aut
title: [The remedy against the troubles of temptations]

text: Almyghty god werketh lyke a leche / for a leche suffreth somtyme the deed flesshe to growe on hym that he hath in cure / but afterwarde he taketh away the same and maketh the quycke flesshe to growe / and soo he heleth the pacyent.
author: Rolle, Richard, of Hampole, 1290?-1349, attributed name. aut
title: [The remedy against the troubles of temptations]

text: And I saye you for trouth so wyll it not be had / but by mekenes moche sooner it may be goten.
author: Rolle, Richard, of Hampole, 1290?-1349, attributed name. aut
title: [The remedy against the troubles of temptations]

text: The thyrde temptacyon is this whan a man in due tyme gyueth hymselfe to honest company & dysporte for the strength and comforte of his soule / and the fende putteth in his mynde his synnes to fore done.
author: Rolle, Richard, of Hampole, 1290?-1349, attributed name. aut
title: [The remedy against the troubles of temptations]

text: And therfore all suche trauayle men ought not to charge but suffre mekely and abyde pacyently tyll god doo remedy therto.

title: [The remedy against the troubles of temptations]

text: So ferynge synne good creatures that they wene to goo out of theyr myndes / But they that ben thus tempted answere the fende thus agayne that he is false and a lyer as his nature is to be.

text: And if ye muſt neade yet a whyle name theym by a diffuſe and a ſtraunge terme, call theym the Sacred wordes: and I am aſſured ye maye awaye wyth Sacred becauſe he ſemeth to be nere of kinne to maiſter Sacryng your good lorde.

text: And hereupon this examinat made reporte to Northcarnes ſecretarie, that the ſayde Ienny was a frende to the Catholykes and the Earles, and is a very truſty frende, and hath ventured his lyfe for the Catholykes.

text: Further the ſayde Story doth ſay, that he was neuer ſworne to King Philip, nor to the Duke of Alua, nor neuer by any meanes was made kyng Philippes ſubiecte or denizen, or otherwyſe naturalized to be Kyng Philippes ſubiect, but remaynes only ſtyll a ſubiect to the Queene of Englande.

text: And the ſaid Story confeſſeth that he wrote to Courteuile, that if about the realme of England there might go a number of ſhyppes, as men went about Ierico, then the Catholykes of Englande woulde take courage to prepare entry for them that went ſo about with the ſaid ſhyppes.

text: For al thoſe thynges which are before recited, are manyfeſtly to be proued, partly by the very wrytynges extant, and in no worde altered, and the reſt by ſufficient witneſſes, whereof I haue hadde good regarde euen for truethes ſake, knowyng that almyghtie God is the auenger of all vntrueth.

text: And to ſhew ſome taſte of their miſchiefes, a gentleman belongyng to Courteuile, a ſecretarie to the Duke of Alua, tolde an Englyſhe man, redye alſo to auowe the ſame, that.

text: And ſo the concluſion in his opinion ſerued for hym that he myght refuſe his naturall liege lady and Queene.

text: And further that Preſtall tolde him he coulde do much with that Englyſhe man in Irelande, wherein this examinat diſcouraged hym.

text: For through their diligence, labour & paynes vnder God, we eate, heare the word of god, laboure, brynge vp youth, householdes be in quietnes, the goodes ther of, with Cities, townes, and villages of the realme.

title: [Godly and most necessary annotations in ye .xiij. chapyter too the Romaynes]

text: There be some so indurate & past grace, that thinke them selues not bound to obey thys order and higher power, appoynted and commaunded of God: but doubtles those shall perysh with their capitaines, as Architophel did with his Absolon.

title: [Godly and most necessary annotations in ye .xiij. chapyter too the Romaynes]

text: For Paule byddeth vs loke vpon the power and autoritie of ye hygher powers: and not vpon theyr manners.

text: If the lawes concerne and appertayne vnto man, and vntoo thinges Ciuil, they must simple wythout exceptyon, be obeyed, except they repugne, and be contrary to the lawe of nature.

title: [Godly and most necessary annotations in ye .xiij. chapyter too the Romaynes]

text: And for a help vnto you, and also to the people in this behalfe, I haue set furth here the. xiii.

title: [Godly and most necessary annotations in ye .xiij. chapyter too the Romaynes]

text: As for the lawe of the fyrste table, whych conteynyth the relygyon of GOD, feare, faythe, loue, prayer, obedyence, pacyence, ryght vse of Sacramentes, wyth souche other as apperteynyth onlye vnto god, and be the fountayne and orygynall of all good workes.
author: Hooper, John, d. 1555.
title: [Godly and most necessary annotations in ye .xiij. chapyter too the Romaynes]

text: First, because the magistrate is the ordinaūce of god then because dysobedyence and breaking of goddes lawes, troubleth the publike and commune peace, & yeueth other stomake and incouraging to dysobey.

title: [Godly and most necessary annotations in ye .xiij. chapyter too the Romaynes]

text: And as he sayd first, they shulde be obeyed, because theyr place and autoritye is the ordynaunce of god: so now in hys seconde cause he sheweth, what great daunger & perill it is, too resyste and dysobaye Goddes ordyaunces.

text: Againe, our Prophet expreſſeth well the promis graūted to the man that conſidereth the poore and néedy, ſaying: He hath diſperſed abroad, and geuen to the poore, his righteouſnes remaineth for euer, his horne ſhall be exalted with glory.
author: Bedel, Henry, fl. 1571.

author: Bedel, Henry, fl. 1571.

author: Bedel, Henry, fl. 1571.

text: The third is here ſet downe moſt plainly, the matter that we muſt preach of, namely the Goſpell.

text: It muſte needes be fulfilled of them which our Sauiour ſpeaketh in an other place, They be blinde leaders of the blinde, and if the blinde lead the blind, both ſhall fall into the ditch, (that is) both the ignoraunt Miniſter and the ignoraunt people ſhall periſhe.

text: That the Indians our friendes did feare, leaſt you with your companie were all ſlaine, and your ſhips ſunke at Cumanaw (for ſo the Spaniards noyſed it amongſt them.) that ſome of Gualtero his frinds with Putijma, were in the mountaines not farre from the hill Aio.

text: We returned therfore another way by the maine riuer on the South ſide: this branch we founde large, deep, and without danger.

text: In the end hee ſent one of his aged followers, to certifie vs, that he was ſicke, olde and weake: that the wayes neere his dwelling are not eaſie: and that therefore he deſired vs to hold him excuſed for not comming.
author: Kemys, Lawrence, d. 1618.

text: That Manoa ſtandeth twentie dayes iourney from the mouth of Wiapoco: ſixteene dayes from Barima: thirteene dayes from Amacur, and ten dayes from Aratoori.
author: Kemys, Lawrence, d. 1618.
title: A relation of the second voyage to Guiana. Perfourmed and written in the yeare 1596. By Lawrence Kemys, Gent

text: O lett not then ſuch an indignitie reſt on vs, as to depraue ſo notable an enterpriſe with falſe rumors, and vaine ſuppoſitions, to ſleepe in ſo ſerious a matter, and renouncing the honour, ſtrength, wealth, and ſoueraingtie of ſo famous conqueſt, to leaue all vnto the Spaniard.

text: Laſtlie, he ſhewed mee that Wariarimagoto the Emperours chiefe Captaine for thoſe partes, hath gathered together manie thouſands of the Epuremai, to keep the borders of the Empire; and that hee lay now on the ſouth ſide of the mountaines, ſome one dayes iourney, or little more from the Spaniard.

text: That it repenteth him of his ambition, euer to haue ſought by the Spaniards meanes, to haue enlarged his countries and people.

text: This Informers verie countenance gaue him to bee ſuſpected, and therefore partlie by threatning, partlie by promiſe of reward we won him to confeſſe the trueth.

text: Where when he ſaw the Prince in armour bright, He cald to him aloud, his caſe to rew, And reſcue him through ſuccour of his might, From that his cruell foe, that him purſewd in ſight.

text: Prouided alſo, that for their partes they remember to loue peace, and modeſtly to conteyne themſelues within their boundes, whereas ſome of them, to the great reproch of their vocation, are become the inſtruments of theſe diſorders.
author: France. Sovereign (1574-1589 : Henry III)
title: The declarations as vvell of the French King, as of the King of Nauarre Concerning the truce agreed vpon betwene their Maiesties: and touching the passage of the riuer of Loire.

text: Of our nobilitie, how many families be there that will not obey the houſe of Lorraine? much leſſe the varlet of varlets? ye houſes honored with the alliance of our kings and princes about vs, who alſo haue this article aboue the reſt.
author: France. Sovereign (1574-1589 : Henry III)
title: The declarations as vvell of the French King, as of the King of Nauarre Concerning the truce agreed vpon betwene their Maiesties: and touching the passage of the riuer of Loire.

text: It is very eaſie to deſire a crowne: it is very eaſie for a people moued and paſſionate againſt their Prince, to thinke vpon the alteration of the Eſtate.
author: France. Sovereign (1574-1589 : Henry III)
title: The declarations as vvell of the French King, as of the King of Nauarre Concerning the truce agreed vpon betwene their Maiesties: and touching the passage of the riuer of Loire.

text: Oh monſters of furie, crueltie and barbarouſneſſe, who neuertheleſſe can not liue long, vnleſſe peraduenture by ſome ſhamefull memory to this world & to the nation that hath borne and doth ſupport them, deteſtable whereſoeuer it commeth to the poſteritie.
author: France. Sovereign (1574-1589 : Henry III)
title: The declarations as vvell of the French King, as of the King of Nauarre Concerning the truce agreed vpon betwene their Maiesties: and touching the passage of the riuer of Loire.

text: Let thoſe townes that haue taken their parte remember in what ſtate they were before, and in what they be now: The traffick (who ſo liſt to ſéeke it) in the midſt of a forreſt?
author: France. Sovereign (1574-1589 : Henry III)
title: The declarations as vvell of the French King, as of the King of Nauarre Concerning the truce agreed vpon betwene their Maiesties: and touching the passage of the riuer of Loire.

text: What can be more effectually spoken to set forthe the maiestie of my iurisdiction whiche I receaued immediatly of the Lord, of the Lord I saye, and of no mā.
author: Foxe, John, 1516-1587, attributed name.
title: A solemne contestation of diuerse popes, for the aduaunsing of theyr supremacie: quoted and collected faithfully out of their own canon law, according to the very wordes, stile, and tenor of the same

text: And agayn where as I haue giuen at sondry times to Ludouicus and other Emperours of my temporall landes and possessions, yet that was donne, not so muche for anye recognising of homage to thē as for keping peace with thē.
author: Foxe, John, 1516-1587, attributed name.
title: A solemne contestation of diuerse popes, for the aduaunsing of theyr supremacie: quoted and collected faithfully out of their own canon law, according to the very wordes, stile, and tenor of the same

text: And for asmuch as some do obiect, yt my pardons cā not extende to thē that be departed, for that it was said to Peter: what so euer thou shalt lose vpō earth, & therfor seyng thei are not vpō earth, they can not be losed of me.
author: Foxe, John, 1516-1587, attributed name.
title: A solemne contestation of diuerse popes, for the aduaunsing of theyr supremacie: quoted and collected faithfully out of their own canon law, according to the very wordes, stile, and tenor of the same

text: Nether must Kinges and Princes thinke it muche to submitte themselfes to my Iudgement for so did Valentinianus the worthy Emperour, so did Theodosius, and also Carolus.
author: Foxe, John, 1516-1587, attributed name.
title: A solemne contestation of diuerse popes, for the aduaunsing of theyr supremacie: quoted and collected faithfully out of their own canon law, according to the very wordes, stile, and tenor of the same

text: Itē to legitimate what persones so euer he please, as touchyng spiritualties? in al places, as touchyng temporalties, as honors, inheritaunce, &c.
author: Foxe, John, 1516-1587, attributed name.
title: A solemne contestation of diuerse popes, for the aduaunsing of theyr supremacie: quoted and collected faithfully out of their own canon law, according to the very wordes, stile, and tenor of the same

text: I am all in all & aboue all, so that God him selfe & I the vicare of God haue both one Consistorie, and am able to do almoste all that God can doe, Claue non errāte.
author: Foxe, John, 1516-1587, attributed name.
title: A solemne contestation of diuerse popes, for the aduaunsing of theyr supremacie: quoted and collected faithfully out of their own canon law, according to the very wordes, stile, and tenor of the same

text: What shoulde I speake here of my dayly reuenues of my first fruites Annates, palles, indulgēces, bulles, confessionales, indultes & rescriptes, testaments, dispensations, priuilegis, elections, prebendes, religious houses and such like whiche come to no small masse of money.
author: Foxe, John, 1516-1587, attributed name.
title: A solemne contestation of diuerse popes, for the aduaunsing of theyr supremacie: quoted and collected faithfully out of their own canon law, according to the very wordes, stile, and tenor of the same

text: For do you not see the neckes of great kinges & princes bēd vnder our knees, yea & thynke thēselfes happy & well defensid, if they maye kisse our hādes?
author: Foxe, John, 1516-1587, attributed name.
title: A solemne contestation of diuerse popes, for the aduaunsing of theyr supremacie: quoted and collected faithfully out of their own canon law, according to the very wordes, stile, and tenor of the same

text: The same hath autoritie in anye election, before it bee made, to pronounce it none, whan it is made.

text: And it is there thenne as Somer in Englonde. ſo in the wynter it is temperate noo colde but lytyll.
title: Informacon for pylgrymes vnto the holy londe

text: And yf ony englyſſhe man catche there that ſykneſſe. it is a grete merueylle but yf he deye therof.
title: Informacon for pylgrymes vnto the holy londe

text: Soo bi.ij. at after noon̄ the ſame Saterday they came to Ieruſalem / where they were receyued in to an hoſpytall a lytyll from the ſepulcre.
title: Informacon for pylgrymes vnto the holy londe

text: And there is the ſepulcre of Zacharie the ſone of Barachie. whyche Iewes ſlewe betwene the temple & the awter.
title: Informacon for pylgrymes vnto the holy londe

text: And there they ſayled vp & downe thre dayes & two nightes in grete peryl beſyde grete rockes. and durſte not paſſe for the wynde was agaynſt them.
title: Informacon for pylgrymes vnto the holy londe

text: The patron̄ of the ſame ſhippe was callyd Luke Mantell. to the nombre of.xlvi. pilgrymes. euery man payend ſome more ſome leſſe as they myghte accorde wyth the patron̄.
title: Informacon for pylgrymes vnto the holy londe

text: Some that myghte paye wel payed.xxxij. dukates. and ſome.xxvi. and.xxiiij. for meete & drynke and paſſage to porte Iaffe.
title: Informacon for pylgrymes vnto the holy londe

text: IN the ſeuen and twenty daye of the monthe of Iune there paſſyd from Venyſe vnder ſaylle out of the hauen of Venyſe acte the ſonne goyng downe. certayn pylgrymes towarde Ieruſalem in a ſhippe of a marchauntes of Venyſe callyd Iohn Moreſon.
title: Informacon for pylgrymes vnto the holy londe

text: There is a foure ſquare ſtoon whyte. where vppon Criſte reſtyd hym wyth his croſſe whan he went towarde the mount of Caluarie.
title: Informacon for pylgrymes vnto the holy londe

text: Alway whan nature / of thyng is moost laudable That thyng men coūteth / moost good & profitable And euery person / in his owne gifte hath ioye The fole in his bable / hath pleasure for to toye.
author: Pius II, Pope, 1405-1464.
title: Here begynneth the egloges of Alexa[n]der Barclay prest wherof the fyrst thre conteyneth the myseryes of courters [et] courtes of all prynces in generall, the matter wherof was translated into Englysh

text: Lo Codrus / I here haue tolde the by and by Of shepherde Cornir / the wofull elegy Wherin he mourned / the greuous payne and harde And last departyng / of noble lorde Hawarde More he endyted / of this good admyrall But truely Codrus / I can nat tell the all.
author: Pius II, Pope, 1405-1464.
title: Here begynneth the egloges of Alexa[n]der Barclay prest wherof the fyrst thre conteyneth the myseryes of courters [et] courtes of all prynces in generall, the matter wherof was translated into Englysh

text: If thy Jupiter / gyue me but onely golde Mercury shall gyue the / giftes manyfolde His pyllion ceptre / his wynges / and his harpe If thou haue all these / thou mayst grathly carpe And ouer all these / gyue the shall Mercury The knot of Hercules enlaced craftely.
author: Pius II, Pope, 1405-1464.
title: Here begynneth the egloges of Alexa[n]der Barclay prest wherof the fyrst thre conteyneth the myseryes of courters [et] courtes of all prynces in generall, the matter wherof was translated into Englysh

text: Joyne we our sterres / let me haue parte of thyne Cōcorde to cheryss he / yu shalte haue parte of myne Make thou Jupiter / be frendely vnto me And our Mercury / shalbe as good to the.
author: Pius II, Pope, 1405-1464.
title: Here begynneth the egloges of Alexa[n]der Barclay prest wherof the fyrst thre conteyneth the myseryes of courters [et] courtes of all prynces in generall, the matter wherof was translated into Englysh

text: So hast thou Codrus / of golde ynough in store And I some cōnyng / though fewe mē care therfore Thou art beholden / to Jupiter truely And I beholden to plesaunt Mercury.
author: Pius II, Pope, 1405-1464.
title: Here begynneth the egloges of Alexa[n]der Barclay prest wherof the fyrst thre conteyneth the myseryes of courters [et] courtes of all prynces in generall, the matter wherof was translated into Englysh

text: He was a pyller / of sober contynence His onely treasure / and iowell was good name But O cursed dethe / thy wrathfull vyolnece By stroke vnwarned / halfe blynded of his fame Who may I accuse? who may I put in blame?
author: Pius II, Pope, 1405-1464.
title: Here begynneth the egloges of Alexa[n]der Barclay prest wherof the fyrst thre conteyneth the myseryes of courters [et] courtes of all prynces in generall, the matter wherof was translated into Englysh

text: This is of our lorde / disposed so my brother Bycause all costes / shulde one haue nede of other.
author: Pius II, Pope, 1405-1464.
title: Here begynneth the egloges of Alexa[n]der Barclay prest wherof the fyrst thre conteyneth the myseryes of courters [et] courtes of all prynces in generall, the matter wherof was translated into Englysh

text: All pleasure present / of men is counted small Desyre obteyned / some counteth nought at all What men hope after / that semeth grete and dere At lyght by dystaunce / apereth great and clere.
author: Pius II, Pope, 1405-1464.
title: Here begynneth the egloges of Alexa[n]der Barclay prest wherof the fyrst thre conteyneth the myseryes of courters [et] courtes of all prynces in generall, the matter wherof was translated into Englysh

text: God for deth / or fortune / or impotent nature God dothe his pleasure / & dethe wyll haue the same Nature was mighty / long able to endure.
author: Pius II, Pope, 1405-1464.

text: Nagera will ſay that he hath no ſuch warrant: then ſhall you aunſwere him that the mā is troubleſome, & that you wil not ſtay for that, ſeeing I haue ſo commaunded you, and that Burgos is deſtitute of money.
author: Jáuregui y Aguilar, Juan de, 1583-1641.

text: It was a great chaunce that I eſcaped all the waye, the Frenche doe ſo range vp and downe.
author: Jáuregui y Aguilar, Juan de, 1583-1641.

text: Concerning the credit and truth of this diſcourſe, it is ſo plaine and ſufficient, that neither all the Spaniardes in the worlde, nor all their fauourites whatſoeuer or whereſoeuer, ſhal be able iuſtlie any maner of way, to impugne or diſgrace the ſame.
author: Jáuregui y Aguilar, Juan de, 1583-1641.

text: In paſſing by, ye ſaid Lorde of Saint Aldegonde went alſo in to his highneſſe, & ſhewed him the ſayde Papers.
author: Jáuregui y Aguilar, Juan de, 1583-1641.
title: A true discourse of the assault committed vpon the person of the most noble prince, William Prince of Orange, Countie of Nassau, Marquesse de la Vere by Iohn Iauregui Spaniarde With the true copies of

text: On the other ſide, the Magiſtrate was as diligent in procéeding againſt the offendors: ſo as finally he atteyned to the truth of the whole matter, as it wil appeare in the depoſitions of the ſayd offendors.
author: Jáuregui y Aguilar, Juan de, 1583-1641.
title: A true discourse of the assault committed vpon the person of the most noble prince, William Prince of Orange, Countie of Nassau, Marquesse de la Vere by Iohn Iauregui Spaniarde With the true copies of

text: Being demaunded whether he knewe, whether the ſayd Iaſper Annaſtro or any other had framed the like practiſe againſt the perſon of the moſt noble Quéene of England, or againſt the moſt noble Duke of Anjou? ſayth that he thinketh no.
author: Jáuregui y Aguilar, Juan de, 1583-1641.
title: A true discourse of the assault committed vpon the person of the most noble prince, William Prince of Orange, Countie of Nassau, Marquesse de la Vere by Iohn Iauregui Spaniarde With the true copies of

text: The blow was giuen the greater is the ſinne, and the good Prince grieuouſlie wounded, the more is the pitie, if the Lord had otherwiſe ſeene it good.
author: Jáuregui y Aguilar, Juan de, 1583-1641.
title: A true discourse of the assault committed vpon the person of the most noble prince, William Prince of Orange, Countie of Nassau, Marquesse de la Vere by Iohn Iauregui Spaniarde With the true copies of

text: Wherefore he requeſteth the Lordes Magiſtrates of this Towne to pardon him hys ſayde offence alſo to adde this to his former confeſſion, and if the other be publiſhed, to publiſh this withal, to the end no man thinke that he dyed in ſo wicked an opinion.
author: Jáuregui y Aguilar, Juan de, 1583-1641.

text: He ſayth yea, and that the ſayd Iohn hauing the Sunday before heard Maſſe, departed out of the houſe about eleuen of the clocke before noone, after he had thrée or foure times gone out and in at the ſaid houſe.
author: Jáuregui y Aguilar, Juan de, 1583-1641.
title: A true discourse of the assault committed vpon the person of the most noble prince, William Prince of Orange, Countie of Nassau, Marquesse de la Vere by Iohn Iauregui Spaniarde With the true copies of

text: I haue deſerued this death ſaide he, and you that are preſent: Example ye may take by me: he then incontinent Did aſke were any there did know, Phillip Sturly by name: Which Capitaine now in Scotland is, ſayes ſome, we know the ſame.
author: Davie, Sampson.
title: [The end and confession of T. Norton and C. Norton rebels who died the 27th of May 1570]

text: The yonger being aſked then, wher he did there beleeue: Saued to be by Chriſte his death, this aunſwere did he geue.
author: Davie, Sampson.
title: [The end and confession of T. Norton and C. Norton rebels who died the 27th of May 1570]

text: Againſt the Papiſts and the Pope, with all your might and powre: Which ſéeke the waies, like raueninge woulen the Goſpel to deuowre.
author: Davie, Sampson.
title: [The end and confession of T. Norton and C. Norton rebels who died the 27th of May 1570]

text: The Preacher then, to him thus ſayde, pray you in Engliſh here: Then will the People pray with you: this anſwer made he there.
author: Davie, Sampson.
title: [The end and confession of T. Norton and C. Norton rebels who died the 27th of May 1570]

text: I neede not here at large reſite, true ſubiectes knowes right well: The troubles greate that chaunſt of late, by ſuch as did rebell Againſt our Sauiour and his word, which he to vs hath ſende, Alſo againſt our noble Quéene, which doth the ſame defende.
author: Davie, Sampson.
title: [The end and confession of T. Norton and C. Norton rebels who died the 27th of May 1570]

text: I do beléeue ſaued to be, by Ieſus Chriſte on hie: For in no other do I truſt, he then immediatly.
author: Davie, Sampson.
title: [The end and confession of T. Norton and C. Norton rebels who died the 27th of May 1570]

text: Did ther deſire the people all, in preſence as they were: That he there died a Chriſtian true, they all ſhould witneſſe beare.
author: Davie, Sampson.
title: [The end and confession of T. Norton and C. Norton rebels who died the 27th of May 1570]

text: With loſſe of landes, of Goods, and lyfe, this haps by Treſon fell: And for the moſt part to all ſuch, as vſe for to rebell.
author: Davie, Sampson.
title: [The end and confession of T. Norton and C. Norton rebels who died the 27th of May 1570]

text: For ſome there be that vſe to faine, and godlineſſe profeſſe: Whiche beare two faces in one hoode, ſuch is their wickedneſſe, To trap and turne ſuch ſwaruing mindes vnto their wicked trade Of Poprie, whiche wee may be ſure, the Deuill himſelf hath made.
author: Davie, Sampson.
title: [The end and confession of T. Norton and C. Norton rebels who died the 27th of May 1570]

text: Nowe you whom both the gods and Fortunes grace, Hath ſau'd from danger in theſe furious broyles, Forbeare to tempt the enemy againe, For feare you feele a third calamitie.
author: Garnier, Robert, 1544-1590.
title: Pompey the Great, his faire Corneliaes tragedie effected by her father and husbandes downe-cast, death, and fortune. Written in French, by that excellent poet Ro: Garnier; and translated into English

text: He that of his departure tooke the ſpoyle, Whoſe fell ambition (founded firſt in blood) By nought but Pompeys lyfe could be with-ſtood.
author: Garnier, Robert, 1544-1590.
title: Pompey the Great, his faire Corneliaes tragedie effected by her father and husbandes downe-cast, death, and fortune. Written in French, by that excellent poet Ro: Garnier; and translated into English

text: Till iealous rage (engendered with reſt,) Returnes them ſharper ſet then at the firſt; And makes them couple when they ſee theyr prize, With briſtled backs, and fire-ſparkling eyes, Tyll tyer'd or conquer'd, one ſubmits or flyes.
author: Garnier, Robert, 1544-1590.
title: Pompey the Great, his faire Corneliaes tragedie effected by her father and husbandes downe-cast, death, and fortune. Written in French, by that excellent poet Ro: Garnier; and translated into English

text: "Fraile men, or mans more fraile defence, "Had neuer power, to practiſe ſtayes "Of this celestiall influence, "That gouerneth and guides our dayes.
author: Garnier, Robert, 1544-1590.
title: Pompey the Great, his faire Corneliaes tragedie effected by her father and husbandes downe-cast, death, and fortune. Written in French, by that excellent poet Ro: Garnier; and translated into English

text: Since thy hard hap, ſince thy fierce deſtinie, (Enuious of all thine honors) gaue thee mee.
author: Garnier, Robert, 1544-1590.
title: Pompey the Great, his faire Corneliaes tragedie effected by her father and husbandes downe-cast, death, and fortune. Written in French, by that excellent poet Ro: Garnier; and translated into English

text: Till (griefe to heare, and hell for me to ſpeake,) My woes waxt ſtronger, and my ſelfe grew weake.
author: Garnier, Robert, 1544-1590.
title: Pompey the Great, his faire Corneliaes tragedie effected by her father and husbandes downe-cast, death, and fortune. Written in French, by that excellent poet Ro: Garnier; and translated into English

text: And thrice detaind, with dolefull ſhreeks and cryes, (With armes to heauen vprea'd) I gan exclaime And bellow forth againſt the Gods themſelues, A bedroll of outragious blaſphemies.
author: Garnier, Robert, 1544-1590.
title: Pompey the Great, his faire Corneliaes tragedie effected by her father and husbandes downe-cast, death, and fortune. Written in French, by that excellent poet Ro: Garnier; and translated into English

text: For yee haue baſely broke the Law of Armes, And out-rag'd ouer an afflicted ſoule; Murdred a man that did ſubmit himſelfe, And iniur'd him that euer vs'd you kindly.
author: Garnier, Robert, 1544-1590.
title: Pompey the Great, his faire Corneliaes tragedie effected by her father and husbandes downe-cast, death, and fortune. Written in French, by that excellent poet Ro: Garnier; and translated into English

text: For then (as if prouokt with pricking goades,) Theyr warlike Armies, (faſt lockt foote to foote,) Stooping their heads low bent to toſſe theyr ſtaues, They fiercely open both Battalions.
author: Garnier, Robert, 1544-1590.
title: Pompey the Great, his faire Corneliaes tragedie effected by her father and husbandes downe-cast, death, and fortune. Written in French, by that excellent poet Ro: Garnier; and translated into English
