text: If that be not a grete faute, so to hurt a mans name, Without sufficient cause: what crime shuld a man blame?
title: A Short answere to the boke called Beware the cat

text: O r els a payre of stockes: if officers do wel, You hurt a harmeles man: which no such tales did tel, As ye were disposed: loude lyes on him to make, Which many witti things: writes for his countreys sake.
title: A Short answere to the boke called Beware the cat

text: Omnia si perdas: famam servare memento: Qua semel amissa postea nullus eris, If thou lese all (sayth he) yet reserve honest fame If that be ones clene gon: go home and suck thy dame.
title: A Short answere to the boke called Beware the cat

text: And now Iuge good hirers: whether he be a good man Of whom I write these things: as truli as I can.

text: Ye had had from his hande: a more precious tresure But in the meane season: content your selfe with this, For your Bagagical boke, a warme a. r. s. you may kys.

text: Certes (sayeth he) I say vnto you, except ye eate my fleshe & drynke my bloud: you shall haue no lyfe in you.
author: Crowley, Robert, 1518?-1588.

author: Crowley, Robert, 1518?-1588.

author: Crowley, Robert, 1518?-1588.

text: Inula is called in greeke Helenion, in engliſhe Alecampane, or Elecampane, in duch Alantz wurtz, in frenche, and in the Poticaries ſhopped Enula cāpana.
author: Turner, William, d. 1568.
title: The names of herbes in Greke, Latin, Englishe, Duche [and] Frenche with the commune names that herbaries and apotecaries vse. Gathered by William Turner.

text: Arum is called in greke aron, in engliſh Cuckopintell, Wake Robin, or Rampe, in duche Pſaffen bynde, in frenche Vidchaen, the Poticarie calleth it Pes vituli, Serpentaria minor, Luph minus groweth in euery hedge almoſt in Englande aboute townes in the ſpryng of the yere.
author: Turner, William, d. 1568.

text: SEeth them in white wine or in Claret, and ſtrain them thick: when they be ſodden: thē take two yolks of egges & thicken it withall: then ſeaſon it with Sinamon, Ginger, and Sugar, and bake it, and ſo ſerue it.
title: [A booke of cookerie, otherwise called the good huswiues handmaid.]

text: TAke of the ſcales, and take foorth the Gall, and with cloues, Mace, and ſalte, ſeaſon it and take corans and prunes, and put about the carpe, and take butter and put it vpon him and let him bake two houres.
title: [A booke of cookerie, otherwise called the good huswiues handmaid.]

text: DReſſe thē faire, & perboil thē, then ſeaſon them wt pepper & ſalt, a few whole cloues amongſt them, and Onions ſmal minced, and ſwéete butter, Vergious, and a litle Sugar.
title: [A booke of cookerie, otherwise called the good huswiues handmaid.]

text: TAke thick almond milke ſéething hot, & ſo wet your flower with it: & ſallet oyle fried, & ſaffron, and ſo miggle your paſte altogether, and that will make good paſte.
title: [A booke of cookerie, otherwise called the good huswiues handmaid.]

text: TAke a Capon and boyle it with veale, or with a marie bone, or what your fancy is.
title: [A booke of cookerie, otherwise called the good huswiues handmaid.]

text: BOil your flank of béef verie tender, til the broth bée almoſt conſumed, then put the broth into a pipkin, & put to it Onions, caret roots ſheed ſmal, being render ſodden before and pepper groſe beaten, vergious; and halfe a diſh of ſwéet butter, and ſo lay it vpon.
title: [A booke of cookerie, otherwise called the good huswiues handmaid.]

text: TAke grated bread and put to it molten butter and a litle Roſewater and ſugar, and the yolks of egs, and put it into your paſte, and bake, and when you ſerue it, cut it in foure quarters and caſt ſugar on it.
title: [A booke of cookerie, otherwise called the good huswiues handmaid.]

text: Make your paſte fine with butter and yolks of egs, and ſugar, rolle it very thin, and ſo lay it in a platter with butter vnderneath, and ſo cut your couer and lay it vpon it.
title: [A booke of cookerie, otherwise called the good huswiues handmaid.]

text: Then put the Creame together in the midſt of the cloth, and hang it on a pin, and let more whey drop out til ye thinke it be well.
title: [A booke of cookerie, otherwise called the good huswiues handmaid.]

text: Firſt howe he dyd gyue hym ſelfe to al hys diſciples and miniſters and in eſpecially to the preachers, beinge an example in waſhinge of theyr fete, that they ſhould do the ſame and be prompte and redy at all tymes to miniſter, and do ſeruice to eueri man.
author: E. T.
title: A sermon declaringe hovv vue [sic] are iustified by faith

text: As yet not redemed to god through faith and borne ſpirituallye as yet not lyghtened with his holy ſprite as yeat not delyuered from the pryſon of darkeneſſe and grafted in the kyngdome of his beloued and gracious ſonne of God.
author: E. T.
title: A sermon declaringe hovv vue [sic] are iustified by faith

text: They cānot finde in the boke of Geneſis that Melchiſedech dyd ſacrifice to God, but that he offered breade and wyne to Abrahame, for ſuſtenaūce of his people, as Chriſte offered to vs hys worde.
author: E. T.
title: A sermon declaringe hovv vue [sic] are iustified by faith

text: And to ſay do this in remē braunce of me, in ſhewynge furth the Lordes death, vntyll he come, is not an offering.
author: E. T.
title: A sermon declaringe hovv vue [sic] are iustified by faith

text: The papiſtes in as muche as in them lyeth, kill and crucifie Chriſte agayne in there ſacrifice of the Maſſe, doinge no other wyſe then if Chriſte as yet were not aſcended into heauen, to hys father he that doeth thys, maketh Chriſte ſubiecte to death and crucifieth hym agayne.
author: E. T.
title: A sermon declaringe hovv vue [sic] are iustified by faith

text: Though they vſed our lordes ſupper, as Chriſte oure mayſter dyd and as S Paule alſo at Corinth: yet they dyd not vſe it as the pyniſhe papiſtes do now the Maſſe.
author: E. T.
title: A sermon declaringe hovv vue [sic] are iustified by faith

text: Vndoubtely al ſuch as do not regard & care for ye only glory of god teach nothing that is godly, true, or in aniwiſe profitable.
author: E. T.
title: A sermon declaringe hovv vue [sic] are iustified by faith

text: For Chriſt is of greater power and reputaciō then that theſe proude popiſh prelates, other can or oughte to offer hym to hys father.
author: E. T.
title: A sermon declaringe hovv vue [sic] are iustified by faith

text: Therefore ſurly ſo muche is contayned in holye ſcripture as is neceſſary vnto ſaluacion to eueri one that beleueth They ſaye coulde the churche erre ſo longe time as it hath?
author: E. T.
title: A sermon declaringe hovv vue [sic] are iustified by faith

text: If any man come to me and hate not his father and mother, and wife, and children, and brethren, and ſiſters, yea and his own life life alſo, he cannot be my diſciple.
author: Woolton, John, 1535?-1594.
title: An armoure of proufe very profitable, as well for princes, noble men; and gentlemen, as all other in authoritie, shewing the firme fortresse of defence, and hauen of rest in these troublesome times an

text: Now if God do any long ſpace trie vs in ye ſtormes of miſerie & calamitie, whereas he is able euery moment to releeue vs, yet doth it not before he perceiueth vs purified and prepared to repē tance.
author: Woolton, John, 1535?-1594.
title: An armoure of proufe very profitable, as well for princes, noble men; and gentlemen, as all other in authoritie, shewing the firme fortresse of defence, and hauen of rest in these troublesome times an

text: The ſpeeche of Chriſt to one of his company caryeth weight with it: Put vppe thy ſwoorde in his place, for all that take the ſwoord, ſhall perith with the ſwoord.
author: Woolton, John, 1535?-1594.
title: An armoure of proufe very profitable, as well for princes, noble men; and gentlemen, as all other in authoritie, shewing the firme fortresse of defence, and hauen of rest in these troublesome times an

text: Which cogitation is verye profitable, not onlie to repreſſe the inſolencie and hautineſſe of mynde, which commonly accompanieth dignitie and authoritie, being very pernitious in all regiment: but alſo much furthereth to the better adminiſtration and diſcharge of their calling in the feare of God.
author: Woolton, John, 1535?-1594.
title: An armoure of proufe very profitable, as well for princes, noble men; and gentlemen, as all other in authoritie, shewing the firme fortresse of defence, and hauen of rest in these troublesome times an

text: Let them rather conſider the terrible threats of God, left in this worlde, whereby men are drawen from fragile to firme things, from fleſh to ſpirit, from mā to God.
author: Woolton, John, 1535?-1594.
title: An armoure of proufe very profitable, as well for princes, noble men; and gentlemen, as all other in authoritie, shewing the firme fortresse of defence, and hauen of rest in these troublesome times an

text: Afterward there came agaynſt him Zerach of Ethiopia, with an hoſte of ten hundreth thouſand men, and three hundreth Chariots.
author: Woolton, John, 1535?-1594.
title: An armoure of proufe very profitable, as well for princes, noble men; and gentlemen, as all other in authoritie, shewing the firme fortresse of defence, and hauen of rest in these troublesome times an

text: Though an hoſt pitched agaynſt me, mine hart ſhoulde not be afrayd Though warre be raiſed agaynſt mee, I will truſt in this.
author: Woolton, John, 1535?-1594.
title: An armoure of proufe very profitable, as well for princes, noble men; and gentlemen, as all other in authoritie, shewing the firme fortresse of defence, and hauen of rest in these troublesome times an

text: For the almightie was his refuge, hys hope, and hys Protectour: and therfore it was vnpoſſible for hym to bee confounded and deſtroyed.
author: Woolton, John, 1535?-1594.
title: An armoure of proufe very profitable, as well for princes, noble men; and gentlemen, as all other in authoritie, shewing the firme fortresse of defence, and hauen of rest in these troublesome times an

text: And Demades that eloquente orator and graue Senator of Greece, giuing as holeſome counſaile in matters touching the commō wealth, as eyther Themistoclēs, Miltiades or Pericles, was wōt to alledge for himſelfe, that frowarde fortune and vnhappie deſteny, did fruſtrate his deuiſes.
author: Woolton, John, 1535?-1594.
title: An armoure of proufe very profitable, as well for princes, noble men; and gentlemen, as all other in authoritie, shewing the firme fortresse of defence, and hauen of rest in these troublesome times an

text: Well siker, I euer feared ye would be nought, your lewde behauiours sore greue my hart: to trayn you to goodnes, al meanes haue I sought, But in vaine, yet wyl I play a brotherly part.
title: A preaty interlude called, Nice wanton ...

text: I am right worshipfull maister wordly shame, The matter that I come now about, Is euen thys, I put you out of dought.
title: A preaty interlude called, Nice wanton ...

text: I haue caught two byrdes, I wyll set for the dame, If I catche her in my clutche, I wyl her tame.
title: A preaty interlude called, Nice wanton ...

text: To loue and feare God, and other allure, And for his sake, to helpe hys neighbour, Then may he well be mery.
title: A preaty interlude called, Nice wanton ...

text: Thus paltyng to scole, I thynke vs vnwyse In sommer dye for thryst, in wynter for colde, And styl to liue in feare of a churle, who would?
title: A preaty interlude called, Nice wanton ...

text: Sirs thys fine woman, had babes three, Twayne the derest darlinges that might be, Ismael and faire Dalila, these two, With the loute Barnabas, I haue nothyng to do.
title: A preaty interlude called, Nice wanton ...

text: For when my brother & sister were of yonge age, You saw they were geuen to ydlenes and play, Would apply no learnyng, but liue in outrage, And mencomplagned on them euery day.
title: A preaty interlude called, Nice wanton ...

text: Then on the other as well would I complayne, But your other sonne is good, and no thank to you These wyl ye make naught by swete Iesu.
title: A preaty interlude called, Nice wanton ...

text: By two chyldren brought vp wantonly in play, Whom ye mother doth excuse, whē she should chastise They delyte in daliaunce and mischief alway, At last they ende theyr lyues in miserable wyse.
title: A preaty interlude called, Nice wanton ...

text: The Archbiſhoppe enquired of hym what he would do, if certain articles wer taken out of his bookes to be ſubmitted to the generall Councell.
author: Melanchthon, Philipp, 1497-1560.
title: A famous and godly history contaynyng the lyues a[nd] actes of three renowmed reformers of the Christia[n] Church, Martine Luther, Iohn Ecolampadius, and Huldericke Zuinglius. The declaracion of Marti

text: And fearing leaſt vnder colour of the holye Ghoſte he ſhoulde abuſe hym ſelfe, he conferred that, that was wrytten, and illuſtrated the darke places, by the plaine, in ſort, that when he preached the ſcripture, euery man might plainely perceiue he was taughte of the holy ghoſt.
author: Melanchthon, Philipp, 1497-1560.
title: A famous and godly history contaynyng the lyues a[nd] actes of three renowmed reformers of the Christia[n] Church, Martine Luther, Iohn Ecolampadius, and Huldericke Zuinglius. The declaracion of Marti

text: There cōtinued ſince a conglutinate mutual loue betwixt Luther & Keynech, proceding either of agreement of nature, either of ſociety in chyldiſh ſtudy.
author: Melanchthon, Philipp, 1497-1560.
title: A famous and godly history contaynyng the lyues a[nd] actes of three renowmed reformers of the Christia[n] Church, Martine Luther, Iohn Ecolampadius, and Huldericke Zuinglius. The declaracion of Marti

text: And therefore they falſelye accuſe hym, that blaſe he beganne wyth plawſible matter, and whereby he myghte get prayſe, to the ende in proceſſe of tyme, he myght chaunge the ſtate of the Common weale, and purchaſe authoritye, eyther for him ſelfe or other.
author: Melanchthon, Philipp, 1497-1560.
title: A famous and godly history contaynyng the lyues a[nd] actes of three renowmed reformers of the Christia[n] Church, Martine Luther, Iohn Ecolampadius, and Huldericke Zuinglius. The declaracion of Marti

text: The cauſe recited in the beginning, moued me (yea truely me, that haue bene a luculent witnes wyth diuers credible perſons, of all theſe thynges wrytten) not to ſwarue from teſtification of the truthe, but faythfully to aduertiſe the ſame.
author: Melanchthon, Philipp, 1497-1560.
title: A famous and godly history contaynyng the lyues a[nd] actes of three renowmed reformers of the Christia[n] Church, Martine Luther, Iohn Ecolampadius, and Huldericke Zuinglius. The declaracion of Marti

text: For after certen propoſitions, he was contented to be reformed, & gaue thankes to God, that he had reuealed the truth vnto hym ſo playnly by hys excellent Organe.
author: Melanchthon, Philipp, 1497-1560.
title: A famous and godly history contaynyng the lyues a[nd] actes of three renowmed reformers of the Christia[n] Church, Martine Luther, Iohn Ecolampadius, and Huldericke Zuinglius. The declaracion of Marti

text: Whileſt Luther was in this courſe of ſtudy, a certaine Dominicke Friernanied Tecel, a moſt impudent Sicophant (if euer there raygned any) cauſed the Popes Indulgences or Pardons to he caryed and ſold about the Country.
author: Melanchthon, Philipp, 1497-1560.
title: A famous and godly history contaynyng the lyues a[nd] actes of three renowmed reformers of the Christia[n] Church, Martine Luther, Iohn Ecolampadius, and Huldericke Zuinglius. The declaracion of Marti

text: Martin Luther & Ierome Schurffe reproued theſe folyes, & other vaine and ridiculous matters, whych Ecke brought forth but modeſtli, as things not ſeruing to the purpoſe.
author: Melanchthon, Philipp, 1497-1560.
title: A famous and godly history contaynyng the lyues a[nd] actes of three renowmed reformers of the Christia[n] Church, Martine Luther, Iohn Ecolampadius, and Huldericke Zuinglius. The declaracion of Marti

text: Truth it is in this poynt I cannot cleare thys yong man of all ſuſpicion of ſynne, although with ſacred deſire to ſerue God, he circumſpectly tooke hede by euyl example to abaſe the authority of heauenly doctrine.
author: Melanchthon, Philipp, 1497-1560.
title: A famous and godly history contaynyng the lyues a[nd] actes of three renowmed reformers of the Christia[n] Church, Martine Luther, Iohn Ecolampadius, and Huldericke Zuinglius. The declaracion of Marti

text: Who may be thought a more conuenyent vocate for synners than he yt neuer dyd synne than he yt suffycyently hath payed for ye raunsome of synne his owne moost precyous blode & paynfull & bytter deth than he that is the sone of almyghty god and that before his owne fader.
author: Fisher, John, Saint, 1469-1535.
title: This sermon folowynge was compyled [and] sayd in the cathedrall chyrche of saynt Poule within ye cyte of London by the ryght reuerende fader in god Iohn̄ bysshop of Rochester, the body beyinge present

text: Impossibile est multo rum p̄ces nō exaudiri sayth saynt Austyn / that is to saye / the prayer of many can not be but herde.
author: Fisher, John, Saint, 1469-1535.
title: This sermon folowynge was compyled [and] sayd in the cathedrall chyrche of saynt Poule within ye cyte of London by the ryght reuerende fader in god Iohn̄ bysshop of Rochester, the body beyinge present

text: Let no man also murmure ayenst this / for this is the grete treasour of the mercy of almyghty god / & ayenst suche murmures is suffycyētly answered in ye same place / for what sholde become of ony of vs ne were this grete mercy.
author: Fisher, John, Saint, 1469-1535.
title: This sermon folowynge was compyled [and] sayd in the cathedrall chyrche of saynt Poule within ye cyte of London by the ryght reuerende fader in god Iohn̄ bysshop of Rochester, the body beyinge present

text: This noble prynce after his confessyon made with all dylygence and grete repentaunce / he promysed thre thynges that is to saye / a true reformacyon of all them that were offycers and ministres of his lawes to the entent that Justyce from hens for warde truly and indyfferently myghte be executed in all causes.
author: Fisher, John, Saint, 1469-1535.
title: This sermon folowynge was compyled [and] sayd in the cathedrall chyrche of saynt Poule within ye cyte of London by the ryght reuerende fader in god Iohn̄ bysshop of Rochester, the body beyinge present

text: The cause of this hope was the true beleue yt he had in god / in his chirche & in the sacramentes therof / whiche he receyued all wt merueylous deuocion / namely in the sacrament of penaūce / the sacrament of ye auter / & the sacrament of anelynge.
author: Fisher, John, Saint, 1469-1535.
title: This sermon folowynge was compyled [and] sayd in the cathedrall chyrche of saynt Poule within ye cyte of London by the ryght reuerende fader in god Iohn̄ bysshop of Rochester, the body beyinge present

text: That same day of his departynge he herde masse of the gloryous virgyn the moder of cryste to whome alwaye in his lyfe he had a synguler & specyall deuocyon.
author: Fisher, John, Saint, 1469-1535.
title: This sermon folowynge was compyled [and] sayd in the cathedrall chyrche of saynt Poule within ye cyte of London by the ryght reuerende fader in god Iohn̄ bysshop of Rochester, the body beyinge present

text: If ony of vs haue synned / let vs not dispayre / for we haue an aduocate for vs before god / our sauyour whiche is Juste & without synne / & he shall be a meane for our synnes / not for ours all onely / but for all ye worldes.
author: Fisher, John, Saint, 1469-1535.
title: This sermon folowynge was compyled [and] sayd in the cathedrall chyrche of saynt Poule within ye cyte of London by the ryght reuerende fader in god Iohn̄ bysshop of Rochester, the body beyinge present

text: The spyder craftely spynneth her thredes and curyously weueth and Joyneth her webbe / but cometh a lytell blast of wynde & dysapoynteth all togyder to the whiche purpose Cietro in his thyrde boke be oratore maketh this exclamacyon.
author: Fisher, John, Saint, 1469-1535.

text: And that I maye ceceyue thy holy body in fourme of breed very God & man, or I departe out of this world in cleane lyfe.

text: For thou cōmaundeſt (I wote) to crye & call vpon the, that thou therby myghte haue occaſyon to gyue vnto vs thy moſt gracyous gyftes.

text: So that in thy ſyght I may appere to be as I am named thy ſone, and a trewe chryſten man.

text: And graūt me good lorde that of all myne actes & dedes done to thy wyl and pleaſure, I may rendre al the honour, laude, and prayſynges vnto the / as vnto whom of very dewtye it belongeth.

text: Thanks gentle ſir, Polidor take him in, And bid him welcome to vnto my houſe, For thou I thinke muſt be my ſecond ſonne, Ferando, Polidor dooſt thou not know Muſt marry Kate, and to morrow is the day.

text: Tis well for you that haue ſuch gentle wiues, Yet in this triall will I not ſit out, It may be Kate will come as ſoone as yours.

text: Come Kate we now will go ſee thy fathers houſe Euen in theſe honeſt meane abilliments, Our purſes ſhallbe rich, our garments plaine, To ſhrowd our bodies from the winter rage, And thats inough, what ſhould we care for more.
title: A pleasant conceited historie, called The taming of a shrew As it was sundry times acted by the Right honorable the Earle of Pembrook his seruants.

text: Faire louely maide yoong and affable, More cleere of hew and far more beautifull, Then pretious Sardonix or purple rockes, Of Amitheſts or gliſtering Hiaſinthe, More amiable farre then is the plain, Where gliſtring Cepherus in ſiluer boures, Gaſeth vpon the Giant Andromede, Sweet Kate entertaine this louely woman.
title: A pleasant conceited historie, called The taming of a shrew As it was sundry times acted by the Right honorable the Earle of Pembrook his seruants.

text: I and that thou ſhalt find I can tell thee and thou Doſt not pleaſe her well, why my Maiſter Has ſuch a doo with hir as it paſſeth and he's euen like a madman.

text: Doo ſo, come Kate, why dooſt thou looke So ſad, be merrie wench thy wedding daies at hand.

text: And his Ma: hath a gracious & hartie compaſſyon of his ſayde obediēt and faythfull ſubiectes (and that no leſſe then is expreſſed by the meſſaungers in theyr wrytinge) becauſe of the ſayde greuous plages.
author: Coverdale, Miles, 1488-1568.
title: The supplicacion: that the nobles and comons of Osteryke made lately by their messaungers, vnto kyng Ferdinandus, in the cause of the Christen religion Item. The kynges answere to the same. Vvherpon f

text: Vvhych yet can not ſo come to paſſe, vnleſſe your Royall Ma. ſhew it ſelfe in moſt gracyous wyſe towarde youre ſayde countre.
author: Coverdale, Miles, 1488-1568.
title: The supplicacion: that the nobles and comons of Osteryke made lately by their messaungers, vnto kyng Ferdinandus, in the cause of the Christen religion Item. The kynges answere to the same. Vvherpon f

text: And euen ſo muſt it enſue, yf we all from oure whole hertes, do not turne vnto hym by true penaunce and vnfayned receauynge of his godly worde.
author: Coverdale, Miles, 1488-1568.
title: The supplicacion: that the nobles and comons of Osteryke made lately by their messaungers, vnto kyng Ferdinandus, in the cause of the Christen religion Item. The kynges answere to the same. Vvherpon f

text: Vvherfore yf we cōſidre well the power and riches of the ſayd Monarchies or Empyres (and the famous prudent men that were amonge them) & compare the ſame to the beeſtlye regyment of the Turkes, we ſhall perceaue, that ſens the great floude, there came neuer a ſorer plage vpō the worlde.
author: Coverdale, Miles, 1488-1568.
title: The supplicacion: that the nobles and comons of Osteryke made lately by their messaungers, vnto kyng Ferdinandus, in the cause of the Christen religion Item. The kynges answere to the same. Vvherpon f

text: Here with (in hope of a right louing anſwere here after) we committe oure ſelues in moſt humble wiſe vnto your Royall Maieſty, as to our moſt gracious doare ſoueraigne Lorde.
author: Coverdale, Miles, 1488-1568.
title: The supplicacion: that the nobles and comons of Osteryke made lately by their messaungers, vnto kyng Ferdinandus, in the cause of the Christen religion Item. The kynges answere to the same. Vvherpon f

text: Vverfore oure moſt humble & erneſt ſupplicacion is, that youre Royall Ma: (acordinge to youre hye and ſuppreme offyce) wyll haue gracious reſpecte here vnto, that the preachers which do ſincerly ſet forth thes articles & the word of God likewiſe in other thinges, maye be ſuffred.
author: Coverdale, Miles, 1488-1568.
title: The supplicacion: that the nobles and comons of Osteryke made lately by their messaungers, vnto kyng Ferdinandus, in the cause of the Christen religion Item. The kynges answere to the same. Vvherpon f

text: Of this is teſtimonye ſufficiēt the captyuyte of Babylon among the Iewes, whych came becauſe they receaued not the Prophetes, and becauſe they ſet vp a new ſeruyng of God contrary to his worde.
author: Coverdale, Miles, 1488-1568.
title: The supplicacion: that the nobles and comons of Osteryke made lately by their messaungers, vnto kyng Ferdinandus, in the cause of the Christen religion Item. The kynges answere to the same. Vvherpon f

text: MOſt noble and mightie Prynce, oure moſt gracious Soueraigne lorde: Where as your royall Ma: (vpō oure moſt humble and erneſt ſupplicacyon) hath graciouſly geuen vs a wrytinge touchinge the cauſe of Religion we haue in moſt hūble wyſe conſidred the ſame, and pondred it with Chriſten, louynge and feruent myndes.
author: Coverdale, Miles, 1488-1568.
title: The supplicacion: that the nobles and comons of Osteryke made lately by their messaungers, vnto kyng Ferdinandus, in the cause of the Christen religion Item. The kynges answere to the same. Vvherpon f

text: But ſeynge that God Almightie dyd thus allure them vnto true repentaunce & to his wholſome word, and they wolde receaue none of hys fatherly monycyons, he therfore ſuffred them to be fynally deſtroyed.
author: Coverdale, Miles, 1488-1568.
title: The supplicacion: that the nobles and comons of Osteryke made lately by their messaungers, vnto kyng Ferdinandus, in the cause of the Christen religion Item. The kynges answere to the same. Vvherpon f

text: Which thynge yf it myght pleaſe you of your goodneſſe to do, I woulde not onelye retracte and wyth all dylygence reuoke agayne all ſuche faultes as your diſcretion ſhall fynde in it, but alſo thynke my ſelfe boūde to praye for your good eſtate ſo longe as my lyfe ſhoulde endure.
author: Bonner, Richard.
title: A treatyse of ye ryght honourynge and wourshyppyng of our sauiour Iesus Christe in the sacrame[n]t of breade and wyne when it is ministred wyth thankes geuing at the holy supper: sette forth by Rychar

text: And ſecondly yt we do forth with vp on thys callyng of vs vnto faith by thys ſacrament, receyue it externally alſo accordyng to hys ordinance, for the ſtrengthenyng & confyrmyng of the ſame fayth the more aſſuredly in vs, and for our better encreaſyng in his moſt godly vertues.
author: Bonner, Richard.
title: A treatyse of ye ryght honourynge and wourshyppyng of our sauiour Iesus Christe in the sacrame[n]t of breade and wyne when it is ministred wyth thankes geuing at the holy supper: sette forth by Rychar

text: And theſe to be miniſtred by the cuppe: take, drinke, thys cuppe is the newe teſtament in my bloude, whych ſhalbe ſhedde for you and for many, to the remiſſion of ſynnes.
author: Bonner, Richard.
title: A treatyse of ye ryght honourynge and wourshyppyng of our sauiour Iesus Christe in the sacrame[n]t of breade and wyne when it is ministred wyth thankes geuing at the holy supper: sette forth by Rychar

text: And vpon the receyuynge of the ſacrament thus, goeth many of the prayers alſo, whiche were made to be ſayd after the communion, and wer therfore called in latyne Poſt communionem, wherof ſome of them dyd begyne thus: Sacramenta que ſumpſimus that is to ſay, that ſacramētes which we haue receyued.
author: Bonner, Richard.
title: A treatyse of ye ryght honourynge and wourshyppyng of our sauiour Iesus Christe in the sacrame[n]t of breade and wyne when it is ministred wyth thankes geuing at the holy supper: sette forth by Rychar

text: Well, thus muche is ſayde, for thys tyme, concernyng the ryght honouryng of our Lorde Ieſu Chriſt in this ſacrament, when it is miniſtred at the holy ſouper.
author: Bonner, Richard.
title: A treatyse of ye ryght honourynge and wourshyppyng of our sauiour Iesus Christe in the sacrame[n]t of breade and wyne when it is ministred wyth thankes geuing at the holy supper: sette forth by Rychar

text: And therfore as thyne owne hart muſt be thy guide in this matter, ſo is it nedefull that thou ſaye thus with Dauid, in goyng to receyue this holy ſouper: directe my foteſteppes, o lord, and teache me to do thy wyll.
author: Bonner, Richard.
title: A treatyse of ye ryght honourynge and wourshyppyng of our sauiour Iesus Christe in the sacrame[n]t of breade and wyne when it is ministred wyth thankes geuing at the holy supper: sette forth by Rychar

text: And ſaint Auſtyne, ſpeakyng of the ſonges that mē vſed by the alter, & makyng mencion of the holy ſouper of the lorde, as it was holden in thoſe dayes, wryteth, that men haue ſonge pſalmes before the offeryng, or as that was dyſtributed whyche was offred.
author: Bonner, Richard.
title: A treatyse of ye ryght honourynge and wourshyppyng of our sauiour Iesus Christe in the sacrame[n]t of breade and wyne when it is ministred wyth thankes geuing at the holy supper: sette forth by Rychar

text: For who ſo did not holde hym ſelfe in the trew doctrine receyued and agreed vpon in the churche (as there were many ſuche in thoſe dayes) with him dyd no deuout byſſhope, pryeſt or clerke, communicate.
author: Bonner, Richard.
title: A treatyse of ye ryght honourynge and wourshyppyng of our sauiour Iesus Christe in the sacrame[n]t of breade and wyne when it is ministred wyth thankes geuing at the holy supper: sette forth by Rychar

text: But to deſire it wyth a pure hearte and good deuocion can doutleſſe be none other thinge, than to deſyre it accordynge to the ordynaunce and inſtitucion of the lorde.
author: Bonner, Richard.
title: A treatyse of ye ryght honourynge and wourshyppyng of our sauiour Iesus Christe in the sacrame[n]t of breade and wyne when it is ministred wyth thankes geuing at the holy supper: sette forth by Rychar

text: God for deth / or fortune / or impotent nature God dothe his pleasure / & dethe wyll haue the same Nature was mighty / long able to endure.
author: Barclay, Alexander, 1475?-1552.
title: The boke of Codrus and Mynalcas

text: To poore and riche / it hath no difference Olde Polycraces / supposyng peryll past With dethe dishonest / ended his exellence Great Alexander by fortune / was downe cast One draught of poyson hym fylled at the last Whom all the worlde / erst coude nat sacyate What is all honour / and power but a blast?
author: Barclay, Alexander, 1475?-1552.
title: The boke of Codrus and Mynalcas

text: So hast thou Codrus / of golde ynough in store And I some cōnyng / though fewe mē care therfore Thou art beholden / to Jupiter truely And I beholden to plesaunt Mercury.
author: Barclay, Alexander, 1475?-1552.
title: The boke of Codrus and Mynalcas

text: Alway whan nature / of thyng is moost laudable That thyng men coūteth / moost good & profitable And euery person / in his owne gifte hath toye The fole in his bable / hath pleasure for to toye.
author: Barclay, Alexander, 1475?-1552.
title: The boke of Codrus and Mynalcas

text: Joyne we our sterres / let me haue parte of thyne Cōcorde to cheryss he / yu shalte haue parte of myne Make thou Jupiter / be frendely vnto me And our Mercury / shalbe as good to the.
author: Barclay, Alexander, 1475?-1552.
title: The boke of Codrus and Mynalcas

text: He was a pyller / of sober contynence His onely treasure / and iowell was good name But O cursed dethe / thy wrathfull vyolnece By stroke vnwarned / halfe blynded of his fame Who may I accuse? who may I put in blame?
author: Barclay, Alexander, 1475?-1552.
title: The boke of Codrus and Mynalcas

text: This is of our lorde / disposed so my brother Bycause all costes / shulde one haue nede of other.
author: Barclay, Alexander, 1475?-1552.
title: The boke of Codrus and Mynalcas

text: London hath scarlot / and Bristo we plesaunt reed Fenne lande hath fyss hes / in other place is leed.

text: If thy Jupiter / gyue me but onely golde Mercury shall gyue the / giftes manyfolde His pylsion ceptre / his wynges / and his harpe If thou haue all these / thou mayst grathly carpe And ouer all these / gyue the shall Mercury The knot of Hercules enlaced craftely.
author: Barclay, Alexander, 1475?-1552.

text: I thinke your meaning is not to haue always two at once to be presented to the ministerie, and then one of them to be chosen by lot: I knowe none of that opinion.

title: The alphabet of prayers very fruitefull to be exercised and vsed of euerye Christian man. Newly collected and set forth, in the yeare of our Lorde, 1564. Seene and allowed according to the order appoi

text: Let all them O Lorde, reioyce and be glad, which ſeeke thee: and let them whiche loue to haue Saluation of thee, ſay: Magnified be the Lorde for euer.

text: Renue my ſpirite, my ſoule, and my body, with thy excellent grace, that I may be made lyke vnto thy holy humanitie, frame me after thine owne hearts deſyre, knit me vnto thee moſte neerely, that I maye be chaunged altogither into thee.

text: So becauſe in theſe laſt times wee abuſe the creatures in riot and exceſſe, God no doubt will according to his word cōſume the whole world with fire.

text: And this pride Saint Paul reproueth, when hee willeth vs not to faſhion our ſelues according to this world.

text: What a dignitie then is this for vs, which indeede are but duſt, earth and aſhes, to be accounted giuers vnto him, which is the giuer of all things?

author: Hill, Adam, d. 1595.

text: Now doe wee ſee our owne faultes, which are in the peece of the wallet that hangeth behinde vs. Thirdly, we are fellow-ſeruants, and being therfore in the ſame condition, wee ſhould liue in charitie which couereth the multitude of ſinnes.
author: Hill, Adam, d. 1595.

text: The Idolator is a breaker of the ſecond precept, the blaſphemer of the third, the prophaner of the ſabaoth is a tranſgreſſour of the fourth, the rebel of the fifth, the oppreſſor of the ſixt, the Sodomite of the ſeauenth; but the Athieſt is a wilfull contemner of all.
author: Hill, Adam, d. 1595.

text: Inordinatly, men ſeeke praiſe: firſt, when they deſire to bee praiſed for thoſe thinges that be not worthye of praiſe, as for riches and temporall thinges which are but vaine.
author: Hill, Adam, d. 1595.

text: Firſt Paul commaundeth them not in his owne name, but by the authoritie of Chriſt, that they ſhould labour.
author: Hill, Adam, d. 1595.

text: Secondly, how was man created? in righteouſnes, holines, mercie, truth: theſe vertues being eſſentiall in God, are accidentall in vs: whoſoeuer therefore murthereth a man, deſtroyeth thoſe vertues, wherein man dooth participate with the nature of God.
author: Hill, Adam, d. 1595.

text: Vſe truthe and ſay truth in that thou goeſt aboute For tyme of althinges the truthe wyll bringe out Shame is the rewarde For lying dewe Then auoyde ſhame and vtter wordes trewe.

text: A voyder vpon the table then haue The trenchers and napkyns therein to receaue The croomes with a napkyn together them ſwepe It at the tables ende In a voydex them kepe.

text: And loue doth moue the mynde to mercie But malice againe doth worke the contrarie. whiche in the wicked wyll euer beare ſtroke Pacience thee teacheth therof to beare the yoke. where pacience aud loue to gether do dwell All hate and debate with malice they expell.
author: F. S. (Francis Segar), fl. 1549-1563.

text: Then men ſhal ſee that grace in the groweth From whom vertues So aboundantly floweth when thou arte come where thy parentes do dwell Thy leaue then takynge Byd thy felowes farewell.
author: F. S. (Francis Segar), fl. 1549-1563.

text: In the churche comly thy ſelfe do behaue In vſage ſober thy countinaunce graue. whyle you be there taulke of no matter Nor one with an other whiſper nor chatter.
author: F. S. (Francis Segar), fl. 1549-1563.

text: O God from whom al good gifts procede To thee we repayre in tyme of our nede That with thy grace thou wouldſt vs endue Vertue to folowe and vyce to exchue: Heare this our requeſt and graunt our deſyre O lorde moſte humbly we do the requyre.
author: F. S. (Francis Segar), fl. 1549-1563.
title: The schoole of vertue and booke of good nourture for chyldren, and youth to learne theyer dutie by. Newely persued, corrected, and augmented by the fyrst auctour. F.S with a briefe declaration of the

text: To fetche or take vp If ought fortune to fall. when they haue done then ready make The table vp fayre In order to take Fyrſte the ſaulte Se that thou couer Hauynge by thee Eyther one or other thynges from thy handes then to conuaye That from the table thou ſhalt take awaye.
author: F. S. (Francis Segar), fl. 1549-1563.

text: But the vtteraunce of truthe is ſo ſimple and playne That it nedeth no ſtudie to forge or to fayne. wherfore ſaye truth how euer ſtand the caſe So ſhalte thou fynde more fauour and grace.
author: F. S. (Francis Segar), fl. 1549-1563.

text: The foirſayd preſbyterie callit and perſewit thame, and ſcarſlie be his Maieſteis authoritie culd be withhaldin from excommunicating the ſaidis Magiſtratis and noblemen, for obeying onely his Hienes lawfull commaund, quhilk the law of al cuntreyis, callit Ius gentium, requyris towards Ambaſſadours of foraine cūtreis.
author: Adamson, Patrick, 1537-1592.
title: A declaratioun of the Kings Maiesties intentioun and meaning toward the lait actis of Parliament

text: And in verie deid it laketh not ane richt intollerable arrogancie in ony ſubiect, callit before his Prince, profeſſing, & authoriſing the ſamin treuth, to diſclame his authoritie: nether do the Prophetes, Apoſtles, nor vthers conductit be the ſpirit of God, miniſter the lyke example.
author: Adamson, Patrick, 1537-1592.
title: A declaratioun of the Kings Maiesties intentioun and meaning toward the lait actis of Parliament

text: Quhilk is only his Maieſt. intentioun to repreſs, and not to tak away ony godly or ſolide ordour in the Kirk, as heirefter ſall appeir.
author: Adamson, Patrick, 1537-1592.
title: A declaratioun of the Kings Maiesties intentioun and meaning toward the lait actis of Parliament

text: Of the quhilk number of the faithfull vnder the heid Chriſt, his Maieſt, acknawlegis him ſelfe to be ane member, baptizit in his name, partaker of the myſterie of the croce and holie communioun, and attending with the faithfull for the cumming of the Lord, and the finall reſtitutioun of Goddis elect.
author: Adamson, Patrick, 1537-1592.
title: A declaratioun of the Kings Maiesties intentioun and meaning toward the lait actis of Parliament

text: Bot this appeareth at this preſent to be ane vntymely and vnprofitable queſtioun, quhilk hes no ground vpoun their parte, bot of the prepoſterus imitatioun of the pretendit iuriſdiction of the Pape of Rome.
author: Adamson, Patrick, 1537-1592.
title: A declaratioun of the Kings Maiesties intentioun and meaning toward the lait actis of Parliament

text: Forther, it is his Hienes will, & expres commandement, that thir biſhops, or commiſsionars, twyſe in the ȝeir, to wit, ten dayes efter the Paſche tyme, & the ſext of September, hald their ſynodall aſſemblies, in euery dioceſe, for the keping of gude ordour thairin.
author: Adamson, Patrick, 1537-1592.
title: A declaratioun of the Kings Maiesties intentioun and meaning toward the lait actis of Parliament

text: And notwithſtanding that his Maieſtie hes reſtabliſhit the ſaid eſtate, it is not his hienes will and intention, that the foirſaid biſhop, ſall haue ſic full power, as to do within his dioceſe quhat he pleaſis.
author: Adamson, Patrick, 1537-1592.
title: A declaratioun of the Kings Maiesties intentioun and meaning toward the lait actis of Parliament

text: HIS Maieſties intentioun is, be the grace of God, to maintene the trew and ſinceir profeſſioun of the Goſpell, and preiching thairof, within this Realme.
author: Adamson, Patrick, 1537-1592.
title: A declaratioun of the Kings Maiesties intentioun and meaning toward the lait actis of Parliament

text: The ſaid M. Andro wllit before his Hienes, preſumptuouſlie anſwerit, that he hald not be iugit be the King and Counſale, becauſe he had ſpok in the ſamein pulpit, quhilk pulpit, in effect, he allegit to be eximit from the Iugement and correction of Princes.
author: Adamson, Patrick, 1537-1592.
title: A declaratioun of the Kings Maiesties intentioun and meaning toward the lait actis of Parliament

text: So iuſtifieth he nat god but hateth hī as a tyrāt / neither careth he for the promyſes / but wyll with his own ſtrēgth be ſauyour of himſelfe / no wiſe glorifyeth he god though he ſeme outwarde to do.
author: Tyndale, William, d. 1536.
title: A path way i[n]to the holy scripture

text: For if oure fearſe and proude herte be nat mekened fyrſt by the lawe / and make vs confeſſe oure ſelfe Synners / we ſhulde neuer be ſaued by Chriſt for he came for to ſaue ſynners and vnrightuous / nat them that be rightuouſe and iuſt / which iuſtify them ſelfe by their workes.
author: Tyndale, William, d. 1536.
title: A path way i[n]to the holy scripture

text: I praye you haue remembraunce of me in your prayers / that I maye worthely walke in the holye worde of god / to the glory of god.
author: Tyndale, William, d. 1536.
title: A path way i[n]to the holy scripture

text: I les at his welth thā at myne owne / if I loue him as well and as moche as my ſelfe / as the law commaundeth me if it were nat ſo: how ſayth Paule?
author: Tyndale, William, d. 1536.
title: A path way i[n]to the holy scripture

text: That is to ſaye / for the fauour that god hath to his ſon chriſt / he giueth vnto vs his fauour & good wyl / & al gyftes of his grace / as a fader to his ſōnes.
author: Tyndale, William, d. 1536.
title: A path way i[n]to the holy scripture

text: For it kylleth oure conſcyences and drweth vs to diſperacyon / in as moche as it requyreth of vs / that which is vnpoſſyble for our nature to do.
author: Tyndale, William, d. 1536.
title: A path way i[n]to the holy scripture

text: Becauſe that as a mā whan he ſhal dye / appoynteth his goodes to be delte and diſtributed after his deth amonge them whiche he nameth to be his heyres.
author: Tyndale, William, d. 1536.
title: A path way i[n]to the holy scripture

text: For whan one reaſoneth with them of ſuche maters / he muſt holde his peace / or ſay as they ſaye / orels they wyll curſe him and make an herityke on him: ſayeng / that he ſpeaketh more than becometh him / or to him belōgeth.
author: Tyndale, William, d. 1536.
title: A path way i[n]to the holy scripture

text: In ſuch a tēptacion there is no remedy but fayth that is to haue full cōfydence & truſt in the promyſes of god / as be theſe.
author: Tyndale, William, d. 1536.
title: A path way i[n]to the holy scripture

text: And as the Authour merits passing well, So doth my friend deserue as greate a meede: That make a worke so hard to vnderstand, So easie that each simple may it reede.

text: But be it blame, or praise yt he deserued: it is most sure, he that refuseth that which euery mā els doth hunt for: sheweth therin, he reproueth or contemneth the common opinion of men.

text: But if wee say: Thou: to suche a one, then wee disgrace him and offer him outrage and wronge: and by suche speach, seeme to make no better reconing of him, then of a knaue and a clowne.

title: Galateo of Maister Iohn Della Casa, Archebishop of Beneuenta. Or rather, A treatise of the ma[n]ners and behauiours, it behoueth a man to vse and eschewe, in his familiar conuersation A worke very nec

text: For, many doe take that ill, and specially suche, as persuade themselues they haue a Ioly grace in telling a tale.

title: Galateo of Maister Iohn Della Casa, Archebishop of Beneuenta. Or rather, A treatise of the ma[n]ners and behauiours, it behoueth a man to vse and eschewe, in his familiar conuersation A worke very nec

text: If a man say: Sir, suche a one willed me to commend him vnto you: They aunswere straite: vvhat haue I too doe vvith his greetings?

text: And ye Mayster of the house, may chaunce to take displesure at that, as if it were done to doe him shame.

title: Galateo of Maister Iohn Della Casa, Archebishop of Beneuenta. Or rather, A treatise of the ma[n]ners and behauiours, it behoueth a man to vse and eschewe, in his familiar conuersation A worke very nec

text: The Curlew is a fowle that feeds commonlye in moyſte groundes and heathes, their fleſh is pleſant to eat, they feed commonly on wormes and ſuch, and they fat them with wheate and fayre water, other feeding I know not what is beſt for them, Thus much for the Bitter & the Curlew.
author: Mascall, Leonard, d. 1589.

text: YE ſhall take ſome Egges of a broode henne, and coloure them with what colour ye will, and put them to the henne, and ye ſhall ſee the Chickens to be of the ſame colour ye coloured the egges.
author: Mascall, Leonard, d. 1589.
title: The husbandlye ordring and gouernmente of poultrie Practised by the learnedste, and suche as haue bene knowne skilfullest in that arte, and in our tyme.

text: TO cut yong Cockrels to make them Capons, the time thereof is beſt to cut or carue them ſoone after their dam haue left them, or whē they cry or pule no more after her, as when they begin to crow and waxe hote to treade the pullets.
author: Mascall, Leonard, d. 1589.
title: The husbandlye ordring and gouernmente of poultrie Practised by the learnedste, and suche as haue bene knowne skilfullest in that arte, and in our tyme.

text: Thus I leaue, vvishing you a proſperous eſtate, vvith increaſe of vvorship long to continue to the pleſure of God.
author: Mascall, Leonard, d. 1589.

text: For I know quoth I, that if ſhe ſhould ſende me to Paris, to louen &c. fourthe with they would burne me.

text: But Bradford put his oracion away in few woordes: that grace was at ye preſent offred vnto his lordſhip, although he receiued it not.
author: Bradford, John, 1510?-1555.
title: All the examinacions of the constante martir of God M. Iohn Bradforde before the Lorde Chauncellour, B. of Winchester the B. of London, [and] other co[m]missioners: whervnto ar annexed, his priuate ta

text: For as I hope and am cercertain, my deathe ſhall pleaſe the Lord: ſo I truſt, I ſhall dye cherfullye, to the comforte of his chyldren. yea, but what if you be deceaued, quoth he: what quoth I, if you dyd ſaye the Sone did not ſhyne nowe.
author: Bradford, John, 1510?-1555.
title: All the examinacions of the constante martir of God M. Iohn Bradforde before the Lorde Chauncellour, B. of Winchester the B. of London, [and] other co[m]missioners: whervnto ar annexed, his priuate ta

text: If I canne dooe you good I wyll, hurte you I wyll not, I am no Prynce, and therefore I cannot promyſe lyfe: excepte you wyll ſubmytte youre ſelf, to the diffinicion of ye church.
author: Bradford, John, 1510?-1555.
title: All the examinacions of the constante martir of God M. Iohn Bradforde before the Lorde Chauncellour, B. of Winchester the B. of London, [and] other co[m]missioners: whervnto ar annexed, his priuate ta

text: Well, quoth I, I praye you hartelye, thancke my Lorde for hys good wil towardes me, I ſhal (as I haue done pray) yt God woulde giue vnto hym, as to my ſelfe, the which is all I can do.
author: Bradford, John, 1510?-1555.
title: All the examinacions of the constante martir of God M. Iohn Bradforde before the Lorde Chauncellour, B. of Winchester the B. of London, [and] other co[m]missioners: whervnto ar annexed, his priuate ta

text: But Bradford ſaid this, My lord ꝙ he, are not theſe woordes take eate, a cōmaundement? and are not theſe woordes, this is my bodye a promyſe?
author: Bradford, John, 1510?-1555.
title: All the examinacions of the constante martir of God M. Iohn Bradforde before the Lorde Chauncellour, B. of Winchester the B. of London, [and] other co[m]missioners: whervnto ar annexed, his priuate ta

text: Vnto whiche woordes Maiſter Harpſfeld ſaid: that he would doe the beſte he could, for he pitied my caſe verie ſore, Sir, quoth I, to deſire any bodie to ſewe for tyme for me, I neuer wil do it by godes helpe.
author: Bradford, John, 1510?-1555.
title: All the examinacions of the constante martir of God M. Iohn Bradforde before the Lorde Chauncellour, B. of Winchester the B. of London, [and] other co[m]missioners: whervnto ar annexed, his priuate ta

text: Sūma to this iſſue we came, that he ſhould draw out of the ſcriptures and doctours, his reaſōs.
author: Bradford, John, 1510?-1555.

text: Lord god, quoth my lord of yorke, howe you delite to leyne to ſo hard, and darke places of ſcripture, yea, quoth my Lord of Chicheſter, I will ſhewe you howe that Luther doth excommunicate zwinglius for this matter, ſo red a place of Luther, making for his purpoſe.
author: Bradford, John, 1510?-1555.

text: Exod. 33. declared all this to ſtande of his mercy, ſaying: I will haue mercie vpon whom it liketh me, and I will ſhew mercie where it ſhall be my pleaſure, for ſo is the meaning of thoſe wordes, I will haue mercy vpon whom I will haue mercy.
author: Gilby, Anthony, ca. 1510-1585.
title: A briefe treatice of election and reprobation with certen ansvvers to the obiections of the aduersaries of thys doctrine: vvritten by Anthonie Gylbie.

text: But the grace of this thy frée Election maketh vs moſt certaine and ſure, ſéeing no creature is able to take oute of thy hande, O God.
author: Gilby, Anthony, ca. 1510-1585.
title: A briefe treatice of election and reprobation with certen ansvvers to the obiections of the aduersaries of thys doctrine: vvritten by Anthonie Gylbie.

text: We knowe that all thinges woorke for the beſte vnto them that loue God, who alſo are called of purpoſe: for thoſe which he knewe before, he alſo predeſtinate, that they ſhoulde be like faſhoned to the ſhape of hys Sonne.
author: Gilby, Anthony, ca. 1510-1585.
title: A briefe treatice of election and reprobation with certen ansvvers to the obiections of the aduersaries of thys doctrine: vvritten by Anthonie Gylbie.

text: And in the chapter before, he ſaith, that it is God which hath begon ye good worke, and will finiſh it.
author: Gilby, Anthony, ca. 1510-1585.
title: A briefe treatice of election and reprobation with certen ansvvers to the obiections of the aduersaries of thys doctrine: vvritten by Anthonie Gylbie.

text: I am ſure that neyther death nor life, neither Angels, nor rule, neither power, neither things preſent, nether things to come, neither high, neither low, neither any other creature, ſhall be able to depart vs from the loue of God in Chriſte Ieſu oure Lorde.
author: Gilby, Anthony, ca. 1510-1585.
title: A briefe treatice of election and reprobation with certen ansvvers to the obiections of the aduersaries of thys doctrine: vvritten by Anthonie Gylbie.

text: By this gratious election was Iacob dearely beloued in his mothers wombe, and Ieremy knowne vnto God before he was faſhioned in his mothers wombe.
author: Gilby, Anthony, ca. 1510-1585.
title: A briefe treatice of election and reprobation with certen ansvvers to the obiections of the aduersaries of thys doctrine: vvritten by Anthonie Gylbie.

text: No, this is the perfect worke maſter whiche worketh all things without faulte or treſpaſſe, all other doo fayle, faulte, and treſpaſſe, and ſinne in all their works, that he may be iuſtified in al his dooings, and al creatures fall downe before his face and preſence.
author: Gilby, Anthony, ca. 1510-1585.
title: A briefe treatice of election and reprobation with certen ansvvers to the obiections of the aduersaries of thys doctrine: vvritten by Anthonie Gylbie.

text: The fyrſte and principall is, leaſte that the wicked do make God the aucthor of ſynne in the Reprobate, the which doubt, we may remone foure maner of wayes.
author: Gilby, Anthony, ca. 1510-1585.
title: A briefe treatice of election and reprobation with certen ansvvers to the obiections of the aduersaries of thys doctrine: vvritten by Anthonie Gylbie.

text: Thou caſtſeſt me from the face of the earth, ſayth he, and I muſt hyde me from thy face.

text: True it is, that the Burgers of Middlebrough and Vlisshing did verie willingly offer their assistance; but they were but fewe: and that was doone vtterlie without aide or assistance of the States.
author: Digges, Thomas, d. 1595.
title: A breife and true report of the proceedings of the Earle of Leycester for the reliefe of the towne of Sluce from his arriuall at Vlisshing, about the end of Iune 1587. vntill the surrendrie thereof 26

text: And albeit the Armie came wearie to that place about noone, yet was it resolued the assault should bee giuen before foure of the clock.

text: In this course, lightlie if the warrant bee for 2 thowsand pounds, the defalcations shall bee 1700. or more, and the cleare debt to the Captaine 300. or lesse.

text: They ought to be persons of great sincerity and vprightnesse, that should make choyce which bills should be first allowed: and which reiected as the Captaines owne debt, and not defalcable on the Companie.
author: Digges, Thomas, d. 1595.
title: A breife and true report of the proceedings of the Earle of Leycester for the reliefe of the towne of Sluce from his arriuall at Vlisshing, about the end of Iune 1587. vntill the surrendrie thereof 26

text: But conceiuing matters (as they are in deede) guided by Gods prouidence, we may learne in all things to giue him all glorie, and modestly acknowledging truly our own priuate Errors and infirmities, to endeuour hereafter to amend them.
author: Digges, Thomas, d. 1595.
title: A breife and true report of the proceedings of the Earle of Leycester for the reliefe of the towne of Sluce from his arriuall at Vlisshing, about the end of Iune 1587. vntill the surrendrie thereof 26

text: Inprimis, if any Captaines take vp Silkes, Gold lace, Iewels, or other like matters for their owne vse amounting to treble their owne entertainement: This being defalked on the warrant for the band, must needs vniustly take from the poore Souldier part of his pay.
author: Digges, Thomas, d. 1595.
title: A breife and true report of the proceedings of the Earle of Leycester for the reliefe of the towne of Sluce from his arriuall at Vlisshing, about the end of Iune 1587. vntill the surrendrie thereof 26

text: IT is a thing too wel knowen, that if al Captaines bills shuld be payd and defalked vpon the warrants for their bands, that both Souldiers many times should vtterly lose a great part of their wages dewe, & the honest Creditors also their debts, by reason of such practises as ensue.
author: Digges, Thomas, d. 1595.
title: A breife and true report of the proceedings of the Earle of Leycester for the reliefe of the towne of Sluce from his arriuall at Vlisshing, about the end of Iune 1587. vntill the surrendrie thereof 26

text: Neuerthelesse it was resolued by the Lord Marshall, and the Militarie councel that without farther delay an attempt should bee made to hewe downe the Pallizado and by scale to enter: and if that tooke not effect, then in the Euening at dead lowe water without sarder delay to march by it.
author: Digges, Thomas, d. 1595.
title: A breife and true report of the proceedings of the Earle of Leycester for the reliefe of the towne of Sluce from his arriuall at Vlisshing, about the end of Iune 1587. vntill the surrendrie thereof 26

text: So that if Sir William Russell Lord Gouernour of Vlisshing, had not verie prouidentlie & earnestly trauailed to send in such prouisions as vpon the sodaine hee prouided: the Towne had beene much more destitute of all meanes to hold out than it was.
author: Digges, Thomas, d. 1595.

text: Your traſh, your toyes, He toke to be his onely ioyes: Therfore, hath wonne, Of you the crowne of martirdome.
author: Peele, Steven.
title: A letter to Rome, to declare to ye Pope, Iohn Felton his freend is hangd in a rope and farther, a right his grace to enforme, he dyed a papist, and seemd not to turne. To the tune of Row well ye marin

text: Yf ye, him ſee, From Purgatorie ſet him free: Let not, trudge than, Fetch Felton out and yf ye can.
author: Peele, Steven.
title: A letter to Rome, to declare to ye Pope, Iohn Felton his freend is hangd in a rope and farther, a right his grace to enforme, he dyed a papist, and seemd not to turne. To the tune of Row well ye marin

text: Now doe, I end, I came to ſhow you as a frend: Whether bleſſe, or curſe, You ſend to me, I am not the worſe.
author: Peele, Steven.

text: For whye? they hang, Vnſhryned each one vpon a ſtang: Thus ſtandes, the caſe, On London gates they haue a place.

text: As now, lately, Your freend Iohn Felton ſeemd to try Therfore, I pray, That you a maſſe for him wyll ſay.
author: Peele, Steven.

text: Sir Pope I ſay? yf you be nere, Bow downe to me your liſtning eare: Come forth, beſturre you then a pace, Fo I haue newes to ſhow your grace.

text: Marie of Scotlande hath had her life ſpared for murdring her husbād & alſo for hoſtilitie and treaſon practiſed againſt Elizabeth Queene of England.
title: A defence of the honorable sentence and execution of the Queene of Scots exempled with analogies, and diuerse presidents of emperors, kings, and popes: with the opinions of learned men in the point, a

text: Now for to ground ſubſtantially this enetrpriſe, and to bring it to good ſucceſſe, you muſte firſte examine deepely what forces aſwell on foote as on horſe, you may raiſe amongeſt you all, and what captaines you ſhall appoint for them in euery ſhire, in caſe a cheife generall cannot bee had.
title: A defence of the honorable sentence and execution of the Queene of Scots exempled with analogies, and diuerse presidents of emperors, kings, and popes: with the opinions of learned men in the point, a

text: Neither doth the rule Par in parem take anie place in that caſe, and ſo in the caſe of an Archbiſhoppe Panormitan and Felin expreſſely ſet downe, that he may by his inferiour Byſhoppe (being not his ſuffragan) receiue condigne puniſhment for the offence, that hee hath committed within the ſayde Byſhoppes dioceſſe.
title: A defence of the honorable sentence and execution of the Queene of Scots exempled with analogies, and diuerse presidents of emperors, kings, and popes: with the opinions of learned men in the point, a

text: Your reaſons to haue ſome generall heade or chiefe me thinkes are verye pertinent, and therefore were it good to ſounde ſome obſcurely for that purpoſe.
title: A defence of the honorable sentence and execution of the Queene of Scots exempled with analogies, and diuerse presidents of emperors, kings, and popes: with the opinions of learned men in the point, a

text: THe two firſt obiections made againſt the ſayde honorable ſentence, are in regarde of the Queene of Scottes perſon: But the two obiections following, doe rather tende to the diſalowance of the lawe, whereupon the ſentence is grounded.
title: A defence of the honorable sentence and execution of the Queene of Scots exempled with analogies, and diuerse presidents of emperors, kings, and popes: with the opinions of learned men in the point, a

text: For the place doth ſo dignifie the perſon, that all ſteine of former actes, is cleane waſhed awaye: and ſo the Queene of Scottes, if ſhee might haue brought her practiſes to execution ment, (as theſe pleaders or rather plodders, about delictum conſummatū mean) to haue eſcaped vnpuniſhed.
title: A defence of the honorable sentence and execution of the Queene of Scots exempled with analogies, and diuerse presidents of emperors, kings, and popes: with the opinions of learned men in the point, a

text: So that ther where he hath offended per omnia diſtringitur etiam quoad perſonam, he may bee puniſhed in all that he hath & that in his perſon, for ratione delicti-ſortitur forum, by reaſon of his offence, hee is now become of another princes iuriſdiction and prerogatiue where he hath offended.
title: A defence of the honorable sentence and execution of the Queene of Scots exempled with analogies, and diuerse presidents of emperors, kings, and popes: with the opinions of learned men in the point, a

text: The firſt obiection is, That Par in parem non habet imperium, that is an abſolute Prince ouer and againſt another abſolute Prince hath no iuriſdiction or ſoueraintie.
title: A defence of the honorable sentence and execution of the Queene of Scots exempled with analogies, and diuerse presidents of emperors, kings, and popes: with the opinions of learned men in the point, a

text: Navve in effect is conteſt vvith Curle, vvith the concurrency of Babington and Ballardes confeſsion, and other of the conſpiracie.
title: A defence of the honorable sentence and execution of the Queene of Scots exempled with analogies, and diuerse presidents of emperors, kings, and popes: with the opinions of learned men in the point, a

text: And lo, my brethren, yet more, beſides our ſelues, even our miniſterie, greater then our ſelues.
author: Pinner, Charles.
title: [A sermon at Marlborough on 1. Tim.iv.16.]

text: Onlie we muſt ſee to this, that this ſeede of our new birth be not corrupted; this milke of our ſpiritual nouriſhment be not mingled, this foode of our foules be not infecred, but alwaies preſerved in all integritie; and ſo it will be able to ſaue our ſoules.
author: Pinner, Charles.
title: [A sermon at Marlborough on 1. Tim.iv.16.]

text: As Moſes alſo ſaith in the fourth of Deuteronomie vnto the people, This is your wiſdome & your vnderſtanding in the ſight of the people, which ſhall heare all theſe Ordinaunces, and ſhall ſay, ſurely this people is wiſe, and of vnderſtanding, and a greate nation.
author: Pinner, Charles.
title: [A sermon at Marlborough on 1. Tim.iv.16.]

text: Where the Lord by the Prophet ſpeaketh vnto the Prieſts, as watchmenne, which had taken the charge of ſounding the trumpet vnto the people: as Saint Paule hereunto Timothie, and in him vnto vs, Take heede vnto doctrine.
author: Pinner, Charles.
title: [A sermon at Marlborough on 1. Tim.iv.16.]

text: Yes, tell it to the very ſkorners, and to the greateſt amongſt them, that never (almoſt) ſuch vowing to the ſinnes of men, by them, that ſhould make all the world to bend.
author: Pinner, Charles.
title: [A sermon at Marlborough on 1. Tim.iv.16.]

text: And our aunſwere is theirs indeede, though not in wordes, for ſo wee doe, as if wee had ſayed.
author: Pinner, Charles.
title: [A sermon at Marlborough on 1. Tim.iv.16.]

text: And out of theſe words of Paul the Apoſtle in the tenth to the Romans, How ſhall they beleeue in him, of whom they haue not heard? and how ſhall they heare without a preacher?
author: Pinner, Charles.
title: [A sermon at Marlborough on 1. Tim.iv.16.]

text: But the propheſie of the Apoſtle is fulfilled in them; & they haue prevailed no longer: for their madnes is manifeſt to al mē, as theirs alſo was.
author: Pinner, Charles.
title: [A sermon at Marlborough on 1. Tim.iv.16.]

text: SIr; your willingnes to haue beene preſent at the preaching of this Sermon, reſtrained only by inſtant, & urgent occaſions, as my ſelfe well know, hath moved me to deliver vnto your minde by reading, that, which otherwiſe you would, but could not receiue by hearing.
author: Pinner, Charles.
title: [A sermon at Marlborough on 1. Tim.iv.16.]

text: For in this diete it may be kepte to the.v. or.vi. day. without any ieoperdie: And than in the mornyng the shauynge of this Guaiacum soden in water must be dronken to the mayntenaunce of halfe an vnce.

text: And therfore if they shulde haue the company of woman, wherby the newe gotten strength is weke and grene, and not yet ryped: it wolde by and by dissolue and destroy the strengthe and myghtis of all the membres for euer.
author: Hutten, Ulrich von, 1488-1523.
title: De morbo Gallico·

text: And therfore I haue harde many experte therin saye, that than Guaiacum maketh an ende of his operation, whan the pacient returneth to his meate and in euery thynge taketh agayne his olde custome of lyuynge.
author: Hutten, Ulrich von, 1488-1523.
title: De morbo Gallico·

text: And more ouer he had great hope, that if this syckenes were thus preuented in the begynnynge, it myght vtterly be purged and clensed, and the syke restored.

title: De morbo Gallico·

text: And Alexander in his problemes sayth, that suche as drinke water onely, are quycker in all senses than other.

text: Secondely bycause all diseases in wynter do fasten their rotes deper and take surer holde / and in sommer contrarye wyse, the humours be styll mouynge, and the body is apte vnto all chaunges.

title: De morbo Gallico·

text: But if it had so fortuned that I myght haue ben in your courte with him (For than ye were away in Germanie) I shulde haue intreated more warely of all these thynges, and sette forthe my booke more perfectly.

title: De morbo Gallico·

text: And Galene cōmendethe rubbynges of the body aboue all thynges, inculcatynge oftentymes and many thinges therof, and specially in his bokes of preseruynge helthe.

title: De morbo Gallico·

text: The moste holsomest fedynge for man (sayth Plinie) is one maner meate, the heapynge of dyuers tastes is pestiferous, and sawces are worse than that.

text: Long in this ſort gan they diſagrée, till at laſt with their enuious emulation they ſtirred vp all the aſſemblie to ſuch ſtrife, as had not the care of the charie Captaine in time reformed, it had brought ſelfe-working harme vpon their owne heads.

text: Spending ye time in theſe villanous practiſes, at length they drew néere home, where readie to intertaine them was the Captaine of theſe cōfederates walking with his wife, a goodly woman, richly attired with the pretious ſpoyles that theſe vnthriftie villaines had forcibly taken away from many true men in their trauaile.

title: The second part of the historie, called The nature of a woman contayning the end of the strife betwixt Perseus and Theseus. Compiled by C.M.

text: At laſt, wonne with the words of this faire foretelling friend, the king wearie with ſolitarie ſitting there alone, and willing alſo to eaſe his head of thoſe cruell cares that ſolitarie diſcontent had clogged him withall, he willingly condeſcends to the others wiſh.

text: AS it fares in the eſtate of al things that are ſo changed from their firſt, as if the Fathers of the firſt world liued to reuiſe this laſt, they ſhould hardlie learne to know that wherein then they liued.

text: And Lord it is high time, for our head Citie is ſicke, hir Siſter Cities grone vnder this burden, their neighbor people are turned to their earth, and no part is frée, from the noyſome peſtilence.

text: Wo worthe your falſhode and doubleneſſe Wo worthe alſo your corrupte iugement Wo worthe delyte in worldly rycheſſe Wo worthe debate without extynguyſſhement Wo worthe your wordes ſo moche impacyent Wo worthe you vnto whome I dyde boote And wo worthe you that tere me at harte roote.

title: The conuercyon of swerers

text: But alſo for drede plonged in neclygence My penne doth quake to preſume to endyte But hope at laſte to recure this ſcyence Exorteth me ryght herdely to wryte To deuoyde ydelneſſe by good appetyte For ydelneſſe the grete moder of ſynne Euery vyce is vedy to lette ynne.
author: Hawes, Stephen, d. 1523?
title: The conuercyon of swerers

text: So hyſtoryagraphes all the worthy dedes Of kynges and knyghtes dyde put in wrytynge To be in mende for theyr memoryall medes How ſholde we now haue knowledgynge Of thynges paſt / but by theyr end ytynge Wherfore we ought to prayſe them doubteles That ſpent theyr tyme in ſuche good buſynes.
author: Hawes, Stephen, d. 1523?
title: The conuercyon of swerers

text: For at the requeſt of good mercy and peaſe I haue forborne you longe and many a daye Yet more and more your ſynnes do encreaſe Wherfore my iuſtyce wyll no more delaye But take vengeaunce for all your proude araye I warne you ofte ye are nothynge the better But ye amende my vengeaunce ſhall be gretter.
author: Hawes, Stephen, d. 1523?
title: The conuercyon of swerers

text: Wo worthe you whiche do me forſake Wo worthe you whiche wyllyngly offende Wo worthe your ſwerynge whiche doth not aſlake Wo worthe you whiche wyll nothynge amende Wo worthe vyce that on you doth atttende Wo worthe your grete vnkyndnes to me Wo worth your hertes withouten pyte.
author: Hawes, Stephen, d. 1523?
title: The conuercyon of swerers

text: Bleſſyd be ye that loue hum ylyte Bleſſyd be ye that loue trouthe and pacyence Bleſſyd be ye folowynge the werkes of equyte Bleſſyd be ye that loue well abſtynence Bleſſyd be ye byrgyngs of excellence Bleſſyd be ye whiche loue well vertu Bleſſyd be ye whiche dothe the worlde eſchue.
author: Hawes, Stephen, d. 1523?
title: The conuercyon of swerers

text: And as a lambe mooſt mekely dyde enclyne To ſuffre the deth for your redempcyon And ye my kynges whiche do now domyne Ouer my comens in terreſtryall mancyon By pryncely premynence and iuredyccyon In your regall courtes do ſuffre me be rent And my tender body with blode all be ſprent.

author: Alfield, Thomas, 1552-1585.

author: Alfield, Thomas, 1552-1585.

author: Hutchins, Edward, 1558?-1629.
title: A sermon preached in S. Peters Church at West-Chester the XXV. of September, 1586 Containing matter fit for the time: by Edward Hutchins Maister of Arts, and fellowe of Brazennose College.

text: Yee wastefull woods beare witnes of my woe, Wherein my plaints did oftentimes abound: Yee carelesse birds my sorrowes well do knoe, They in your songs were wont to make a sound.
author: Smith, William, fl. 1596.
title: Chloris, or The complaint of the passionate despised shepheard. By William Smith

text: If my deere loue would once but pittie showe, To quench these flames which in my breast do broile, Or dry these springs which from mine eies do flowe: Not onely Hellespont but Ocean seas, For hir sweete sake to forde I would attempt.
author: Smith, William, fl. 1596.
title: Chloris, or The complaint of the passionate despised shepheard. By William Smith

text: The breach is made I giue thee leaue to enter, Thee to resist great god I dare not venter.
author: Smith, William, fl. 1596.
title: Chloris, or The complaint of the passionate despised shepheard. By William Smith

text: The stately Lion and the furious Beare The skill of man doth alter from their kinde, For where before they wilde and sauage were, By art both tame and meeke, you shall them finde.
author: Smith, William, fl. 1596.
title: Chloris, or The complaint of the passionate despised shepheard. By William Smith

text: Nor of thine eies which heauenly stars excell, Nor of thine azurde vaines which are so cleere, Nor of thy paps where Loue himselfe doth dwell, Which like two hils of violets appeere.
author: Smith, William, fl. 1596.
title: Chloris, or The complaint of the passionate despised shepheard. By William Smith

text: But I which neuer fauor reaped yet, Nor had one pleasant looke from hir faire brow, Content my selfe in silent shade to sit In hope at length my cares to ouerplow.
author: Smith, William, fl. 1596.
title: Chloris, or The complaint of the passionate despised shepheard. By William Smith

text: But curteous shepheard, if they run astray Conduct them, that they may the path vvay finde, And teach them hovv, the meane obserue they may.
author: Smith, William, fl. 1596.
title: Chloris, or The complaint of the passionate despised shepheard. By William Smith

text: And thou the Genius of my ill tun'de note, Whose beautie vrged hath my rustick vaine, Through mighty Oceans of despaire to flote, That I in rime thy crueltie complaine: Vouchsafe to reade these lines both harsh and bad, Nuntiates of wo with sorrow being clad.
author: Smith, William, fl. 1596.
title: Chloris, or The complaint of the passionate despised shepheard. By William Smith

text: Which I powre foorth vnto a cruell Saint, Who mercilesse my praiers doth attend: Who Tiger-like doth pittie my complaint, And neuer eare vnto my woes will lend.
author: Smith, William, fl. 1596.
title: Chloris, or The complaint of the passionate despised shepheard. By William Smith

text: Let the people prayſe thée G God, now let them all thee prayſe: In this our moſt troubleſome time, and in theſe heauy dayes.
author: Pits, John.
title: A poore mannes beneuolence to the afflicted Church

text: Well ſaith our Sauiour Chriſt, happy are ye when men reuile you & perſecute you for my names ſake, for you ſhal not loſe your rewarde.
author: Pits, John.
title: A poore mannes beneuolence to the afflicted Church

text: He that is of God, heareth Gods word: yf any man kepe my worde, he ſhall neuer ſee death.
author: Pits, John.
title: A poore mannes beneuolence to the afflicted Church

text: Who dwelth ī truth, doth dwel in God and God in him lykewyſe: So, dwel in Truth, & then haue God to make thée perfect wyſe.
author: Pits, John.
title: A poore mannes beneuolence to the afflicted Church

text: If any man loueth me, he wyl kepe my worde, my father wyl loue him, and we ſhal come to him, and dwel with him.
author: Pits, John.
title: A poore mannes beneuolence to the afflicted Church

text: Stand faſt to Truth ſticke to your hold feare not the cruell kyng: He ſhall not hurt you (be you bold) in any maner thyng.
author: Pits, John.
title: A poore mannes beneuolence to the afflicted Church

text: Walke therfore in Truth ye godly, let yll men walke their way: To God and Truth do ye now hy, and take your ioyfull day.
author: Pits, John.
title: A poore mannes beneuolence to the afflicted Church

text: STand in the courte of the Lordes houſe, and ſpeake vnto al the cities of Juda which come to worſhip in the Lords houſe, al the wordes that I haue cōmaūded thee to ſpeake, kepe not a word backe.
author: Pits, John.
title: A poore mannes beneuolence to the afflicted Church

text: My ſhepe do heare it, and I do know them, and they do folow me, and I geue them euerlaſtyng life.
author: Pits, John.
title: A poore mannes beneuolence to the afflicted Church

text: Though it come ſomewhat late, I doubt not but it will breed ſome pleaſure, bicauſe the remembrance of pleaſures paſſed are alwaies delightſome.
author: Ubaldini, Petruccio, 1524?-1600?
title: A discourse concerninge the Spanishe fleete inuadinge Englande in the yeare 1588 and ouerthrowne by Her Ma[ies]ties nauie vnder the conduction of the Right-honorable the Lorde Charles Howarde highe Ad

text: In which time the E. of Suſſex, the L. Buckhurſt, ſir George Carie knight, and the captaines of the fortes and caſtels thereabout, ſent their men with powder, ſhot and victuals, to the L. Admirall to aſſiſt and helpe the armie.
author: Ubaldini, Petruccio, 1524?-1600?
title: A discourse concerninge the Spanishe fleete inuadinge Englande in the yeare 1588 and ouerthrowne by Her Ma[ies]ties nauie vnder the conduction of the Right-honorable the Lorde Charles Howarde highe Ad

text: In the meane ſeaſon the L. Seymer and ſir William Winter ioined with the L. Admirall, wherby the Engliſh fléete increaſed to the number of 140. ſhips of all ſorts.
author: Ubaldini, Petruccio, 1524?-1600?
title: A discourse concerninge the Spanishe fleete inuadinge Englande in the yeare 1588 and ouerthrowne by Her Ma[ies]ties nauie vnder the conduction of the Right-honorable the Lorde Charles Howarde highe Ad

text: The which miſhap ioined with the difficultie of ſtirring themſelues in their defence, bred ſuch a deſpaire in euery man, that the greater ſort lept into the water to ſaue themſelues by ſwimming into the hauen, although many of them periſhed in the water.
author: Ubaldini, Petruccio, 1524?-1600?
title: A discourse concerninge the Spanishe fleete inuadinge Englande in the yeare 1588 and ouerthrowne by Her Ma[ies]ties nauie vnder the conduction of the Right-honorable the Lorde Charles Howarde highe Ad

text: This thing was diligently and effectually brought to paſſe vnder the charge of captaine Yoong and captaine Prewſe, two valiant and couragious men.
author: Ubaldini, Petruccio, 1524?-1600?
title: A discourse concerninge the Spanishe fleete inuadinge Englande in the yeare 1588 and ouerthrowne by Her Ma[ies]ties nauie vnder the conduction of the Right-honorable the Lorde Charles Howarde highe Ad

text: This day alſo and the next being the 27. the Spaniards followed their courſe quietly before the Engliſh fléete.
author: Ubaldini, Petruccio, 1524?-1600?
title: A discourse concerninge the Spanishe fleete inuadinge Englande in the yeare 1588 and ouerthrowne by Her Ma[ies]ties nauie vnder the conduction of the Right-honorable the Lorde Charles Howarde highe Ad

text: And thus this daies worke ended: whereof I may ſay, that the conflict was no whit ſhorter then the day it ſelfe.
author: Ubaldini, Petruccio, 1524?-1600?
title: A discourse concerninge the Spanishe fleete inuadinge Englande in the yeare 1588 and ouerthrowne by Her Ma[ies]ties nauie vnder the conduction of the Right-honorable the Lorde Charles Howarde highe Ad

text: This example may ſerue to inſtruct ſuch as command ouer others, how they ought to behaue themſelues with leſſe inſolencie: inaſmuch as the minde of man is alwaies readie to reuenge, after the cuſtome of this our bloodie age, if he be not borne vtterly void of a quicke wit and liuely ſpirit.
author: Ubaldini, Petruccio, 1524?-1600?
title: A discourse concerninge the Spanishe fleete inuadinge Englande in the yeare 1588 and ouerthrowne by Her Ma[ies]ties nauie vnder the conduction of the Right-honorable the Lorde Charles Howarde highe Ad

text: Therfore the two Lords, viz. the L. Howard, and the L. Sheffeild: Roger Townſend, Iohn Hawkins and Martin Frobiſher were called foorth, and the order of knighthoode giuen them by the L. Admirall as their generall.
author: Ubaldini, Petruccio, 1524?-1600?
