text: From the head of that Riuer to Hochelaga, there is about thrée hundred leagues: the originall beginning of it is in the riuer that commeth from Saguenay, which riſeth and ſpringeth among high and ſtéepe hilles: it entreth into that Riuer before it commeth to the prouince of Canada on the North ſide.
author: Cartier, Jacques, 1491-1557.
title: A shorte and briefe narration of the two nauigations and discoueries to the northweast partes called Newe Fraunce: first translated out of French into Italian, by that famous learned man Gio: Bapt: Ra

text: There are likewiſe great quantitie of the ſaid Aphothuys taken by the inhabitours of the Coūtry, ſo that there is as gret concourſe and méeting in that place as is at Bordeous in Fraunce at euery tide.
author: Cartier, Jacques, 1491-1557.
title: A shorte and briefe narration of the two nauigations and discoueries to the northweast partes called Newe Fraunce: first translated out of French into Italian, by that famous learned man Gio: Bapt: Ra

text: It is a playne Countrey, but an ill ſoyle: and in the middeſt of the entrance thereof, there is an Iland.
author: Cartier, Jacques, 1491-1557.
title: A shorte and briefe narration of the two nauigations and discoueries to the northweast partes called Newe Fraunce: first translated out of French into Italian, by that famous learned man Gio: Bapt: Ra

text: That Ilande is enuironed rounde about with ſande, and hath a very good roade about it thrée or four faddome déepe.
author: Cartier, Jacques, 1491-1557.
title: A shorte and briefe narration of the two nauigations and discoueries to the northweast partes called Newe Fraunce: first translated out of French into Italian, by that famous learned man Gio: Bapt: Ra

text: They are aboute the bigneſſe of a Purpois, yet nothing like them, of bodye verye well proportioned, headed lyke Graye-houndes, altogither as white as Snowe, wythout anye ſpotte, within which Riuer there is great quantitie of them: they do liue altogyther betwéene the Sea and the freſhe Water.
author: Cartier, Jacques, 1491-1557.
title: A shorte and briefe narration of the two nauigations and discoueries to the northweast partes called Newe Fraunce: first translated out of French into Italian, by that famous learned man Gio: Bapt: Ra

text: The ſaide hauen wherin we ſtayed, is as it were but a ſluce of the waters that riſe by the floud, and but of ſmal accompt, we named them S. Iohns Iſleetes, bycauſe we founde them, and entred into thē the day of the beheading of that Saint.
author: Cartier, Jacques, 1491-1557.
title: A shorte and briefe narration of the two nauigations and discoueries to the northweast partes called Newe Fraunce: first translated out of French into Italian, by that famous learned man Gio: Bapt: Ra

text: They haue this vertue and propertie in them, they wyll ſtoppe or ſtench any bléeding at the noſe, for we haue proued it.
author: Cartier, Jacques, 1491-1557.
title: A shorte and briefe narration of the two nauigations and discoueries to the northweast partes called Newe Fraunce: first translated out of French into Italian, by that famous learned man Gio: Bapt: Ra

text: On the North ſide of whiche about halfe a league there lyeth a lowe Ilande, that Cape we named the Cape of Milke.
author: Cartier, Jacques, 1491-1557.
title: A shorte and briefe narration of the two nauigations and discoueries to the northweast partes called Newe Fraunce: first translated out of French into Italian, by that famous learned man Gio: Bapt: Ra

text: They ploughe theyr groundes with certain péeces of wood, as big as halfe a ſworde, on whiche grounde groweth theyr corne, The call it Offici: it is as bigge as our ſmall Peaſon there is great quantitie of it growing in Braſil.
author: Cartier, Jacques, 1491-1557.
title: A shorte and briefe narration of the two nauigations and discoueries to the northweast partes called Newe Fraunce: first translated out of French into Italian, by that famous learned man Gio: Bapt: Ra

text: From hence therefore euen presently, my iorney I will take, And hye me fast for tyme it is, to myne infernall lake.
author: Garter, Thomas.

text: Dispatche I pray thée, for yonder I sée, the Iudges are comming, And therefore take payne, I say once agayne, let vs doe something.
author: Garter, Thomas.

text: The fewter of her formed face, the glistering of her eyne, Her shoulders that are quadrant to, her nose that is so fyne.
author: Garter, Thomas.
title: The commody of the moste vertuous and godlye Susanna neuer before this tyme printed. Compiled by Thomas Garter. Eyght persons may easyly play it. 1. The Prologue and the Saylour for one. 2. Ioachim an

text: This ioyfull lyfe did he leade still, till death the Deuill and Hell, By disobeying of thy doome did spite his state so well, He fell from that and now is come, into such weakenesse Lord, As what a loue of him doth come, by thée it is abhorde.
author: Garter, Thomas.
title: The commody of the moste vertuous and godlye Susanna neuer before this tyme printed. Compiled by Thomas Garter. Eyght persons may easyly play it. 1. The Prologue and the Saylour for one. 2. Ioachim an

text: Her brestes that are so round and fayre, her armes that are so long, Her fyngers straight with vaynes beset, of blew and white among.
author: Garter, Thomas.
title: The commody of the moste vertuous and godlye Susanna neuer before this tyme printed. Compiled by Thomas Garter. Eyght persons may easyly play it. 1. The Prologue and the Saylour for one. 2. Ioachim an

text: The one from the beginning of a word a sillable may cut, The other from the end, another may shut.
author: Garter, Thomas.
title: The commody of the moste vertuous and godlye Susanna neuer before this tyme printed. Compiled by Thomas Garter. Eyght persons may easyly play it. 1. The Prologue and the Saylour for one. 2. Ioachim an

text: God also did make Maiestrates, the pore to helpe and stay, Yet some doe vyle examples show, which now doe beare a sway, I speake it not I will you know, the worst man to offende, But for that such as guiltie be, their guilt may soone amende.
author: Garter, Thomas.
title: The commody of the moste vertuous and godlye Susanna neuer before this tyme printed. Compiled by Thomas Garter. Eyght persons may easyly play it. 1. The Prologue and the Saylour for one. 2. Ioachim an

text: And I vse to be short, and in few wordes to tell, God sende thée a thousande plagues more then euer were found in hell, These and ten thousand when thou art layde in thy bed, To recompence thy trauayle light vpon thy head.
author: Garter, Thomas.
title: The commody of the moste vertuous and godlye Susanna neuer before this tyme printed. Compiled by Thomas Garter. Eyght persons may easyly play it. 1. The Prologue and the Saylour for one. 2. Ioachim an

text: And if you cannot smell, Then are you not well, For reasons by gis: Will doe you small good, But chaunge your good blood, To stinking ywis.
author: Garter, Thomas.

text: And for the time perchaunce, I was accepted then, And promiſed to haue aduaunce, as ſoone as other men.
author: Saparton, John.
title: Sapartons alarum, to all such as do beare the name of true souldiers, in England, or els wheare.

text: Eſteeme not my yll hap, Nor weye it ought at all, The wight that ſcapes the Cannons clap, Runnes yet to further thrall.
author: Saparton, John.
title: Sapartons alarum, to all such as do beare the name of true souldiers, in England, or els wheare.

text: Some youthfull Imps I knowe, that beares a paſſing grace: If they to pitched fielde ſhould goe, durſt ſcarſly ſhew their face.
author: Saparton, John.
title: Sapartons alarum, to all such as do beare the name of true souldiers, in England, or els wheare.

text: Could neuer force me yet, the enemies face to ſhonne: If Captaines courage ſemed fit, the conqueſt to haue wonne.
author: Saparton, John.
title: Sapartons alarum, to all such as do beare the name of true souldiers, in England, or els wheare.

text: Though Venus ſtriue with Mars, to get the vpper grounde: At length yet ſhall the barded Horſe, exceede doth Hauke and Hounde.
author: Saparton, John.
title: Sapartons alarum, to all such as do beare the name of true souldiers, in England, or els wheare.

text: O Mars, bewaile thy man, Becauſe he hath ſuche wronge, In dolefull tunes, O ruſtick Pan, Now helpe to waile this ſonge.
author: Saparton, John.
title: Sapartons alarum, to all such as do beare the name of true souldiers, in England, or els wheare.

text: Tis not the curled head, nor yet the friſled heare: That courage giues in time of neede, to weld thunweldy Speare.
author: Saparton, John.
title: Sapartons alarum, to all such as do beare the name of true souldiers, in England, or els wheare.

text: In faith then I am he, ſuch one that for my parte Haue ready bin full willinglye, with hand, and eeke with harte.
author: Saparton, John.
title: Sapartons alarum, to all such as do beare the name of true souldiers, in England, or els wheare.

text: But when that all is don, Tis manhood makes the man: Match not the Candell with the Sunne, no praiſe deſerue you than.
author: Saparton, John.
title: Sapartons alarum, to all such as do beare the name of true souldiers, in England, or els wheare.

text: GEntlemen; the laſt Terme there came forth a little toy of mine, intituled, The affectionate Shepheard: In the which, his Country Content found ſuch friendly fauor, that it hath incouraged me to publiſh my ſecond fruites.
author: Barnfield, Richard, 1574-1627.
title: Cynthia VVith certaine sonnets, and the legend of Cassandra.

text: But what? (fond man) he laughes her skil to ſcorne, And icſteth at her diuination: Ah to what vnbeliefe are Princes borne?
author: Barnfield, Richard, 1574-1627.
title: Cynthia VVith certaine sonnets, and the legend of Cassandra.

text: This is my wiſh: the which your honorable excellent giftes doe promiſe me to obtaine: and whereof theſe few rude and vnpolliſhed lines, are a true (though an vndeſeruing) teſtimony.
author: Barnfield, Richard, 1574-1627.
title: Cynthia VVith certaine sonnets, and the legend of Cassandra.

text: VVhich when Aurora ſaw, and ſaw t'was ſhee, Euen ſhee her ſelfe whoſe far-renowmed fame Made all the world to wonder at her beauty, It mou'd compaſſion in this ruthfull Dame: And thinking on her Sonnes ſad deſtnie.
author: Barnfield, Richard, 1574-1627.
title: Cynthia VVith certaine sonnets, and the legend of Cassandra.

text: Happy are they, that neuer liu'd to know What t'is to liue in this world happily: Happy are they which neuer yet felt woe: Happy are they, that die in infancie: Whoſe ſins are cancell'd in their mothers wombe: Whoſe cradle is their graue, whoſe lap their tomb.
author: Barnfield, Richard, 1574-1627.
title: Cynthia VVith certaine sonnets, and the legend of Cassandra.

text: Wondring thus at Natures worke, (Wherein many maruailes lurke) Me thought I heard a dolefull noiſe, Conſorted with a mournfull voice, Drawing nie to heare more plaine, Heare I did, vnto my paine, (For who is not pain'd to heare Him in griefe whom heart holdes deare?)
author: Barnfield, Richard, 1574-1627.
title: Cynthia VVith certaine sonnets, and the legend of Cassandra.

text: He (noble Lord) feareleſſe of hidden treaſon, Sweetely ſalutes this weeping Crocodile: Excuſing euery cauſe with inſtant reaſon That kept him from her ſight ſo long a while: Shee, faintly pardons him: ſmiling by Art: (For life was in her lookes, death in her hart.)
author: Barnfield, Richard, 1574-1627.
title: Cynthia VVith certaine sonnets, and the legend of Cassandra.

text: When, thinking that it would ſtrāge Magique proue, He open'd it: and taking off the couer, He ſtraight perceau'd himſelfe to be my Louer.

text: In ſtede of the nominatyue where you prayed for your ſelfe: you maye now praye for all thoſe that do byde in payne for any defaute or offence done by your exā ple or occaſion.

text: And yf you haue portunyte there vpon it / ſhalbe full conuenyent for you to be confeſſed on the nexte morowe.

text: In all thynges eſteme and acoūt your ſelfe moſt vyle / and moſt ſymple / & as very nought in reſpecte / and regarde of vertue and thynke / ſuppoſe / and byleue that all perſons ben good / and better than you be / for ſo ſhall you moche pleaſe our lorde.

title: Here begynneth a goodly treatyse, and it is called a notable lesson, otherwyse it is called the golden pystle

text: Fyrſt by Rotable leſ. reaſon of your body: you were cōceyued of the moſt fylthy abomynable mater of man / ſhamefull to be ſpoken / fetre more vyle then the ſluche / or ſlyme of the erthe / and after borne in a ſynfull ſoule / and purged onely by grace.

text: And ſo to auoyde thoſe: you ſhal here (the better) ſuffre / and for our lorde the more pacyently bere al theſe that now be preſent or may come here after.

text: Vf you intende to pleaſe god / & wolde obteyne grace to fulfyll the ſame / two thynges ben vnto you very neceſſarye.

text: Dany yf there be any that hath ani matter in this ſeſcions houſe, let hym enter his accione for my lord iuge is ready to heare yt Iuge. danyell call forthe that woman ther Danye, mother meſſe ſtande forthe at the bare here.

text: Vuiſd. brother knowleg I pray you where is hir moſt abydīg & comē trade where I maye lay wayte for hir.

text: Meſſe. marye I ſay I am very wel content, vviſ antipus I do cōmand you in the kīgs nāe to lay this womā faſt in newgate that ſhe maye be forthe commīg to morow at ye Seſcione houſe.
author: Punt, William.
title: A new dialoge called the endightment agaynste mother Messe

text: BRother knowledge cā ſte thou tel me what newes ys now abrode amonge the people concernīg godes word. knovvledg brother veryte I here no newes but yt it ſhal floryſh according to godes wil for eany thing that I cāneperceyue.
author: Punt, William.
title: A new dialoge called the endightment agaynste mother Messe

text: Brother knowlege & veryte you muſt be at the ſeſſciō howſſe at.viii. of the clocke to morow to put your inditment agaīſt mother meſſe. knouv. and I praye you brother wyſdome haue you gotten hir.

title: A new dialoge called the endightment agaynste mother Messe

text: Iuge. no that ſhe ſhall not for yt way chāce that ſhe maye do moche harme in the weye as ſhe gotthe, Stifnec my lorde yf yt pleaſe you to ſet two honeſt men to ouer ſe hyr my brother couetes and I wylbe glad to beare there coſts what ſo euer yt be.
author: Punt, William.
title: A new dialoge called the endightment agaynste mother Messe

text: Well then That ſame bodye after it had Suffred death and roſe agayne yt aſſended vp to heauen and let hym downe on the ryght hande of his father & there tarieth tyll his foes, be made hys fote ſtole, nowe that bodye is in heauen you wyll graunt me thys.
author: Punt, William.
title: A new dialoge called the endightment agaynste mother Messe

text: Brother veryte I haue no dought but that he ſhal take hyr tyght wel al though it belōg firſt Wherfore I beſech ye lord be his ſpede. very.

text: And in their going they doo carry theyr head so hye, as if they were kinges ouer the heardes of the Cattell: and if it be true that Iupiter when hée did carry Io away, was transformed into a Bull, surely then I thinke it was into an Aegyptian.
author: Achilles Tatius.

text: Hauing spoken thus, incensed with furie, she flung it into my face, which when I vnderstood I was astonied, and cast down my head as if I hadde béene guilty of some hainous crime.
author: Achilles Tatius.

text: The Phisition being come, deuised with himselfe what this sodaine sicknesse might be: wherefore first hee gaue her a potion to sléepe, that the sicknesse might leaue some of his force: for sleepe is the remedie for all sicknesse.
author: Achilles Tatius.

text: That is the lawe among the Barbarians, the Scythians, and them which inhabite the mountaine Taurus, to sacrifice to Diana with mens blood.

text: But Melite bad her be of good chéere, saying: I will deliuer thee from these miseries, and afterwards thou shalt dwell with me at home.

text: O sea! thou hast preserued a Sayler, but by preseruing him, thou hast cast him into greater daungers: two dead persons are reuiued again to my perdition, as though one Leucippe were not sufficient: but let her liue, so that Clitiphon do not liue in sorrow.
author: Achilles Tatius.

text: Therefore know this for certaintie, that hée is Melites husband, which you sawe héere in the Countrey, and the chéefest in birth amongest the Ionians: whose stocke surpasseth his wealth, but his gentlenesse excelleth all his riches.
author: Achilles Tatius.

text: Tush, friends are hard to finde, true friendship seeld appeares: A man may misse to haue a friend, that liues olde Nestors yeares.

text: She wary of the time, and carefull for her nest: Debated wisely with her selfe, what thing to doo were best: For to abide the rage. of cruell Reapers hand: She knew it was to perilous, with safetie for to stand.
author: Bourcher, Arthur.

text: But when she heard of kin, she laughing cried amaine: A pin for kin, a figge for friends, yet kinne the worst of twaine.

text: Who giues me glozing wordes, and faile me at my need: May in my Pater noster be, but neuer in my Creede.

text: Now foloweth the third diſprayſe and fault which is layed in olde age, becauſe (ſaye they) it is wythoute pleaſure, and muſte forgoe voluptuous appetites.
author: Cicero, Marcus Tullius.
title: The worthye booke of old age othervvyse entituled the elder Cato contayning a learned defence and praise of age, and aged men: writen in latine by that father of eloquence Marcus Tullius Cicero, and n

text: But truly the cauſe therof is not proprely to be imputed to the old age, but commonelye to lacke of health.
author: Cicero, Marcus Tullius.
title: The worthye booke of old age othervvyse entituled the elder Cato contayning a learned defence and praise of age, and aged men: writen in latine by that father of eloquence Marcus Tullius Cicero, and n

text: The fourth cauſe, whyche moſte of all greueth & diſquieteth old men, remaineth yet behind vndiſcuſſed, which is the approching of death, & the néereneſſe therof, which truly can not be farre of frome olde age.
author: Cicero, Marcus Tullius.
title: The worthye booke of old age othervvyse entituled the elder Cato contayning a learned defence and praise of age, and aged men: writen in latine by that father of eloquence Marcus Tullius Cicero, and n

text: Seuerity and ſterneneſſe in old age I well allow and commend, ſo that a moderate meane therin (as in al other thinges) be obſerued, but bitterneſſe and rigorous dealinge I can in no wyſe brooke nor away withall.
author: Cicero, Marcus Tullius.
title: The worthye booke of old age othervvyse entituled the elder Cato contayning a learned defence and praise of age, and aged men: writen in latine by that father of eloquence Marcus Tullius Cicero, and n

text: Neither do I feare, whē I read the Epitaphes and inſcripcions of Tombes & graues, leaſt I ſhould therby, (as the cō mō credulity of people is) loſe my memory and remembraunce: for in reading of them I am brought into remembraunce of thoſe that are deceaſſed.
author: Cicero, Marcus Tullius.
title: The worthye booke of old age othervvyse entituled the elder Cato contayning a learned defence and praise of age, and aged men: writen in latine by that father of eloquence Marcus Tullius Cicero, and n

text: Plato alſo the noble A thenian Philoſopher, was preſent & heard him ſpeake theſe wordes, whom I do in olde hiſtories fynd, that he came and arriued at Tarento, when L. Aemilius and Appius Claudius were Conſuls.
author: Cicero, Marcus Tullius.
title: The worthye booke of old age othervvyse entituled the elder Cato contayning a learned defence and praise of age, and aged men: writen in latine by that father of eloquence Marcus Tullius Cicero, and n

text: The race and courſe of age is certayne, and there is but one way of nature and the ſame ſimple, and to euery part of a mans life and age, are géeuen hys conuenyente tymes and propre tempeſtiuytyes.
author: Cicero, Marcus Tullius.
title: The worthye booke of old age othervvyse entituled the elder Cato contayning a learned defence and praise of age, and aged men: writen in latine by that father of eloquence Marcus Tullius Cicero, and n

text: For pleaſure being a deadly and mortall enemye to reaſon, hindereth vertuous action and prudent conſultacion, and the eyes of the mind thereby are ſo iuggled and bewitched, that it can haue no felowſhip nor compaignie with vertue.
author: Cicero, Marcus Tullius.
title: The worthye booke of old age othervvyse entituled the elder Cato contayning a learned defence and praise of age, and aged men: writen in latine by that father of eloquence Marcus Tullius Cicero, and n

text: Accept therfore (Right noble Lord this poore earneſt penye of my vnfayned good vvil into your tuition, vvherby I ſhal be anymated and encouraged hereafter perhappes to attempte ſome vvaightier matter.
author: Cicero, Marcus Tullius.
title: The worthye booke of old age othervvyse entituled the elder Cato contayning a learned defence and praise of age, and aged men: writen in latine by that father of eloquence Marcus Tullius Cicero, and n

text: The englyshe men sente agayne for Etheldred out of Normandye, who by the healpe of the Normans, and present assistance of his commons, expelled Canutus. but shortly Canutus returned agayne into Englande, where he spared nothynge that myght be destroyed with sworde & fyre.
author: Stow, John, 1525?-1605.
title: A summarie of Englyshe chronicles conteynyng the true accompt of yeres, wherein euery kyng of this realme of England began theyr reigne, howe long they reigned: and what notable thynges hath bene doon

text: But the people stil folowed him as thei before had doone: and he made to them certaine orations openly, taking for his Theme this sentence, Haurietis aquas in gaudeo de fontibus Saluatoris, Whiche is to saie: Ye shall drawe in ioie, waters forth of the welles of your Sauiour.
author: Stow, John, 1525?-1605.

text: An other is Landaeffe, the thirde Bangor, and the fourthe All Saint Asaph. whiche, be vnder Tharchbyshoppe of Canterburye.
author: Stow, John, 1525?-1605.

text: EDwarde, the Elder sonne of Alured, began his reign ouer the most parte of Englande, and gouerned this land well and nobly. xxiiii. yeares.
author: Stow, John, 1525?-1605.
title: A summarie of Englyshe chronicles conteynyng the true accompt of yeres, wherein euery kyng of this realme of England began theyr reigne, howe long they reigned: and what notable thynges hath bene doon

text: Dyuers gentylmen in England were appeached of treason, and for fauoryng the conspiracie of Parkyn Warbeck: of whiche some were pardoned, and some put to death.
author: Stow, John, 1525?-1605.
title: A summarie of Englyshe chronicles conteynyng the true accompt of yeres, wherein euery kyng of this realme of England began theyr reigne, howe long they reigned: and what notable thynges hath bene doon

text: In October on sainct Edwardes eue, was borne at Hampton courte, the noble Prince Edwarde, and shortely after, Quene Iane lefte her lyfe, the.14. day of October.
author: Stow, John, 1525?-1605.
title: A summarie of Englyshe chronicles conteynyng the true accompt of yeres, wherein euery kyng of this realme of England began theyr reigne, howe long they reigned: and what notable thynges hath bene doon

text: The.xxiii. of Nouember Cardinall Poole came oute of Brabant into Englande, and was receyued with muche honour in all places as he passed.
author: Stow, John, 1525?-1605.
title: A summarie of Englyshe chronicles conteynyng the true accompt of yeres, wherein euery kyng of this realme of England began theyr reigne, howe long they reigned: and what notable thynges hath bene doon

text: This yeare one willyam Serle was taken in the marches of Scotlande, and brought to London, and there hanged, drawen, and quartred for the murdring of the duke of Gloucester at Calice.
author: Stow, John, 1525?-1605.
title: A summarie of Englyshe chronicles conteynyng the true accompt of yeres, wherein euery kyng of this realme of England began theyr reigne, howe long they reigned: and what notable thynges hath bene doon

text: For prince Ed. being now set at libertie, allied him wt the erle of Glocester & gathering to hī a great power, warred so freshly vpon Symon of Leicester, that at the ende he and Hughe spencer with many others of the nobles, were slayn in the battayle at Euishā in Worcester shyre.
author: Stow, John, 1525?-1605.
title: A summarie of Englyshe chronicles conteynyng the true accompt of yeres, wherein euery kyng of this realme of England began theyr reigne, howe long they reigned: and what notable thynges hath bene doon

text: Your Grace hath alreadye heard by that is paſt, howe infamous the firſt hath beene vnto the Countrey Magiſtrate: The ſecond hath not feared to ſlander the court: but this third, in plain tearmes, hath preſumed to touch your owne perſon.
author: Rich, Barnabe, 1540?-1617.
title: The aduentures of Brusanus Prince of Hungaria, pleasant for all to read, and profitable for some to follow. / Written by Barnaby Riche, seauen or eight yeares sithence, and now published by the great

text: Die thē Moderna, Moderna die: better were it for thée to periſh with high deſires, then to liue in baſe thoughts: thus throwing her ſelfe vpon her bed, drawing the Curtaines, ſhee turned too and fro, as if ſhee would haue hidden her ſelfe from her owne thoughts.
author: Rich, Barnabe, 1540?-1617.
title: The aduentures of Brusanus Prince of Hungaria, pleasant for all to read, and profitable for some to follow. / Written by Barnaby Riche, seauen or eight yeares sithence, and now published by the great

text: Let Bruſanus looke better of his text, and he ſhal find it to bee ſo, and that Adam could neuer after haue riſen againe, but by the ſeed of a woman.
author: Rich, Barnabe, 1540?-1617.
title: The aduentures of Brusanus Prince of Hungaria, pleasant for all to read, and profitable for some to follow. / Written by Barnaby Riche, seauen or eight yeares sithence, and now published by the great

text: THe poore man hauing thus finiſhed his ſpeache, was willed to ſtand by, and Glorioſus was now to inferre againſt Martianus, who procéeded in this wiſe.
author: Rich, Barnabe, 1540?-1617.
title: The aduentures of Brusanus Prince of Hungaria, pleasant for all to read, and profitable for some to follow. / Written by Barnaby Riche, seauen or eight yeares sithence, and now published by the great

text: AFter the gentleman had bene in this ſort qualified, he was willed to infourme what hee had againſt Corynus, and in this wiſe hee beganne to tell his tale.
author: Rich, Barnabe, 1540?-1617.
title: The aduentures of Brusanus Prince of Hungaria, pleasant for all to read, and profitable for some to follow. / Written by Barnaby Riche, seauen or eight yeares sithence, and now published by the great

text: Bruſanus and Doreſtus, beeing nowe growen to a mutuall loue, and both of them deſirous to approoue their owne vallour, came into the liſtes amongſt the reſt gallantly mounted, and moſt richly armed.
author: Rich, Barnabe, 1540?-1617.
title: The aduentures of Brusanus Prince of Hungaria, pleasant for all to read, and profitable for some to follow. / Written by Barnaby Riche, seauen or eight yeares sithence, and now published by the great

text: And to make deniall, ſhee thought would either incurre diſpleaſure, or mooue ſuperſtition: but her father liſtening what ſhe would ſay, ſhe thought in this manner to haue ſtopt his mouth, and thus ſhe anſwered.
author: Rich, Barnabe, 1540?-1617.
title: The aduentures of Brusanus Prince of Hungaria, pleasant for all to read, and profitable for some to follow. / Written by Barnaby Riche, seauen or eight yeares sithence, and now published by the great

text: Thus the pore louer findes his pleaſure tranſlated into a quality of bitternes, and his hope ſo turned into diſpaire, that hee hath no other refuge then in death, and yet in him he hardly finds medicine.
author: Rich, Barnabe, 1540?-1617.
title: The aduentures of Brusanus Prince of Hungaria, pleasant for all to read, and profitable for some to follow. / Written by Barnaby Riche, seauen or eight yeares sithence, and now published by the great

text: But why doſt thou moue doubtes Moderna? miſdéeming either Bruſanus or thy ſelfe: ſhall the reward of loue be loathing? doth good wil deſerue hatred? or fancie defiaunce: or what is there in thee that Bruſanus ſhould miſlike.
author: Rich, Barnabe, 1540?-1617.
title: The aduentures of Brusanus Prince of Hungaria, pleasant for all to read, and profitable for some to follow. / Written by Barnaby Riche, seauen or eight yeares sithence, and now published by the great

text: I did with a milde countenance beholde ſuch counſailours as tickled mine eares: but thoſe that ſpake vnto mee with a free minde, I put farre from me.
author: António, Prior of Crato, 1531-1595.
title: Psalmes of confession found in the cabinet of the most excellent King of Portingal, Don Antonio, first of that name, written with his owne hand. Wherein the sinner calleth vpon the mercie of God for h

text: Neither did I only not ſeeke a medicine for my ſoule, that was ſicke vnto death, but refuſed it being offered: yea, with an vnreuerent and vntamed mind was wroth againſt them, that would miniſter it vnto me.
author: António, Prior of Crato, 1531-1595.
title: Psalmes of confession found in the cabinet of the most excellent King of Portingal, Don Antonio, first of that name, written with his owne hand. Wherein the sinner calleth vpon the mercie of God for h

text: The ſorowes of death compaſſe me rounde about: and being filled with many ſorowes without, I feele inwardly no ſorowe that may worke vnto ſaluation.
author: António, Prior of Crato, 1531-1595.
title: Psalmes of confession found in the cabinet of the most excellent King of Portingal, Don Antonio, first of that name, written with his owne hand. Wherein the sinner calleth vpon the mercie of God for h

text: For thou art iuſt, O Lord, and righteous is thy iudgement, and thou rendereſt to euery man according to his workes.
author: António, Prior of Crato, 1531-1595.
title: Psalmes of confession found in the cabinet of the most excellent King of Portingal, Don Antonio, first of that name, written with his owne hand. Wherein the sinner calleth vpon the mercie of God for h

text: I haue willingly forſaken the right way, and as a ſheepe that refuſeth his ſhepheard, I haue beene caried farre and wide round about through drie vnwatered places, wandring in the wilderneſſe, and not in the way.
author: António, Prior of Crato, 1531-1595.
title: Psalmes of confession found in the cabinet of the most excellent King of Portingal, Don Antonio, first of that name, written with his owne hand. Wherein the sinner calleth vpon the mercie of God for h

text: Yea I haue wickedly and vainely conſumed thy talent, and by looſe liuing I haue ſpent thy goods. ſurely I haue ſpoken fooliſhly, by ſaying liuing: for I ſhould better haue ſayed by dying.
author: António, Prior of Crato, 1531-1595.
title: Psalmes of confession found in the cabinet of the most excellent King of Portingal, Don Antonio, first of that name, written with his owne hand. Wherein the sinner calleth vpon the mercie of God for h

text: I waxed olde and gray, and did not walke in thy wayes: but as a child of an hundred yeres, being nowe an olde man, I liue childiſhly.
author: António, Prior of Crato, 1531-1595.
title: Psalmes of confession found in the cabinet of the most excellent King of Portingal, Don Antonio, first of that name, written with his owne hand. Wherein the sinner calleth vpon the mercie of God for h

text: Wherefore then doeſt thou feare to goe, thou that art not called by a cruell iudge, but by the father of mercies, that thou mayeſt obtaine mercie: therefore goe now willing being called to mercie, that thou be not compelled hereafter to goe vnto iudgement.
author: António, Prior of Crato, 1531-1595.
title: Psalmes of confession found in the cabinet of the most excellent King of Portingal, Don Antonio, first of that name, written with his owne hand. Wherein the sinner calleth vpon the mercie of God for h

text: I payed not my debt to them that did lende vnto me, and did borowe to ſatisfie my inordinate deſire.
author: António, Prior of Crato, 1531-1595.
title: Psalmes of confession found in the cabinet of the most excellent King of Portingal, Don Antonio, first of that name, written with his owne hand. Wherein the sinner calleth vpon the mercie of God for h

text: The Lorde blesse vs and saue vs, the Lorde make his face to shine vppon vs, and bee mercifull vnto vs: the Lord turne his fauourable countenance vnto vs, and graunte vs his peace.
author: Dering, Edward, 1540?-1576.
title: Godly priuate prayers for housholders to meditate vpon, and to say in their families

text: Cast out al hirelings, time seruers, & dumb dogs, which to fill their bellies only, haue thrust themselues among thy sheep, & do pitifully suffer the flock of Christ thy sonne, to be deuowred and scattered of the woolfe.
author: Dering, Edward, 1540?-1576.
title: Godly priuate prayers for housholders to meditate vpon, and to say in their families

text: Reueale not thy secretes to thy wife, nor to thy children: for women, and children, say all they know.
author: Dering, Edward, 1540?-1576.
title: Godly priuate prayers for housholders to meditate vpon, and to say in their families

text: And I know (O Lord God) that thou art true and iust, & canst not abide sinne and wickednesse, but wilt iustly punish euerie sinne, euen with the selfe same tormentes of hell whiche thy iustice hath appointed, euen for euery sinne.
author: Dering, Edward, 1540?-1576.
title: Godly priuate prayers for housholders to meditate vpon, and to say in their families

text: Defende her, O Lord, from all conspiracies, treasons, and rebellions, and so woorke in the hearts of all her Subiects, that knowing her authoritie doth come from thy Heauenly Maiestie, they may with obedient heartes humbly obey her in thee and for thee.
author: Dering, Edward, 1540?-1576.
title: Godly priuate prayers for housholders to meditate vpon, and to say in their families

text: Beholde the ende ere thou beginne, Haue mynde on death, and feare to sinne: For death shall reape that lyfe hath sovvne, And lyfe shall spring vvhere death hath movvne.
author: Dering, Edward, 1540?-1576.

text: Wherefore I thinke as I haue alreadie ſayd, that this departure out of Babylon, which is done both in body and ſoule, is the moſt ſure and happy.

text: I maruell what newe chriſtianitie ſuch men will bring vs, and to what ende they thinke Ieſus Chriſt hath ſayde: who ſo denyeth mee before men, I will denie him before my father & his angels.
author: Viret, Pierre, 1511-1571.
title: An epistle to the faithfull necessary for all the children of God: especially in the s[o] dangerous dayes. Written by Maister Peter Viret in french, and englished by F.H. Esquier.

text: We ſee by experience, that where the Prince or chiefe Magiſtrate fauoureth the profeſſion of the Goſpel, the moſt part wilbe Goſpellers.

title: An epistle to the faithfull necessary for all the children of God: especially in the s[o] dangerous dayes. Written by Maister Peter Viret in french, and englished by F.H. Esquier.

text: Wherefore departe from the middeſt of them, and ſeparate your ſelues from them, ſaith the Lord, and touch not any defiled thing, and I wil receaue you, and be your father, and you ſhall be my ſonnes and daughters.
author: Viret, Pierre, 1511-1571.
title: An epistle to the faithfull necessary for all the children of God: especially in the s[o] dangerous dayes. Written by Maister Peter Viret in french, and englished by F.H. Esquier.

text: Although the body be there, yet we conſent not in heart, and yet we auoyde offence and perſecution.

text: If it be not poſſible to ſerue God and riches, howe can we ſerue God and Idols, and the diuel in them?

text: Come out of Babylon, flee from the Chaldeans, depart ye, goe out from thence, touch no vncleane thing, goe out of the middeſt of her, be ye cleane, ye that beare the veſſels of the Lord, flye out from the middeſt of Babylon, and deliuer euery man his ſoule.
author: Viret, Pierre, 1511-1571.
title: An epistle to the faithfull necessary for all the children of God: especially in the s[o] dangerous dayes. Written by Maister Peter Viret in french, and englished by F.H. Esquier.

text: I knowe not howe wee maye ſpeake this more ciuilly, if we will not correct the ſpeech, which the ſpirit of GOD hath vttered by his Prophets, whiche commonly vſe theſe kinde of ſpeeches, when they preache agaynſt the Idolatrye of the chyldren of Iſraell.

text: But to you, whome the Lord hath ſeaſoned by a better ſpirit, then to profeſſe for faſhions ſake, let me ſpeake boldly without offence.

title: An epistle to the faithfull necessary for all the children of God: especially in the s[o] dangerous dayes. Written by Maister Peter Viret in french, and englished by F.H. Esquier.

text: The man that is borne vnder this ſign of Aquarius ſhalbe worſhipped, he ſhal be good and true, and wel beloued, & haue often headach, he ſhall haue a fall from riches, but he ſhal be happy in the weaſt countrey, and he ſhall be in perrill of water.
author: Moulton, Thomas.
title: The mirrour or glasse of health Necessary and needefull for euery person to looke in, that will keepe their bodye from the sickenesse of the pestylence, and it sheweth how the planets do reygne euery

text: Take the iuice of henbane & put it in to thyne eares and it wil take away the ach and ſlea the worms in them.
author: Moulton, Thomas.

text: Take fayre clere water, and boyle it well, and ſcum it, and put therin ſhiuers of browne bread, and let thē lie therin an houre, till the water be almoſt cold, and thē drink therof two or three dayes by dyuers times, and he ſhall amend in ſhorte time.
author: Moulton, Thomas.

text: The man that is borne vnder the ſign of Aries, by kind of complexyon is Chollorick, & ſhalbe witty and wyſe, and deceyueable, ſmall of bones, yellow of collour and kynd of heart.
author: Moulton, Thomas.
title: The mirrour or glasse of health Necessary and needefull for euery person to looke in, that will keepe their bodye from the sickenesse of the pestylence, and it sheweth how the planets do reygne euery

text: Alſo it were needefull to haue this water diſtilled of theſe herbs, of Detan of Scabious of Turmentill, of Vyolets, of Endiue, and Letiſe, and for to drinke theſe mingled wt whyte wytte of Gaſcan, or elſe of Rochell witte, and namely, the whilſt that vnkindly heate reigneth.
author: Moulton, Thomas.
title: The mirrour or glasse of health Necessary and needefull for euery person to looke in, that will keepe their bodye from the sickenesse of the pestylence, and it sheweth how the planets do reygne euery

text: Alſo keepe thee from haunting of lechery, for that both openeth the pores, and deſtroyeth the kynde naturall, and alſo enfeebleth the ſpirituall members, and the liuely ſpyrytes of man.
author: Moulton, Thomas.
title: The mirrour or glasse of health Necessary and needefull for euery person to looke in, that will keepe their bodye from the sickenesse of the pestylence, and it sheweth how the planets do reygne euery

text: Take an herbe that is called Mare clee in french, and frye it well in oyle Olife, and lay it to the ſtones that is ſo ſwolen, as hote as it may be ſuffred eyghte dayes, or more and neede bee, for this will heale the ſwelling.
author: Moulton, Thomas.
title: The mirrour or glasse of health Necessary and needefull for euery person to looke in, that will keepe their bodye from the sickenesse of the pestylence, and it sheweth how the planets do reygne euery

text: Take Mylfoyle, and Plantyne, of euerich a like much, ſtampe them well togither and keepe it, and whan thou wilt take thereof, and temper it with wyne, and let the pacient drink it, and he ſhalbe hole.
author: Moulton, Thomas.

text: Take and roſte Sorell in a wet linnen cloth, the ſpace of an halfe hower vnder the hote embers, & then ſtamp it with fyne clarified hony, and laye that to the ſore, and without doubt it will do away the brenning blacknes and ſtinck, and heale it perfectly.
author: Moulton, Thomas.

text: The which (my ſoueraigne Lorde) hath not beene either in cauſes or effects, more deepely or cleerelier ſeene by any other, then onely your Maiestie.
author: Henry IV, King of France, 1553-1610.
title: The declaration of the King of Nauarre touching the slaunders published against him in the protestations of those of the League that are rysen up in armes in this realme of Fraunce. With priuiledge. T

text: Here is the whole ſomme of al things, whereby the Kyng of Nauarre canne be blamed with theſe fayre tyrles of heretique, Relaps, perſecutor of the Church, enemie of the Catholiques, and diſturber of this eſtate.
author: Henry IV, King of France, 1553-1610.
title: The declaration of the King of Nauarre touching the slaunders published against him in the protestations of those of the League that are rysen up in armes in this realme of Fraunce. With priuiledge. T

text: It pleaſed King Charles, to cauſe the ſaid King of Nauarre repayre to his Coart, and to honour him with Marriage of his ſiſter.
author: Henry IV, King of France, 1553-1610.
title: The declaration of the King of Nauarre touching the slaunders published against him in the protestations of those of the League that are rysen up in armes in this realme of Fraunce. With priuiledge. T

text: To conclude, it wilbe founde that they haue encreaſed Simony in the Churche, and brought in the ſale of the temporalties for their owne profite, to be reuanged vppon their memies, vnder coulour of bereſſe.
author: Henry IV, King of France, 1553-1610.
title: The declaration of the King of Nauarre touching the slaunders published against him in the protestations of those of the League that are rysen up in armes in this realme of Fraunce. With priuiledge. T

text: And in the ſame haue gone about by all manner of ſlaunders, to bring me in ſuſpition with your Maiesty, into hatred with all orders and eſtates, and into the great miſliking of all Princes and nations of Chriſtendome.
author: Henry IV, King of France, 1553-1610.
title: The declaration of the King of Nauarre touching the slaunders published against him in the protestations of those of the League that are rysen up in armes in this realme of Fraunce. With priuiledge. T

text: Firſt therefore the ſaid king of Nauarre, proteſteth in his conſcience before God, that with all his hart, he deſireth and wiſheth proſperous and long life, to the King his ſoueraigne Lord, and neuer entred into any conceipt or opinion, to builde any deuiſe or purpoſe either vpon his death or after.
author: Henry IV, King of France, 1553-1610.
title: The declaration of the King of Nauarre touching the slaunders published against him in the protestations of those of the League that are rysen up in armes in this realme of Fraunce. With priuiledge. T

text: Gyuen at Bergerac the tenth day of Iune, in the yéere of our Lorde, a thouſand, fiue hundred, foureſcore and fyue.

text: If any offend theyr brethren, eyther by manifeſt adultery, or whoredome, or inceſt, or drunkennes, or much ſwearing, or baudry, or vſurie, or any other vncleanes and wickednes of life, let the churchwardens warne them brotherly and freendly, to amende.
author: Church of England.
title: A booke of certaine canons, concernyng some parte of the discipline of the Churche of England In the yeare of our Lord. 1571.

text: And no licence to preach, ſhall hereafter ſtande in force, but that which hath bene obtayned after the laſt day of Aprill, which was in the yeare, 1571.
author: Church of England.
title: A booke of certaine canons, concernyng some parte of the discipline of the Churche of England In the yeare of our Lord. 1571.

text: But they ſhall alwayes teach that, which may make for edifying, and may vnite the hearers in Chriſtian peace and loue.

text: Scholemaiſters ſhall teach no Grammer, but onely that, which the Queenes Maieſtie hath commaunded to be read in all Scholes, through the whole Realme, neyther any other Latine Catachiſme, then that which was ſette forth, in the yeare. 1570.
author: Church of England.
title: A booke of certaine canons, concernyng some parte of the discipline of the Churche of England In the yeare of our Lord. 1571.

text: But chiefly they ſhal ſo order and frame the tongues of children, that they may pronounce openly, plainly, and diſtinctly.

text: They ſhall ſuffer ringing onely at thoſe tymes, which are appoynted in the booke of aduertiſementes, and to that onely vſe, and after that onely order.
author: Church of England.
title: A booke of certaine canons, concernyng some parte of the discipline of the Churche of England In the yeare of our Lord. 1571.

text: And he beyng once admitted into the holy miniſtery, ſhall from thencefoorth neuer departe from it, nor ſhall vſe himſelfe as a laye man, eyther in apparell, or in any part of his lyfe.
author: Church of England.
title: A booke of certaine canons, concernyng some parte of the discipline of the Churche of England In the yeare of our Lord. 1571.

text: CHurchewardens according to the cuſtome of euery pariſhe, ſhalbe choſen by the conſent of theyr pariſhioners, and theyr miniſter: otherwiſe they ſhall not be churchwardens: neyther ſhall they continew any lenger then one yeare in that office, except perhaps they be choſen againe.
author: Church of England.
title: A booke of certaine canons, concernyng some parte of the discipline of the Churche of England In the yeare of our Lord. 1571.

text: None of theſe, neyther Chauncellor, Commiſſary nor Officiall ſhal proceede in examination of matters vnto the ſentence of excommunication, but onely in cauſes of inſtances.
author: Church of England.
title: A booke of certaine canons, concernyng some parte of the discipline of the Churche of England In the yeare of our Lord. 1571.

text: Pirrhus play, which he inuented in Creete for the souldiours to exercise themselues in Armes, wherein he taught diuers iestures, and sundry shyfts in mouings, whence first proceeded much the vse of warres, was a kinde of dauncing in Armes, as Dionisius Halicarnassaeus in his 7. booke testifieth.

title: Politeuphuia VVits common wealth.

text: The worlde in the foure ages thereof, may bee compared vnto the foure seasons of the yeere; the first resembling the spring-tyme, the second, sommer, the third, autumne, and the fourth, winter.
author: N. L. (Nicholas Ling), fl. 1580-1607.
title: Politeuphuia VVits common wealth.

text: Some new heads I haue inserted, corrected many where I found it necessary, and almost euery one in some sort augmented.
author: N. L. (Nicholas Ling), fl. 1580-1607.
title: Politeuphuia VVits common wealth.

text: As it is not necessary to credite the oath of an infidell, so it is not lawfull for a Christian to breake his vowe, although it bee made to a Sarazine.
author: N. L. (Nicholas Ling), fl. 1580-1607.
title: Politeuphuia VVits common wealth.

text: Clisthenes King of Sicyon, hauing a daughter marrigeable, commaunded that it should bee proclaimed at the games of Olympus, that he that would bee counted Clisthenes son in lawe, shoulde within threescore dayes repaire to Sicyon.
author: N. L. (Nicholas Ling), fl. 1580-1607.
title: Politeuphuia VVits common wealth.

text: All thinges are resolued into those thinges whereof they are compounded, the body of man being earth, shall returne to earth, and the soule beeing immortall, shall enter into immortality.
author: N. L. (Nicholas Ling), fl. 1580-1607.
title: Politeuphuia VVits common wealth.

text: All worldly gladnes rideth vppon the wings of Time, and but in heauen, no perfect ioy is found.
author: N. L. (Nicholas Ling), fl. 1580-1607.
title: Politeuphuia VVits common wealth.

text: The difference betweene an old man and a young man is thys; the one is follovved as a friend to others, the other is eschewed as an enemy to himselfe.
author: N. L. (Nicholas Ling), fl. 1580-1607.
title: Politeuphuia VVits common wealth.

text: Haunt not too much thy friends house, for that ingendereth no great loue, neyther bee thou long frō thence, for that begetteth hate, but vse a meane in all things.
author: N. L. (Nicholas Ling), fl. 1580-1607.
title: Politeuphuia VVits common wealth.

text: For the Grecians, as, many of them haue wise men in litle reuerence, so they accompt their precepts méere contemptible: notwithstanding (to say the trueth) they bée such, as lack neither learning nor grauitie.

text: I would to God my fortune had béene so happie: then had not he béene so combersome vnto vs. But it was your déede, ful of manhood and prówesse: in which, for so muche as it is past, I woulde I were able to giue you any counsell.

text: Beware ye neuer entermedle with this herbe, without the aduyſement and coūceyll of ſome experte and well learned Phyſycyon.
author: Arnaldus, de Villanova, d. 1311.
title: Here is a newe boke, called the defence of age, and recouery of youth, translated out of the famous clarke and ryght experte medycyne Arnold de Noua Uilla, very profytable for all men to knowe

text: The naturall hete then & the meate cōmyng to the membres beyng decayed or corrupted, which cōmeth of putryfyed colour, furthwith enſueth corrugacyon, and olde lokynge as ye may ſe in ſuch as are ſcaby, in any parte of theyr body, for that parte beynge enfected, it ſemeth ryuyled and olde ſkynne.
author: Arnaldus, de Villanova, d. 1311.
title: Here is a newe boke, called the defence of age, and recouery of youth, translated out of the famous clarke and ryght experte medycyne Arnold de Noua Uilla, very profytable for all men to knowe

text: And for the preſeruacyō of the powres, is no better thynge then a ſyrupe made of wyne and ſuger, myxte togyther. iii. partes of wyne, &. ii. partes of ſuger dronke with fayre water, or borage water.
author: Arnaldus, de Villanova, d. 1311.
title: Here is a newe boke, called the defence of age, and recouery of youth, translated out of the famous clarke and ryght experte medycyne Arnold de Noua Uilla, very profytable for all men to knowe

text: Theſe thynges may be amended with thus, earynge of chekyns, and chekyn broth, with due reſt and ſlepe, and alſo with ſwete and odoryferous thynges, and ſuche other lyke.
author: Arnaldus, de Villanova, d. 1311.
title: Here is a newe boke, called the defence of age, and recouery of youth, translated out of the famous clarke and ryght experte medycyne Arnold de Noua Uilla, very profytable for all men to knowe

text: It cōforteth the herte, and clenſeth it, and to ſpeke of the prayſe of this medycyne wolde requyre a longe proceſſe.
author: Arnaldus, de Villanova, d. 1311.
title: Here is a newe boke, called the defence of age, and recouery of youth, translated out of the famous clarke and ryght experte medycyne Arnold de Noua Uilla, very profytable for all men to knowe

text: And the fore ſayd ſpyced wyne, when it is receyued of man, it ſpredeth it ſelfe abrode in ye partes of the body and comforteth all the partes of the body, and dryeth vp the ſuperfluous humydyties of the body, alſo the powder of the ſame ſpyces vſed with meate, profyteth wonderfully.
author: Arnaldus, de Villanova, d. 1311.
title: Here is a newe boke, called the defence of age, and recouery of youth, translated out of the famous clarke and ryght experte medycyne Arnold de Noua Uilla, very profytable for all men to knowe

text: But amonge all other thyngꝭ there is nothynge, the which ſo ſtrongly doth cauſe a man to loke oldely, as feare and deſperacion.
author: Arnaldus, de Villanova, d. 1311.
title: Here is a newe boke, called the defence of age, and recouery of youth, translated out of the famous clarke and ryght experte medycyne Arnold de Noua Uilla, very profytable for all men to knowe

text: THe cōſeruaciō of youth and withſtandyng of age, conſyſteth in the mayntenynge of the powres, the ſpyrites, & the naturall heate of the body in theyr ſtate and temperancy: & in the cōfortyng and repayrynge of theym beynge defertyue.
author: Arnaldus, de Villanova, d. 1311.
title: Here is a newe boke, called the defence of age, and recouery of youth, translated out of the famous clarke and ryght experte medycyne Arnold de Noua Uilla, very profytable for all men to knowe

text: Sall twiſe ilk zeir, at the feaſt of Whitſunday and Martimes, make ane roll of all Evidents, preſented and marked be him, the halfe zeir preceeding, and ſall affix the ſame on ſome publick place of the towne quhair he remaines, that the ſame may come to al parties knawledge.
author: Scotland.
title: Ane acte anent the registring of saisings, reversiones, and some vther writtes, for the better tryall o[f] the falsettis daylie invented and occurring within this realme

text: And the ſaidis regiſters, after the filling of the ſame, to be reported to the ſaid Secretare, to remayne with him, and be patent to all our Soveraine Lords lieges, that fall haue a-doe with the ſame.
author: Scotland.
title: Ane acte anent the registring of saisings, reversiones, and some vther writtes, for the better tryall o[f] the falsettis daylie invented and occurring within this realme

text: And to the effect the ſaid office may preſently, & in al time cumming, be the mair faithfully miniſtrat: STATVTES & ordaines, the ſame to be annext & incorporat with the office of Secretarie.
author: Scotland.
title: Ane acte anent the registring of saisings, reversiones, and some vther writtes, for the better tryall o[f] the falsettis daylie invented and occurring within this realme

text: Ane in the Burgh of Dundie, for the Schireffedome of Forfare: Ane in the Burgh of Perth, for the Schireffedome of Perth, and Stewartrie of Stratherne: Exceptand the Stewartrie of Menteith.
author: Scotland.
title: Ane acte anent the registring of saisings, reversiones, and some vther writtes, for the better tryall o[f] the falsettis daylie invented and occurring within this realme

text: Ane in the Burgh of Innernes, for the Schireffedomes of Innernes and Cromartie: Ane in the Burgh of Elgin, for the Schireffedomes of Elgin, Forres, and Narne: Ane in the Burgh of Abirdene, for the Schireffdoms of Abirdene, Banff, and Kincardin.
author: Scotland.
title: Ane acte anent the registring of saisings, reversiones, and some vther writtes, for the better tryall o[f] the falsettis daylie invented and occurring within this realme

text: And the ſaids Regiſters, for the greater eaſe of the Lieges, to be eſtabliſhed in the particular places following: That is to ſay, Ane in the towne of Kirkwall in Orknay, for the haill inhabitants and Lands, lyand within the Schireffedome of Orknay and Zetland.
author: Scotland.
title: Ane acte anent the registring of saisings, reversiones, and some vther writtes, for the better tryall o[f] the falsettis daylie invented and occurring within this realme

text: As for the price of ilk leafe of his Regiſter, written on baith the ſids: And according thereto, ſal tak proportionally, for regiſtring of every ane of the ſaids Evidents.
author: Scotland.
title: Ane acte anent the registring of saisings, reversiones, and some vther writtes, for the better tryall o[f] the falsettis daylie invented and occurring within this realme

text: And the ſaids regiſters to be filled be the ſaids deputes, to be marked be the Secretare or his deputes, to be appoynted be him to that effect, with ane note of the particular number of the leaues, that the ſame ſall conteine.
author: Scotland.
title: Ane acte anent the registring of saisings, reversiones, and some vther writtes, for the better tryall o[f] the falsettis daylie invented and occurring within this realme

text: And the ſaids evidents to be regiſtrat in the particular buikes, appoynted for ilk Schireffedome, as ſaid is.
author: Scotland.
title: Ane acte anent the registring of saisings, reversiones, and some vther writtes, for the better tryall o[f] the falsettis daylie invented and occurring within this realme

text: In reading it thou mayst likewise remember, That great Cyty called Sodom and Gommor: To be in great perill to sinke without succour, Which wil not God alone in fear & faith honor.
author: I. A.
title: The great wonders that are chaunced in the realme of Naples with a great misfortune happened at Rome and in other places, by an earth quake in the moneth of December last past. Translated out of Frenc

text: Whereof did come that God, his wrath did still restrayne: Repent therefore in tyme I say, so mayst thou styll remayne.
author: I. A.
title: The great wonders that are chaunced in the realme of Naples with a great misfortune happened at Rome and in other places, by an earth quake in the moneth of December last past. Translated out of Frenc

text: Amend my country still, I thée desire and pray: For I a member of thy state, were loth thou shouldst decay.
author: I. A.
title: The great wonders that are chaunced in the realme of Naples with a great misfortune happened at Rome and in other places, by an earth quake in the moneth of December last past. Translated out of Frenc

text: Before long haire she hath, behinde she quite is polde: Put to thy hande, and of her lockes, sée that thou take good holde.
author: I. A.
title: The great wonders that are chaunced in the realme of Naples with a great misfortune happened at Rome and in other places, by an earth quake in the moneth of December last past. Translated out of Frenc

text: Beholde thy louing Lorde, his sworde is in his hande: Thée to the earth to fling in yre what can his force withstande: Can mighty gates of brasse, can Castels strongly builte: His force withstande? his very breath, these Castels quite hath spilte.
author: I. A.
title: The great wonders that are chaunced in the realme of Naples with a great misfortune happened at Rome and in other places, by an earth quake in the moneth of December last past. Translated out of Frenc

text: Beholde what noble things are come to ruine great: When fruites are rype, thou well doest know, then are they pluct to eate: The sinne is very rype, the bankes doe ouer flowe: The tyme wyll come when thou shalt be, like these be brought as lowe.
author: I. A.
title: The great wonders that are chaunced in the realme of Naples with a great misfortune happened at Rome and in other places, by an earth quake in the moneth of December last past. Translated out of Frenc

text: For thus he playne doth say, when sinners shall relente: And turne from sinne, I euen then lykewise my selfe repente.
author: I. A.
title: The great wonders that are chaunced in the realme of Naples with a great misfortune happened at Rome and in other places, by an earth quake in the moneth of December last past. Translated out of Frenc

text: Of all the plagues which I vpon them thought to bring: Lo here the mercy great I say, of our most heauenly king: Their sinnes Ill quite forgette, if they will turne to me: I will remember them no more, though thousandes that there be.
author: I. A.
title: The great wonders that are chaunced in the realme of Naples with a great misfortune happened at Rome and in other places, by an earth quake in the moneth of December last past. Translated out of Frenc

text: The Ryuer of Tiber was séene couered with suche a quantity of dead fyshes, that they thinke not so many to be left lyuing in the sayd Riuer, as there was sene deade.
author: I. A.
title: The great wonders that are chaunced in the realme of Naples with a great misfortune happened at Rome and in other places, by an earth quake in the moneth of December last past. Translated out of Frenc

text: THe ryche peraduenture oppreſſeth nowe and than, The pore man in dede: but who is cauſe of this?
author: Bieston, Roger.
title: The bayte [and] snare of fortune Wherin may be seen that money is not the only cause of mischefe and vnfortunat endes: but a necessary mean to mayntayne a vertuous quiet lyfe. Treated in a dialoge bet

text: For Auarice of the owne nature is vnſaciable, accordyng to the ſaying of the Sage in the fift Chapter of Eccleſiaſtes.
author: Bieston, Roger.
title: The bayte [and] snare of fortune Wherin may be seen that money is not the only cause of mischefe and vnfortunat endes: but a necessary mean to mayntayne a vertuous quiet lyfe. Treated in a dialoge bet

text: SAynt Paule Doctor of veritie, ſayeth that Auarice is the Roote and beginnyng of all euylles: Algates the men of this tyme preſent, be therto much enclined.
author: Bieston, Roger.
title: The bayte [and] snare of fortune Wherin may be seen that money is not the only cause of mischefe and vnfortunat endes: but a necessary mean to mayntayne a vertuous quiet lyfe. Treated in a dialoge bet

text: But noble wiſemen that reaſon haue in ſtore With connyng and conſcience, and caſt for no colluſion By theſe is Iuſtice exalted evermore.
author: Bieston, Roger.
title: The bayte [and] snare of fortune Wherin may be seen that money is not the only cause of mischefe and vnfortunat endes: but a necessary mean to mayntayne a vertuous quiet lyfe. Treated in a dialoge bet

text: I am the poſt and piller vnto all Adams ſeede, The father of the faith ſumtime is made by me, The Pope I meane, Gods vicar, and captaine of his crede, Great Emperours and Kinges I crowne in mageſtie, Duke, Marquiſe, earle, baron, and Lordes of eche degree.
author: Bieston, Roger.
title: The bayte [and] snare of fortune Wherin may be seen that money is not the only cause of mischefe and vnfortunat endes: but a necessary mean to mayntayne a vertuous quiet lyfe. Treated in a dialoge bet

text: That man cannot be ſaued from endles paine Without thy fauour, thine aide and amitie, Wherin I ſay no reaſon doeth remaine: Full many a ſoule (more pitie it is certaine) Is damned by thee to euerlaſting fire.
author: Bieston, Roger.
title: The bayte [and] snare of fortune Wherin may be seen that money is not the only cause of mischefe and vnfortunat endes: but a necessary mean to mayntayne a vertuous quiet lyfe. Treated in a dialoge bet

text: Grace and good maners for thee he doeth auoyde: No reaſon can be layed to this, nor replication.
author: Bieston, Roger.
title: The bayte [and] snare of fortune Wherin may be seen that money is not the only cause of mischefe and vnfortunat endes: but a necessary mean to mayntayne a vertuous quiet lyfe. Treated in a dialoge bet

text: But ſith he cannot be content with meaſure, Much trauaile and payne behoueth it him to take Pennies to purchaſe with riche ſubſtaunce and treaſure.
author: Bieston, Roger.
title: The bayte [and] snare of fortune Wherin may be seen that money is not the only cause of mischefe and vnfortunat endes: but a necessary mean to mayntayne a vertuous quiet lyfe. Treated in a dialoge bet

text: But baratours and brayneles brybours met in fere, Theyr maker they diſmember, and on his name they wunder, At table, at tauerne, at churche, and euery where: Great horror is to hear, howe they rent hym aſunder.
author: Bieston, Roger.
title: The bayte [and] snare of fortune Wherin may be seen that money is not the only cause of mischefe and vnfortunat endes: but a necessary mean to mayntayne a vertuous quiet lyfe. Treated in a dialoge bet

text: If we cal theſe to mynd, and caſt of them into our cuppe (conſyderyng what he was, what he ſuffred, of whom, for whom, to what ende, and what came ther of) ſurely we cannot lothe oure medicine, but wynke and drynke it luſtely.
author: Bradford, John, 1510?-1555.
title: An exhortacion to the carienge of Chrystes crosse wyth a true and brefe confutacion of false and papisticall doctryne.

text: But, I trow they wil not ſuffer the laie men, to ſay maſſe another whyle now for them.
author: Bradford, John, 1510?-1555.
title: An exhortacion to the carienge of Chrystes crosse wyth a true and brefe confutacion of false and papisticall doctryne.

text: As for ye victorye geuen to ye Quenes hyghnes, yf mē had ani godli wit, thei might ſe many thynges in it.
author: Bradford, John, 1510?-1555.
title: An exhortacion to the carienge of Chrystes crosse wyth a true and brefe confutacion of false and papisticall doctryne.

text: And thus much for you ſecondlye to conſyder, that afflyccion, perſecucion and trouble is no ſtraūge thyng to gods children: and therfore it ſhoulde not diſmaye, dyſcourage or diſcomfort vs, beyng none other thyng, then al godes deare frēdes haue taſted in their iourney to heauen warde.
author: Bradford, John, 1510?-1555.
title: An exhortacion to the carienge of Chrystes crosse wyth a true and brefe confutacion of false and papisticall doctryne.

text: So very oftē doth he deliuer vs by ſuche meanes, as haue bene thought moſt folyſh and litle to be regarded.
author: Bradford, John, 1510?-1555.
title: An exhortacion to the carienge of Chrystes crosse wyth a true and brefe confutacion of false and papisticall doctryne.

text: The other ſayth: he is our aduocate, that is, a ſpokeſman, cō forter, interceſſor, and mediator.
author: Bradford, John, 1510?-1555.
title: An exhortacion to the carienge of Chrystes crosse wyth a true and brefe confutacion of false and papisticall doctryne.

text: Commodities of the croſſe, ioyne thys thirde, of gods ſyngular wyſdome: that it may be coupled with his iuſtice and mercy.
author: Bradford, John, 1510?-1555.
title: An exhortacion to the carienge of Chrystes crosse wyth a true and brefe confutacion of false and papisticall doctryne.

text: Now, dearly beloued, the wicked world reioyceth: the papiſts are puft vp agaynſt poore chriſt and his people, after their olde kynde: now crye they: where are theſe newe founde preachers?
author: Bradford, John, 1510?-1555.
title: An exhortacion to the carienge of Chrystes crosse wyth a true and brefe confutacion of false and papisticall doctryne.

text: Now what we are god knoweth, and all the worlde ſeeth: more mete a great deale to haue the deuils decrees, then gods religion, ſo great is our contempte in it.
author: Bradford, John, 1510?-1555.
title: An exhortacion to the carienge of Chrystes crosse wyth a true and brefe confutacion of false and papisticall doctryne.

text: I set my shéeld betwéene him and his foes, and him bestrid: And savde the dastards lyfe. small prayse redoundes of that I did.
author: Ovid, 43 B.C.-17 or 18 A.D.
title: The. xv. bookes of P. Ouidius Naso, entytuled Metamorphosis, translated oute of Latin into English meeter, by Arthur Golding Gentleman, a worke very pleasaunt and delectable. 1567.

text: O dearer vnto mée Than is my selfe, my soule I say, stay: lawfull we it sée For valiant men to kéepe aloofe.
author: Ovid, 43 B.C.-17 or 18 A.D.
title: The. xv. bookes of P. Ouidius Naso, entytuled Metamorphosis, translated oute of Latin into English meeter, by Arthur Golding Gentleman, a worke very pleasaunt and delectable. 1567.

text: He also is reported too haue heawen in wicked wyse The groue of Ceres, and to fell her holy woods which ay Had vndiminisht and vnhackt continewed to that day There stood in it a warrie Oke which was a wood alone.
author: Ovid, 43 B.C.-17 or 18 A.D.
title: The. xv. bookes of P. Ouidius Naso, entytuled Metamorphosis, translated oute of Latin into English meeter, by Arthur Golding Gentleman, a worke very pleasaunt and delectable. 1567.

text: The day would end, And Phebus panting stéedes should in the Ocean déepe descend, Before all alterations I in woordes could comprehend.
author: Ovid, 43 B.C.-17 or 18 A.D.

text: And to pray and thynke not, is but in vayne The Godly prophet herein agreeth wt me All theſe are dyſhonour to Gods holy name.

text: There ſhall be no waylyng, nor cryenge, nor ſorowe any more: Yea there is no ioy or comfort, that can be wiſhed for, but it is there moſt plentifully.

text: This is the very honour and duetie, whiche not onely the chyldren do owe vnto theyr parentes, but alſo all ſubiectes & inferiours, to theyr heades and rulers.

text: It ſygnifieth alſo, that we muſt obey vnto his wyll, as well in al our inwarde thoughtes and affections, as alſo in al our outwarde actes and dedes, and that we muſt abhorre all vyce, and not wiſhe or deſyre of god, any euyll or vngodly thing.

text: For as ſaint Barnarde ſayth: Lyke as the backebiter caryeth the deuyll in his mouthe: ſo the hearer carieth the deuyll in his eare.

text: And generally all euyll chriſten men, which profeſſe the name of Chriſte, and liue not accordynge to their profeſſion, do alſo take the name of god in vayne, in wordes confeſſynge Chriſte, and denyinge hym in deedes.

text: For as god can not be tempted to euyll, ſo he tempteth no man to euyll, but euerye man is tempted drawen, and allured by his owne concupiſcence: than concupiſcence whan ſhe hath conceyued, bringeth furth ſynne.

text: That this muſte nedes be graunted: that there is not ſo greate ſinne in thys kinde of vſurie, as in that, by the which vſurie is taken of the pore, which crueltie is forbidden, not onely, by the lawes of Chriſte, but alſoo by the lawes of nature.

text: On the other ſide, he that taketh vſurie of his monei: he gathereth as it were a yearelye fruite, without any dekey of the ſtock, which bi theſe meās he mai reſerue hole vnto his heires.
author: Musculus, Wolfgang, 1497-1563.

text: For we ſeke not our owne, but the profet of others, widowes & fatherles: and ſo we fulfil the worke of charite, and we do as we are bonden by promes vnto them.
