text: Yet I my selfe with al my hart doo dayne, To reue thy life, and cause thee to complayne.
author: Blenerhasset, Thomas.
title: The seconde part of the Mirrour for magistrates conteining the falles of the infortunate princes of this lande, from the conquest of Cæsar, vnto the commyng of Duke William the Conquerour.

text: Which when the wrathful Duke once vnderstoode, He raysde my Realme, and by his myght and powre I lost my lyfe, my Crowne, and Princely bowre.
author: Blenerhasset, Thomas.
title: The seconde part of the Mirrour for magistrates conteining the falles of the infortunate princes of this lande, from the conquest of Cæsar, vnto the commyng of Duke William the Conquerour.

text: Geue leaue therefore good Memory, I may Not here repeate my tedious Tragedy, Inquiry, let me nowe departe away.
author: Blenerhasset, Thomas.
title: The seconde part of the Mirrour for magistrates conteining the falles of the infortunate princes of this lande, from the conquest of Cæsar, vnto the commyng of Duke William the Conquerour.

text: O Fancye fonde, thy fuminges hath mee fed, The stinking stinch of thyne inclined hest, Hath poysoned al the vertues in my brest.
author: Blenerhasset, Thomas.
title: The seconde part of the Mirrour for magistrates conteining the falles of the infortunate princes of this lande, from the conquest of Cæsar, vnto the commyng of Duke William the Conquerour.

text: And wil you not you wretched wightes assent To helpe me here to tell that drierie tale, Which may amongst men liuing much preuayle?
author: Blenerhasset, Thomas.
title: The seconde part of the Mirrour for magistrates conteining the falles of the infortunate princes of this lande, from the conquest of Cæsar, vnto the commyng of Duke William the Conquerour.

text: Me thought I could winne al the worlde in haste, But fyrst I ment the Romane state to waste.
author: Blenerhasset, Thomas.
title: The seconde part of the Mirrour for magistrates conteining the falles of the infortunate princes of this lande, from the conquest of Cæsar, vnto the commyng of Duke William the Conquerour.

text: My deedes at home, inrichte me with renowne, My talke abroade, with proper filed phrase, Adornde my head euen with a Laurell crowne.
author: Blenerhasset, Thomas.
title: The seconde part of the Mirrour for magistrates conteining the falles of the infortunate princes of this lande, from the conquest of Cæsar, vnto the commyng of Duke William the Conquerour.

text: So I in vaine who had the victorie, Within fewe dayes was forst againe to fight, My strength halfe spoylde, the rest wounded and wearie, His campe was comne vnwares within my sight, There was no hope to flee by day nor night.
author: Blenerhasset, Thomas.
title: The seconde part of the Mirrour for magistrates conteining the falles of the infortunate princes of this lande, from the conquest of Cæsar, vnto the commyng of Duke William the Conquerour.

text: Looke backe (I say) confesse it is much better, To hide a lesser sinne doe not a greater.
author: Sabie, Francis.
title: Adams complaint. The olde vvorldes tragedie. Dauid and Bathsheba

text: He saw how vice had growne vnto a head, Injustice all the earth had ouerspread: He saw how sinne and vile impietie Vanted themselues against his Deitie.
author: Sabie, Francis.
title: Adams complaint. The olde vvorldes tragedie. Dauid and Bathsheba

text: But thou (O Sathan) proud infernall deuill, Chiefe actor in this dolefull tragedie: Lord of ambition, maister of all euill, Thy fatall fall behold I prophecie: From out the woman shall an issue spring, VVhich will preuayle against thy deadly sting.
author: Sabie, Francis.
title: Adams complaint. The olde vvorldes tragedie. Dauid and Bathsheba

text: Most lothsome be thou of Iehouahs worke, Enuyed both of man and feeding cattell: In vnfrequented valleyes shalt thou lurke, And with thy stinging tongue still menace battell.
author: Sabie, Francis.
title: Adams complaint. The olde vvorldes tragedie. Dauid and Bathsheba

text: Alas, no sooner night-expelling morning, Al.-hyding heauen from her blacke rug exempteth: But viewing me, and mine offences scorning, Her snowie cheekes with rednes she besprenteth, Disdaining Sols bright beams should long behold me In Sable night bright Hesperus doth fold me.
author: Sabie, Francis.
title: Adams complaint. The olde vvorldes tragedie. Dauid and Bathsheba

text: This sayd; he turn'd him to the vntill'd field, VVhere vncoth weeds, and fruitlesse brambles breed, The earth which earst most fragrant hearbs did yeeld, VVith thornes and thistles now was ouer-spread.
author: Sabie, Francis.
title: Adams complaint. The olde vvorldes tragedie. Dauid and Bathsheba

text: Now shall rush in the fiery thirst of gaine, And golde in bowels of the earth inclosed: Which men by toyle and labour will obtaine, And coffer vp from his darke dungeon losed.
author: Sabie, Francis.
title: Adams complaint. The olde vvorldes tragedie. Dauid and Bathsheba

text: Learne heer (O all posterities) the shrewdnesse Of Sathan, and his treacherous assaultes: VVho hauing once seduced man to lewdnesse, Exaggerates the greatnesse of his faults, Making him blush like Adam in the garden.
author: Sabie, Francis.
title: Adams complaint. The olde vvorldes tragedie. Dauid and Bathsheba

text: Ah no, ye cannot, his all-seeing eie VVill find you out, where euer you doe lie.
author: Sabie, Francis.
title: Adams complaint. The olde vvorldes tragedie. Dauid and Bathsheba

text: And thus the herte whiche was thappalaunte Out of his tente yssues ryght manly Whiche bare as he that was ryght valeaunt A spere heed with sorowe sekerly The eye from his pauylyon by and by Yssued also in his hande a launce The whiche he gyded full gentylmanly Herte & eye.
author: Map, Walter, fl. 1200.
title: Here begynneth a lytel treatyse called the dysputacyon or co[m]playnt of the herte thorughe perced with the lokynge of the eye

text: Than the eye whiche hym gretly applyed To fynde matere to his saluacyons With ryght goodly aduyse anone replyed Unto the hertes composycyons And sayd I se well by his accyons That he hath ben at scole I trowe of loue Whiche bryngeth forth plesaunte Intencyon Hymselfe further for his owne behoue.
author: Map, Walter, fl. 1200.
title: Here begynneth a lytel treatyse called the dysputacyon or co[m]playnt of the herte thorughe perced with the lokynge of the eye

text: The day and the houre aboue sayd Whan the herte sholde fyght ayenst the eye Loue came hym selfe with his wynges dysplayd Dyscendynge downe of his scafolde trewely And in his chayre he sat downe softely A robe on hym embrodered with rych stones And fyne perles sette full craftely Browderede of emeraudes for the nones.
author: Map, Walter, fl. 1200.
title: Here begynneth a lytel treatyse called the dysputacyon or co[m]playnt of the herte thorughe perced with the lokynge of the eye

text: For whiche I made to blowe hornes hye And houndes syxe score and mo certayne Whiche made me thought a Ioyous melodye.
author: Map, Walter, fl. 1200.
title: Here begynneth a lytel treatyse called the dysputacyon or co[m]playnt of the herte thorughe perced with the lokynge of the eye

text: Wherfore I complayne me thus ryghtfully Of grete iniurye that the eye hath done And my cause is mente moost faythfully Wherfore to you I do submyssyon And on my trouth I make promyssyon To fyght with hym in loues hygh presence Byfore the whiche we shall knowe soone The ryght fro wronge without more dyffence.
author: Map, Walter, fl. 1200.
title: Here begynneth a lytel treatyse called the dysputacyon or co[m]playnt of the herte thorughe perced with the lokynge of the eye

text: Her lady venus of loue goddesse With a sote salue she dyde her presente And sayd madame to your hygh noblenesse Are come these two knyghtes of grete prowess.
author: Map, Walter, fl. 1200.
title: Here begynneth a lytel treatyse called the dysputacyon or co[m]playnt of the herte thorughe perced with the lokynge of the eye

text: The herte and the eye to knowe your entente Whome loue hath drede and with humblenesse Now at this tyme by me to you hath sente.
author: Map, Walter, fl. 1200.
title: Here begynneth a lytel treatyse called the dysputacyon or co[m]playnt of the herte thorughe perced with the lokynge of the eye

text: He had also a bowe of vnycorne And two strynges made of grete substaunce Of golde of cypresse at eche ende A shefe of arowes set in ordenaunce To teche the louers his trace to daunce Federed with fyne rubyes bryght and shene Whiche gaue hym for a grete pleasaunce Poynted with dyamondes sharpe and kene.
author: Map, Walter, fl. 1200.
title: Here begynneth a lytel treatyse called the dysputacyon or co[m]playnt of the herte thorughe perced with the lokynge of the eye

text: In whose companye came honoure also Hardynesse / prowesse / and eke gentylnesse Thought and good hope and many other mo That were of his alyaunce as I gesse All clothed lyke for theyr worthynesse With roses reed and also with lylyes whyte Chapelettes they had eke for theyr noblenesse Of lauendre a floure of grete delyte.
author: Map, Walter, fl. 1200.
title: Here begynneth a lytel treatyse called the dysputacyon or co[m]playnt of the herte thorughe perced with the lokynge of the eye

text: Say me Reinald Greene-leafe Wilt thou dwell with me, and euery yeare I will thee giue twenty marke to thy fee.
title: A merry iest of Robin Hood and of his life, vvith a newe play for to be plaied in May-games. Very pleasant and full of pastime.

text: Nay for God ſaid the Monk Me rueth I came ſo neere For better chepe I might haue dined in Blithe or Dancaſter.
title: A merry iest of Robin Hood and of his life, vvith a newe play for to be plaied in May-games. Very pleasant and full of pastime.

text: Sir Roger of Dancaſtre by the prioreſſe he lay, And there they betrayed Robin hood through their falſe play: Chriſt haue mercy on his ſoule that died on the rood, For he was a good outlaw and did poore men much good.
title: A merry iest of Robin Hood and of his life, vvith a newe play for to be plaied in May-games. Very pleasant and full of pastime.

text: Then was there a faire Caſtle a little within the wood, double ditched it was about, and walled by the Rood: And there dwelt that gentle Knight ſir Richard of the Lee that Robin had lent his good vnder the greene wood tree.
title: A merry iest of Robin Hood and of his life, vvith a newe play for to be plaied in May-games. Very pleasant and full of pastime.

text: Sith you will not dine ſaid little Iohn I ſhall giue you to drinke: and thogh you liue this hundreth winter on little Iohn ſhall ye thinke: Little Iohn eat and alſo drunke the while that he would: the Sheriffe had in the kitchin a Cooke a ſtout man and a bold.
title: A merry iest of Robin Hood and of his life, vvith a newe play for to be plaied in May-games. Very pleasant and full of pastime.

text: Then beſpake good Robin hood, to dine I haue no luſt till I haue ſome bould Baron or ſome vnketh geſt that may pay for the beſt Or ſome Knight, or ſome Squire that dwelleth heere by weſt.
title: A merry iest of Robin Hood and of his life, vvith a newe play for to be plaied in May-games. Very pleasant and full of pastime.

text: Blowe on ragged knaue without any doubt, vntill both thine eyes ſtart out: Heere is a ſorte of ragged knaues come in Clothed all in kendall greene and to thee they take their way now.
title: A merry iest of Robin Hood and of his life, vvith a newe play for to be plaied in May-games. Very pleasant and full of pastime.

text: There the king was wont to ſee heards many a one, He could vnneth finde any Deere that bare any good horne. the King was wonder wroth withall and ſwore by the Trinitie, I would I had Robin hood with eyes I might him ſee.
title: A merry iest of Robin Hood and of his life, vvith a newe play for to be plaied in May-games. Very pleasant and full of pastime.

text: Mercy then ſaid Robin to our King vnder this truſly tree, Of thy goodnes and thy grace for my men and for mee.
title: A merry iest of Robin Hood and of his life, vvith a newe play for to be plaied in May-games. Very pleasant and full of pastime.

text: Whan I wryte of theyr order and begynnynge, and beholde them now, yf in my mynde I conpare them together that were than and be now, my thynke I wryte of Chriſte and take the deuell for an enſample, and make hym a brother of Chriſtes couente.
author: Coverdale, Miles, 1488-1568, attributed name.
title: The original [and] sprynge of all sectes [and] orders by whome, wha or were they beganne. Translated out of hye Dutch in Englysh.

text: The begynnyng was of thys maner: Amonge thē of Albania roſe a peſtilent hereſy, which cauſed a great diſſenſion amonge them of Rome.
author: Coverdale, Miles, 1488-1568, attributed name.
title: The original [and] sprynge of all sectes [and] orders by whome, wha or were they beganne. Translated out of hye Dutch in Englysh.

text: By thys commeth it that many folyſh Iewes drynke no wyne, counterfaytynge other therin, as we alſo playe the apes in oure orders: yee lyke Manaſſes dyd counterfayte Abraham in offrynge vp of hys chylde.
author: Coverdale, Miles, 1488-1568, attributed name.
title: The original [and] sprynge of all sectes [and] orders by whome, wha or were they beganne. Translated out of hye Dutch in Englysh.

text: The Abbeſſe ſhulde haue the primacy on S. Brydes behalfe, & ye brethren to be vnder her: ſo yt ſhe ſhuld prouyde both man & womā meate, drynke & clothyng Amōge the brethrē ſhulde one be called Prior, warden or Cōfeſſoure, and be aboue ye other.
author: Coverdale, Miles, 1488-1568, attributed name.
title: The original [and] sprynge of all sectes [and] orders by whome, wha or were they beganne. Translated out of hye Dutch in Englysh.

text: Such as force not whether they are ſene or not, or haue not dreth ynough, they draw downe the cole from theyr heades, & ſcourge thēſelfes ſo openly.
author: Coverdale, Miles, 1488-1568, attributed name.
title: The original [and] sprynge of all sectes [and] orders by whome, wha or were they beganne. Translated out of hye Dutch in Englysh.

text: To be ſhorte and playne for thyne vnerſtandynge: Ionadab a ſonne of Rechab commaunded hys chylderen neuerto drynke wyne, buylde no houſes, ſowe no feldes, plante no vynes, but only to dwell in tentes.
author: Coverdale, Miles, 1488-1568, attributed name.
title: The original [and] sprynge of all sectes [and] orders by whome, wha or were they beganne. Translated out of hye Dutch in Englysh.

text: Theyr rule is to confeſſe Chriſt with the mouth, but to denye his power, in trueth, to abrenoūce him, and to truſt in theyr owne workes.
author: Coverdale, Miles, 1488-1568, attributed name.
title: The original [and] sprynge of all sectes [and] orders by whome, wha or were they beganne. Translated out of hye Dutch in Englysh.

text: IN Ungary are rych ſpiritual Lordes & an order which weare a white cote, & a reede cloke theron, where vpon they haue a grene croſſe.
author: Coverdale, Miles, 1488-1568, attributed name.
title: The original [and] sprynge of all sectes [and] orders by whome, wha or were they beganne. Translated out of hye Dutch in Englysh.

text: Noman wēt aboute to begyle ony mā by craftynes at thys tyme, no ſtraū ger was oppreſſed, all hatred ceaſſed, and alenuy turned to peace: Thys cōtinued ye ſpace of. iii. monethes.
author: Coverdale, Miles, 1488-1568, attributed name.
title: The original [and] sprynge of all sectes [and] orders by whome, wha or were they beganne. Translated out of hye Dutch in Englysh.

text: Now this kinde of vsurie and vsurers no man that hath his right wits and senses, will once dare to challenge or condemne generally as vnlawfull.
author: Mosse, Miles, fl. 1580-1614.
title: The arraignment and conuiction of vsurie That is, The iniquitie, and vnlawfulnes of vsurie, displayed in sixe sermons, preached at Saint Edmunds Burie in Suffolke, vpon Prouerb. 28.8. By Miles Mosse,

text: And lastly, it is so farre from approuing any, as that it punisheth vsurie euen to the lowest degree and measure.
author: Mosse, Miles, fl. 1580-1614.
title: The arraignment and conuiction of vsurie That is, The iniquitie, and vnlawfulnes of vsurie, displayed in sixe sermons, preached at Saint Edmunds Burie in Suffolke, vpon Prouerb. 28.8. By Miles Mosse,

text: But among many other thinges, I may not forget that our late English Canons agréed vpon by the Conuocation house for this prouince of Canterbury, do couple vsurie with the most gréeuous sinnes of heresie, schisme, periurie, incest, and Adulterie.
author: Mosse, Miles, fl. 1580-1614.
title: The arraignment and conuiction of vsurie That is, The iniquitie, and vnlawfulnes of vsurie, displayed in sixe sermons, preached at Saint Edmunds Burie in Suffolke, vpon Prouerb. 28.8. By Miles Mosse,

text: In the handling of which point, I must of necessitie conioyne those thrée kindes of vsurie together, whereof I haue seuerally discoursed before: lest otherwise the treatise should growe infinite, and too tedious to the hearers.
author: Mosse, Miles, fl. 1580-1614.
title: The arraignment and conuiction of vsurie That is, The iniquitie, and vnlawfulnes of vsurie, displayed in sixe sermons, preached at Saint Edmunds Burie in Suffolke, vpon Prouerb. 28.8. By Miles Mosse,

text: In such cases as this, by like suppositions, it is growne into a prouerbe, Qui tacet consentire videtur: He that holdeth his peace, and replyeth not, seemeth to consent.
author: Mosse, Miles, fl. 1580-1614.
title: The arraignment and conuiction of vsurie That is, The iniquitie, and vnlawfulnes of vsurie, displayed in sixe sermons, preached at Saint Edmunds Burie in Suffolke, vpon Prouerb. 28.8. By Miles Mosse,

text: Secondly, he requireth not againe the selfesame particular which he lent, but the like or the worth onely: none of both which are done in the contract of accommodatiō.
author: Mosse, Miles, fl. 1580-1614.
title: The arraignment and conuiction of vsurie That is, The iniquitie, and vnlawfulnes of vsurie, displayed in sixe sermons, preached at Saint Edmunds Burie in Suffolke, vpon Prouerb. 28.8. By Miles Mosse,

text: And surely it is no maruaile, though the worde of God, and others speaking by an extraordinarie spirite, haue forbidden and condemned vsurie.
author: Mosse, Miles, fl. 1580-1614.
title: The arraignment and conuiction of vsurie That is, The iniquitie, and vnlawfulnes of vsurie, displayed in sixe sermons, preached at Saint Edmunds Burie in Suffolke, vpon Prouerb. 28.8. By Miles Mosse,

text: Note (saith one) that vsurie cannot bee committed, but onely in such thinges which are subiect to that kinde of lending which wée mutuation: that is to say, in such things as consist in number, waight, and measure.
author: Mosse, Miles, fl. 1580-1614.
title: The arraignment and conuiction of vsurie That is, The iniquitie, and vnlawfulnes of vsurie, displayed in sixe sermons, preached at Saint Edmunds Burie in Suffolke, vpon Prouerb. 28.8. By Miles Mosse,

text: To them which iustifie vsurie to be lawfull, I stand not here to make answer: for to that end serueth the treatise following.
author: Mosse, Miles, fl. 1580-1614.
title: The arraignment and conuiction of vsurie That is, The iniquitie, and vnlawfulnes of vsurie, displayed in sixe sermons, preached at Saint Edmunds Burie in Suffolke, vpon Prouerb. 28.8. By Miles Mosse,

text: I Hymenaeus hight whoſe force you do obay, In whom (twiſe happy may you bee) if you do rightly ſtay.
author: Student in Cambridge.
title: A poore knight his pallace of priuate pleasures Gallantly garnished, with goodly galleries of strang inuentio[n]s and prudently polished, with sundry pleasant posies, [et] other fine fancies of dainty

text: Morpheus replyde agayne, I finde none other cauſe, Why ſuch reſort of mortall men, vnto her tent ſhee drawes, But that ſhee dooth delight the minde of man and beaſt, And tickleth forth the willing minde, vnto Dame Venus neaſt.
author: Student in Cambridge.
title: A poore knight his pallace of priuate pleasures Gallantly garnished, with goodly galleries of strang inuentio[n]s and prudently polished, with sundry pleasant posies, [et] other fine fancies of dainty

text: With whom my God departed thence, beckning his hand at mee, As who ſhould ſay, goe pack away, I cannot come to thee.
author: Student in Cambridge.
title: A poore knight his pallace of priuate pleasures Gallantly garnished, with goodly galleries of strang inuentio[n]s and prudently polished, with sundry pleasant posies, [et] other fine fancies of dainty

text: There Paris hath a Tombe, far diſtant from the reſt, A gorgious Tombe no doubt it was, excelling all the beſt.
author: Student in Cambridge.
title: A poore knight his pallace of priuate pleasures Gallantly garnished, with goodly galleries of strang inuentio[n]s and prudently polished, with sundry pleasant posies, [et] other fine fancies of dainty

text: For why in trickes of childiſh yéeres, hee cauſeth them to ſtay, Neglecting duties of great waight, delighting nought but play.
author: Student in Cambridge.
title: A poore knight his pallace of priuate pleasures Gallantly garnished, with goodly galleries of strang inuentio[n]s and prudently polished, with sundry pleasant posies, [et] other fine fancies of dainty

text: Let Iuno ſerue for Ioue, ſufficing for his wife, And let not Neptune with his mate, diſpiſe to lede his life.
author: Student in Cambridge.
title: A poore knight his pallace of priuate pleasures Gallantly garnished, with goodly galleries of strang inuentio[n]s and prudently polished, with sundry pleasant posies, [et] other fine fancies of dainty

text: Then muſt I néedes reioyce my freend, that fortune doth reueale, That thing to mee, which thou from mee didſt purpoſe to conceale.
author: Student in Cambridge.
title: A poore knight his pallace of priuate pleasures Gallantly garnished, with goodly galleries of strang inuentio[n]s and prudently polished, with sundry pleasant posies, [et] other fine fancies of dainty

text: Lo Sextus Boſcius is accuſed, by Scilla and his traine, And Tully muſt come tell his tale, to ſet him frée againe.
author: Student in Cambridge.
title: A poore knight his pallace of priuate pleasures Gallantly garnished, with goodly galleries of strang inuentio[n]s and prudently polished, with sundry pleasant posies, [et] other fine fancies of dainty

text: Yet ſith the Fates haue cut their clewes, ſith Lacheſis hath ſayd, That ſhee would ſtretch her hand no more, then be you well apayde.
author: Student in Cambridge.
title: A poore knight his pallace of priuate pleasures Gallantly garnished, with goodly galleries of strang inuentio[n]s and prudently polished, with sundry pleasant posies, [et] other fine fancies of dainty

text: For althoughe he ſhould go from them as concernyng the body, yet for all that he would not forſake them, but be preſent with them in his ſpirite euen vnto the ende of the worlde.
author: Zwingli, Ulrich, 1484-1531.
title: A briefe rehersal of the death resurrectio[n], [and] ascension of Christ gathered together oute of ye foure euangelistes and actes of the apostles by the most godly and great learned man Huldriche Zui

text: A iudge ought not to haue a reſpect to the fauoure or diſpleaſure of men, but vnto the rule of equitie and lawe.
author: Zwingli, Ulrich, 1484-1531.
title: A briefe rehersal of the death resurrectio[n], [and] ascension of Christ gathered together oute of ye foure euangelistes and actes of the apostles by the most godly and great learned man Huldriche Zui

text: The magiſtrate as long as he vſeth the ſword laufully, he himſelfe doth not ſtrike, but God by him.
author: Zwingli, Ulrich, 1484-1531.
title: A briefe rehersal of the death resurrectio[n], [and] ascension of Christ gathered together oute of ye foure euangelistes and actes of the apostles by the most godly and great learned man Huldriche Zui

text: But the feaſt of the Paſſeouer by Iohn, doth ſeme to be the day followyng the eatyng of the Lambe.
author: Zwingli, Ulrich, 1484-1531.
title: A briefe rehersal of the death resurrectio[n], [and] ascension of Christ gathered together oute of ye foure euangelistes and actes of the apostles by the most godly and great learned man Huldriche Zui

text: Thou knoweſt all thinges, thou knoweſt that I loue thee: Ieſus ſayed vnto him, fede my ſhepe.
author: Zwingli, Ulrich, 1484-1531.
title: A briefe rehersal of the death resurrectio[n], [and] ascension of Christ gathered together oute of ye foure euangelistes and actes of the apostles by the most godly and great learned man Huldriche Zui

text: Take therfore and eate, do this in remē braunce of me, I go now from you, ſo that frō henceforth I ſhall not eate and drynke wyth you after the accuſtomed maner.
author: Zwingli, Ulrich, 1484-1531.

text: Gyue me now and euer grace to drede the / to loue the and to ſerue the / with all my harte and mynde / with all my wyll & reaſon / wt all my myght power & ſtrength of body and ſoule.

text: LOgique is an Arte to define the nature of things, to deuide them into parts, to knit true arguments, and to detect the false.
author: Evans, Lewis, fl. 1574.
title: [The abridgement of logique]

text: The repugnancie of propsitions, is the diuersitie of two perfect sentences, consisting of two, and the selfe same partes.
author: Evans, Lewis, fl. 1574.
title: [The abridgement of logique]

text: And herevnto may we referre the dutie of euery man: as to teach, to write, to play the lawyer or merchaunt. &c.
author: Evans, Lewis, fl. 1574.

text: A conditionall proposition is euermore true when the partes are so knit together, that the latter must néedes follow vpon the first.
author: Evans, Lewis, fl. 1574.
title: [The abridgement of logique]

text: Where let none thinke, that I contemne authorities, but only wishe, Sine ratione vt non valeret authoritas, that authoritie without reason or scripture, should not take place, and preuaile.

title: [The abridgement of logique]

text: The third figure hath the double repeate in the former part of both propositions, and there be sixe moodes, appertayning vnto the same: Darapti, Felapton, Disamis, Datisi, Bocardo, Ferison, the vowels lykewise wherof, are as afore, specially to be considered.
author: Evans, Lewis, fl. 1574.
title: [The abridgement of logique]

text: This vnperfect argument consisteth partly of likelyhoodes, and partly of infallible reasons, therefore it must be foreséene, that lykelyhoodes bée not taken for necessarie reasons.

title: [The abridgement of logique]

text: For to saye the troth, some receyued of many as authorities, be so fonde, vt aures à cōmemoratione abhorreant.

text: Euerye perfect sentence is two wayes deuyded, eyther it is single, as modestie is a vertue: or else it is double, as if modestye be a vertue: it is praise worthy.

text: Alſo ye ſhall inquire of al petye Hoſteryes, and blynde alehouſes, that is to ſaye, they that kepe any lodging in their houſes, and haue not a ſygne at theyr dore, or ſel ale, and be not auctoriſed by the Iuſtices and other officers.

text: Alſo ye ſhall inquire yf there be anye man that kepeth any Greyhounde, that may not diſpende xl. s. by the yeare, or yf there be any preſt that kepeth any Greyhounde that maye not dyſpende ten pounde by the yeare.
author: Southwark (London, England)
title: The articles of lete and courte for the lyberties of Southwarke

text: Alſo ye ſhal inquyre yf all the officers within thys lordeſhyp, that is to ſay, the baylyfe concerning his office, the conſtable concernynge his office, the Ale conner concernynge his offyce the Scauengers, concerning his office haue wel and truely done the ſame, without any maner of extortion or other miſdemenure.
author: Southwark (London, England)
title: The articles of lete and courte for the lyberties of Southwarke

text: Alſo ye ſhal inquire of all Huxſters, and Tapſters that ſell Beare, Ale, and breade, by any vnlaweful diſhes, booles, cuppes, & meaſures vnſealed wherby the Quenes liege people are dyſceaued, not knowing what they haue.
author: Southwark (London, England)
title: The articles of lete and courte for the lyberties of Southwarke

text: Alſo ye ſhal inquire if anye Brydge be broken, or yf anye houſe, hedge, or pale, be caſte downe and lie in the high way, wherby the Quenes liege people be letted of ther common paſſage to market, or to the churche or otherwyſe.
author: Southwark (London, England)
title: The articles of lete and courte for the lyberties of Southwarke

text: Alſo, ye ſhal inquyre of all pounde and cage berkers, which is an offence, and fynable by the lawe, that is to ſay, the pound brech. v. li. and the cage breking is finable as in caſes of reſcus.
author: Southwark (London, England)
title: The articles of lete and courte for the lyberties of Southwarke

text: Alſo ye ſhall preſente whether that all ſuche as be inherytours of any eſtate of anye landes or Tenementes, do kyll or cauſe to be kylled all Crowes, Chowes, Rowkes, that brede vpon the poſſeſſioners, accordyng to the Statute vpon payne of the penaltye conteyned in the ſame.
author: Southwark (London, England)
title: The articles of lete and courte for the lyberties of Southwarke

text: Alſo ye ſhal inquire of al them that vſe to ſel by double or falſe waightes, and meaſures, that is to ſay, to by a great, and ſel by a leſſer, lackynge the iuſt weyght, length, gage, and quantiof the ſtanderd.

text: Wickedly doubtleſſe did Pharao, that ſo cruelly entreated Gods owne people, the Iſraelites: iuſtly and mercifully dealed God, who not onely ouerwhelmed bothe him, and all his horſemen and chariots in the redde ſea: but mightily deliuered them out of his handes, whom he ſo maliciouſly purſued.

text: That then whiche nowe we haue already ſpoken touching the cauſe of ſinne, we ſée it ſo manifeſt and plaine a matter, that it néedeth not to bée diſcourſed vppon with any longer proceſſe.
author: Cradock, Edward.

text: But ſeeing we enioy by their occaſion no ſmall ſafetie and quietneſſe, and not one of vs all is able to do all thinges at all tymes as we ſhoulde: it were more reaſon we ſhoulde diſpoſe oure ſelues (if néede were) to be bearers, than to bée headlong and raſh diſturbers.
author: Cradock, Edward.

text: He at my wealth doth ioy that loues both me and mine: The ſpitefull man hates me, and at my welfare doth repine.

text: And vndoutedlye there is nothynge that longer mayntayneth concorde and quyetnes nor more increſeth perfecte loue in maryage, then ſwete & fayre wordes, gentyll and frendelye dedes, and wyth a louyng patyens to take all thynges to the beſte.

text: For they that will not worke (ſayeth ſaynte Paul) let them not eate, therefore put them to learne ſome honeſte ſcyens or crafte, wherunto of nature they be moſte apte.

text: For chyldren is the verye ſure bande and laſt knot of loue Matrymony all, by the whyche the parentes can neuer be clerelye ſeparatyd a ſunder, In aſmuch as that whyche is of them both can not be deuyded, ſeyng both haue parte in euerye one.
author: Wied, Hermann von.

text: And chyldren are theyre parentes chefe ioye comforte and felycite nexte vnto GOD, theyr ſtaye and ſtaffe & vpholders of their age, and in theyr chyldren do the parentes leue (in a maner) after theyr death.
author: Wied, Hermann von.

author: Wied, Hermann von.

text: And not to meddle of Princes actes, What they will do nor of there factes, If occupied, well we thus abyde: The Lorde for vs will well prouide.
author: Bette, Thomas.
title: A nevve ballade intituled, Agaynst rebellious and false rumours To the nevve tune of the Blacke Almaine, vpon Scissillia.

text: With loſſe of many a man, Since firſt that ſturre began: And many a Noble hath bene ſlayne, A Duke, and eake a Prince certayne.
author: Bette, Thomas.
title: A nevve ballade intituled, Agaynst rebellious and false rumours To the nevve tune of the Blacke Almaine, vpon Scissillia.

text: And euery one to ſtaye, His tongue and nothing ſaye: But of the thinges he hath in hand, And ſée his beſynes well be ſcand?
author: Bette, Thomas.
title: A nevve ballade intituled, Agaynst rebellious and false rumours To the nevve tune of the Blacke Almaine, vpon Scissillia.

text: And leaue this murmoring ſpight, Which God doth not delight: The Scripture playnely doth declare, The Iſralites they plagued weare: Becauſe the murmered at there God, Therin we do deſarue lyke rod.
author: Bette, Thomas.
title: A nevve ballade intituled, Agaynst rebellious and false rumours To the nevve tune of the Blacke Almaine, vpon Scissillia.

text: We haue hard in Fraunce the Rumur there That hath bene many a daye: There countrey ſpoyled in Ruth and feare, Vnto there cleane decaye.
author: Bette, Thomas.
title: A nevve ballade intituled, Agaynst rebellious and false rumours To the nevve tune of the Blacke Almaine, vpon Scissillia.

text: Doth tell them ſo abrode, And thus they laye on lode: And filles the peoples eares with lyes, Thus Rumor ſtill abrode he flyes.
author: Bette, Thomas.
title: A nevve ballade intituled, Agaynst rebellious and false rumours To the nevve tune of the Blacke Almaine, vpon Scissillia.

text: Of Flemminges fled from Tirantes hand, Which dayly commeth to this land: Whoſe harts in wrath full long hath boyld And eake there Countrye cleane diſpoyld.
author: Bette, Thomas.
title: A nevve ballade intituled, Agaynst rebellious and false rumours To the nevve tune of the Blacke Almaine, vpon Scissillia.

text: Which weare the chiefe ſtayes of that land, Wherfore in hazarde now they ſtande, For where the chiefe are taken awaye, The reſt muſt nedes runne to decaye.
author: Bette, Thomas.
title: A nevve ballade intituled, Agaynst rebellious and false rumours To the nevve tune of the Blacke Almaine, vpon Scissillia.

text: It is a shame for a Phisiciō to be so spotted & pocky, that it shall maye iustly be sayde to him, Phisiciō heale thy selfe.

text: Than shulde prestes be honored as fathers, and laye men coūt thē selues as theyr chyldren, gyuing them reuerence and double honour as the scripture commaūdeth.

title: An inuectyue agenst the moost wicked [and] detestable vyce of swearing, newly co[m]piled by Theodore Basille

text: Let not dome, sayth he, and all vnclennes or couetousnes, or fylthynes, or folyshe talkynge, or iestynge be once named among you, as it becommeth saynctes, but rather thanckes gyuyng.
author: Becon, Thomas, 1512-1567.
title: An inuectyue agenst the moost wicked [and] detestable vyce of swearing, newly co[m]piled by Theodore Basille

text: For we haue both hearde and sene, that goodes wrongfully gottē be soone dispersed abrode & come to nought.
author: Becon, Thomas, 1512-1567.
title: An inuectyue agenst the moost wicked [and] detestable vyce of swearing, newly co[m]piled by Theodore Basille

text: I maruell howe they could euer pacify theyr consciences afterwarde, seynge they made so solemne a vowe, and yet brake it.
author: Becon, Thomas, 1512-1567.
title: An inuectyue agenst the moost wicked [and] detestable vyce of swearing, newly co[m]piled by Theodore Basille

text: If they at onye tyme sweare, lette them fyrste of all be admonysshed of theyr faute, and tolde how great an offēce it is before God wyckedly and vaynely to sweare.
author: Becon, Thomas, 1512-1567.
title: An inuectyue agenst the moost wicked [and] detestable vyce of swearing, newly co[m]piled by Theodore Basille

text: For all theues shall be iudged after this boke, and al swearers shal be iudged accordyng to the same.
author: Becon, Thomas, 1512-1567.
title: An inuectyue agenst the moost wicked [and] detestable vyce of swearing, newly co[m]piled by Theodore Basille

text: Here vnto pertaynethe the sayeng of S. Ambrose, that Dauid dyd not fulfyll hys ooth by the shed dynge of bloude, it was the greater godlynes.
author: Becon, Thomas, 1512-1567.
title: An inuectyue agenst the moost wicked [and] detestable vyce of swearing, newly co[m]piled by Theodore Basille

text: A man that vseth much swearyng, shall be fylled wyth wyckednes, and the plage shall neuer go from hys house.
author: Becon, Thomas, 1512-1567.

author: Herbert, William, Sir, 1553?-1593.

text: O Eternall God and heauenly Father, whoſe might is ineffable, whoſe mercies ineſtimable, we thy poore creatures & moſt vnprofitable ſeruants in all humblenes of minde, do proſtrate our ſelues before the throne of thy maieſtie, yelding vnto thee with moſt feruent harts and faith vnfained, the Sacrifice of prayſe & thankſgiuing.

text: I vvas cheefe actor in the Iewish spight, I vvas a captaine to that rascall rout, I vvrought the tumult of that guilty night, I vvas blind guide, to that they vvent about, They all expected notice come from me, Till craft had kist, they knew not vvhich vvas he.
author: Rowlands, Samuel, 1570?-1630?
title: The betraying of Christ Iudas in despaire. The seuen words of our Sauior on the crosse. With other poems on the Passion.

text: Though Salomon vvas Israels crowne successour, And gain'd his kingly fathers state and throne; Of Dauids mercy seemes he no possessour, Funerall cost, or teares vve read of none: But Scriptures recommend the honour done In Iacobs buriall, by his gratefull sonne.
author: Rowlands, Samuel, 1570?-1630?
title: The betraying of Christ Iudas in despaire. The seuen words of our Sauior on the crosse. With other poems on the Passion.

text: Three euils in one I did commit, in this That gainst the King of glory I haue done: Deceit betray'd vvith shew of kind-ment kisse, Couetousnesse incenst, that sinne begun, Impudent boldnesse did intrude the deed, Ere any mou'd or vvisht me to proceed.
author: Rowlands, Samuel, 1570?-1630?
title: The betraying of Christ Iudas in despaire. The seuen words of our Sauior on the crosse. With other poems on the Passion.

text: Lead on despaire, confounder of my sprite, Direct vnto some nooke of hellish shade, For shames sake, be it gloomier then that night In vvhich by me heav'ns brightnesse was betraide: Blacker then death, more sable hew'd then hell, Where sulpher flames, vvith vtter darknesse dwell.
author: Rowlands, Samuel, 1570?-1630?
title: The betraying of Christ Iudas in despaire. The seuen words of our Sauior on the crosse. With other poems on the Passion.

text: In eies he suffred monefull showres of teares, His face had spittings and dispightfull blowes, Blasphemous speech vpbraid his sacred eares, Most loathsome carrion stinckes entred his nose, Gaule in his mouth, the holiest hands were bound, Hands, feet, heart, head, were nailed, pierc'd & crownd.
author: Rowlands, Samuel, 1570?-1630?
title: The betraying of Christ Iudas in despaire. The seuen words of our Sauior on the crosse. With other poems on the Passion.

text: He vvould not haue our sinnes ascend vp so, That they should come vnto his fathers sight, Nor yet his fathers vengeance fall so low, That on vs sinne committers it should light, But plac'd himselfe betwixt both vvrath and sinne, True reconcilement, by true loue to vvinne.
author: Rowlands, Samuel, 1570?-1630?
title: The betraying of Christ Iudas in despaire. The seuen words of our Sauior on the crosse. With other poems on the Passion.

text: But fearefull guerdon for so foule attempt, All-seeing eies beheld my rags bevvray'd, And most seuerely thence he did exempt, Bind him both hand and foot (his iustice said) And cast him out, no such may here partake, The Lambe vvith Sion, Sathan and the Lake.
author: Rowlands, Samuel, 1570?-1630?
title: The betraying of Christ Iudas in despaire. The seuen words of our Sauior on the crosse. With other poems on the Passion.

text: Alſo it is ſaid that the moſte patt of there camp goeth toward Paris, to ſet the againſt the ſtraūge Princes.
author: One of the camp, of the Prince of Conde.

text: God forbid that wée ſhould make fleſhe or blood our arme, or to put anye conridence in the multitude of horſemen.
author: One of the camp, of the Prince of Conde.

text: And as for our victories whiche God hath giuen vs: wée haue taken by force of weapon theſe townes following.
author: One of the camp, of the Prince of Conde.
title: The copy of a letter sent by one of the camp, of the Prince of Conde (touching the feats of war as of late haue been doon) to a freend of his, the xxx. of December last past. Anno Domini. 1568

text: One of my Lord Admirals lackeis hath for his part ſixe and thirtie péeces of ſiluer veſſels whiche did belonge to the lord of Guiſe.
author: One of the camp, of the Prince of Conde.
title: The copy of a letter sent by one of the camp, of the Prince of Conde (touching the feats of war as of late haue been doon) to a freend of his, the xxx. of December last past. Anno Domini. 1568

text: And yet wée wil not ceaſſe, or leaue of: but go forward as place and time ſhall ſerue.
author: One of the camp, of the Prince of Conde.
title: The copy of a letter sent by one of the camp, of the Prince of Conde (touching the feats of war as of late haue been doon) to a freend of his, the xxx. of December last past. Anno Domini. 1568

text: Touching the méeting and a ſkirmiſhe betwéen vs fiue wéeks ago: they loſt ſeuen or eyght hundreth men, & the ſpoile was about two hundreth M. crownes worthe, but they ſaued them ſelues by the means of a riuer, ſome within Poytiers, ſome other at Luſignam.
author: One of the camp, of the Prince of Conde.

author: One of the camp, of the Prince of Conde.

text: Wo be to you when all men ſpeake well of you: (for as he ſayth in an other place) that which is highly esteemed amongſt men, is moſt commonly abhominable in the ſight of God.
author: L'Espine, Jean de, ca. 1506-1597.
title: An excellent and learned treatise of apostasie made by the most reuerend and godly learned man M. Iohn de l'Espine minister of the word of God in the churche of Angers in the dukedome of Anjou. Direct

text: All that then, which we could poſſibly loſe in the worlde, we doe recouer, to followe Ieſus Chriſt; not two folde or foure folde, but an hundred folde: and ouer and beſides life euerlaſting, which can not be meaſured.
author: L'Espine, Jean de, ca. 1506-1597.
title: An excellent and learned treatise of apostasie made by the most reuerend and godly learned man M. Iohn de l'Espine minister of the word of God in the churche of Angers in the dukedome of Anjou. Direct

text: Who promiſed it vnto all thoſe who ſhould beleeue in his name? ſaying: He that beleeueth in me, (as ſaith the Scripture) out of his belly ſhall flowe riuers of water of life.
author: L'Espine, Jean de, ca. 1506-1597.
title: An excellent and learned treatise of apostasie made by the most reuerend and godly learned man M. Iohn de l'Espine minister of the word of God in the churche of Angers in the dukedome of Anjou. Direct

text: He is our light and wiſedome, what are we then without him but darkenes, and ſilly blind men groping and going at all aduentures, vntill we haue found the pit euen to caſt our ſelues headlong into the ſame?
author: L'Espine, Jean de, ca. 1506-1597.
title: An excellent and learned treatise of apostasie made by the most reuerend and godly learned man M. Iohn de l'Espine minister of the word of God in the churche of Angers in the dukedome of Anjou. Direct

text: Seing then we now belong vnto him, and not vnto our ſelues, and that he is Lord of our life, and of our death; is not the one and the other in his diſpoſition, to doe with them, as it ſhall ſeeme good vnto him.
author: L'Espine, Jean de, ca. 1506-1597.
title: An excellent and learned treatise of apostasie made by the most reuerend and godly learned man M. Iohn de l'Espine minister of the word of God in the churche of Angers in the dukedome of Anjou. Direct

text: And otherwiſe, Giue vs helpe againſt trouble, for vaine is the helpe of man: Thorough God we ſhall do valiauntly for he ſhall treade downe our enemies.
author: L'Espine, Jean de, ca. 1506-1597.
title: An excellent and learned treatise of apostasie made by the most reuerend and godly learned man M. Iohn de l'Espine minister of the word of God in the churche of Angers in the dukedome of Anjou. Direct

text: THere are three things which cauſe the delayers to ſlumber, which they euer ſet before their eyes, to flatter themſelues in their ſluggiſhnes, and which the deuill can vſe marueilous well, to keepe them faſt in his bands, & to hold them from going from him.
author: L'Espine, Jean de, ca. 1506-1597.
title: An excellent and learned treatise of apostasie made by the most reuerend and godly learned man M. Iohn de l'Espine minister of the word of God in the churche of Angers in the dukedome of Anjou. Direct

text: When a branche of the vine is ſhred of, ſhall we ſay it is yet of the vine, or any member to be yet of the bodie after it is cut of?
author: L'Espine, Jean de, ca. 1506-1597.
title: An excellent and learned treatise of apostasie made by the most reuerend and godly learned man M. Iohn de l'Espine minister of the word of God in the churche of Angers in the dukedome of Anjou. Direct

text: The Scripture teacheth how God was greeuouſly prouoked againſt Moſes, Ieremy and Ionas, in that they were wayward in taking the charge and commiſſion which he was to giue them, & in obeying that which he commaunded them.
author: L'Espine, Jean de, ca. 1506-1597.
title: An excellent and learned treatise of apostasie made by the most reuerend and godly learned man M. Iohn de l'Espine minister of the word of God in the churche of Angers in the dukedome of Anjou. Direct

text: And heape of workes of a new mā thou shalt finde in the epistle of Paul to the Galathiās the.v. chapter.
author: Sarcerius, Erasmus, 1501-1559.
title: Co[m]mon places of Scripture ordrely and after a co[m]pendious forme of teachyng set forth with no litle labour, to the gret profit and help of all such studentes in Gods worde as haue not had longe e

text: Againe other some say they be so called, hauinge respect to sin yt is irremissible, which is the syn agaynst the holy ghost.
author: Sarcerius, Erasmus, 1501-1559.
title: Co[m]mon places of Scripture ordrely and after a co[m]pendious forme of teachyng set forth with no litle labour, to the gret profit and help of all such studentes in Gods worde as haue not had longe e

text: Therfore Chryste sayth, that the holy ghost shall come to thintent that he maye repreue the world of synne, of rightousnesse, and of iudgement, all which thinges the worlde oughte to condemne in them selues, yf they wyll be partakers of the ryghtousnes of Christ.
author: Sarcerius, Erasmus, 1501-1559.
title: Co[m]mon places of Scripture ordrely and after a co[m]pendious forme of teachyng set forth with no litle labour, to the gret profit and help of all such studentes in Gods worde as haue not had longe e

text: To holde that eyther we be otherwise to be baptysed thē in the name of the father, the son, & the holy ghost, or that this forme suffyseth not.
author: Sarcerius, Erasmus, 1501-1559.
title: Co[m]mon places of Scripture ordrely and after a co[m]pendious forme of teachyng set forth with no litle labour, to the gret profit and help of all such studentes in Gods worde as haue not had longe e

text: Also forasmoch as suche affections & thoughtes be the actes of the vyce styckynge in nature: Therfore actuall synnes must be vnderstanded not only outward wordꝭ and dedes but also inwarde affections and thoughtes wherfore in this wyse oweth actuall synne to be defyned.
author: Sarcerius, Erasmus, 1501-1559.
title: Co[m]mon places of Scripture ordrely and after a co[m]pendious forme of teachyng set forth with no litle labour, to the gret profit and help of all such studentes in Gods worde as haue not had longe e

text: It is also an erroure to saye that the conscience of men can not be saued & kept from desperacion, oneles, we wyl snstre and permyte the commaundementes of god to be turned into counsels & giuen onely to men of more perfection to be fulfylled.
author: Sarcerius, Erasmus, 1501-1559.
title: Co[m]mon places of Scripture ordrely and after a co[m]pendious forme of teachyng set forth with no litle labour, to the gret profit and help of all such studentes in Gods worde as haue not had longe e

text: To holde that all sinnes are to be confessed to gither with all the circumstaunces be longinge to the same.
author: Sarcerius, Erasmus, 1501-1559.
title: Co[m]mon places of Scripture ordrely and after a co[m]pendious forme of teachyng set forth with no litle labour, to the gret profit and help of all such studentes in Gods worde as haue not had longe e

text: Also absolucion & excō munīcaciō formed of the word of god, all which I make here to be signes and sure markes wherby the true churche is kowen.
author: Sarcerius, Erasmus, 1501-1559.
title: Co[m]mon places of Scripture ordrely and after a co[m]pendious forme of teachyng set forth with no litle labour, to the gret profit and help of all such studentes in Gods worde as haue not had longe e

text: There is no riches, no treasure, no substaūce of this world greter, than is the catholyque fayth, which saueth synful mē, lyghtneth ye blynde. ac.
author: Sarcerius, Erasmus, 1501-1559.
title: Co[m]mon places of Scripture ordrely and after a co[m]pendious forme of teachyng set forth with no litle labour, to the gret profit and help of all such studentes in Gods worde as haue not had longe e

text: Haue they not (trow you) in ſo praiſing Luther, ſhewed men a candle to ſee by it their owne fowle faces, and a light wherby to runne out of their cōpany?
author: Bristow, Richard, 1538-1581.
title: A briefe treatise of diuers plaine and sure waies to finde out the truth in this doubtfull and dangerous time of heresie Conteyning sundrie worthy motiues vnto the Catholike faith, or considerations t

text: But that, which afore I ſaide, is certaine, as it is alſo moſt worthy to be conſidered, that the Fathers in their times hauing manie Sees Apoſtolike, yet chieflie looked themſelues, and directed others to the Apoſtolike See of Rome.
author: Bristow, Richard, 1538-1581.
title: A briefe treatise of diuers plaine and sure waies to finde out the truth in this doubtfull and dangerous time of heresie Conteyning sundrie worthy motiues vnto the Catholike faith, or considerations t

text: And here doth Charity compell me, to admoniſh certaine Prieſtes of their dutie who will of vs be counted Catholiks, & yet doe for the penny giue them ſelues to the miniſterie of this new Seruice, and flatter themſelues therein, as though it were no ſin.
author: Bristow, Richard, 1538-1581.
title: A briefe treatise of diuers plaine and sure waies to finde out the truth in this doubtfull and dangerous time of heresie Conteyning sundrie worthy motiues vnto the Catholike faith, or considerations t

text: And ſo ſhal it be: when any man, ſhall any more play the Falſeprophet, there ſhal ſay vnto him his Father and his Mother that did begett him, Thou ſhalt not liue, by cauſe thou haſt ſpoken a lie in the name of our Lord.
author: Bristow, Richard, 1538-1581.
title: A briefe treatise of diuers plaine and sure waies to finde out the truth in this doubtfull and dangerous time of heresie Conteyning sundrie worthy motiues vnto the Catholike faith, or considerations t

text: And therefore vnto euery one that will heare Chriſts voice, muſt they be ſicut Ethnicus & Publicanus, as Ethnikes & Publicans, no credit to be giuen vnto them, no cō panie to be kept with them.
author: Bristow, Richard, 1538-1581.
title: A briefe treatise of diuers plaine and sure waies to finde out the truth in this doubtfull and dangerous time of heresie Conteyning sundrie worthy motiues vnto the Catholike faith, or considerations t

text: As certaine therefore as this is, that Chriſt & truth chaungeth not: ſo certainely ſhall it be proued in this part, that theſe men be Heretikes, and their doctrine Hereſie.
author: Bristow, Richard, 1538-1581.
title: A briefe treatise of diuers plaine and sure waies to finde out the truth in this doubtfull and dangerous time of heresie Conteyning sundrie worthy motiues vnto the Catholike faith, or considerations t

text: Wee therefore, that obediently receaue, al ſuch Councels, reiecting no one of them, in no one point what ſo euer: is it not manifeſt, that wee are of the ſame one catholike Church and ſociety that they were of?
author: Bristow, Richard, 1538-1581.
title: A briefe treatise of diuers plaine and sure waies to finde out the truth in this doubtfull and dangerous time of heresie Conteyning sundrie worthy motiues vnto the Catholike faith, or considerations t

text: As if we now ſhould againſt the Heretikes of this time, reaſon out of priuate mens beades, and out of the publike praiers vvhich are in the Portuiſe or Breuiary, in the Miſſal, & other Church bookes.
author: Bristow, Richard, 1538-1581.
title: A briefe treatise of diuers plaine and sure waies to finde out the truth in this doubtfull and dangerous time of heresie Conteyning sundrie worthy motiues vnto the Catholike faith, or considerations t

text: Crie they not out alowd, that they be and haue bene alwaies, ſome of them theſe twelue hundred yeares and vpward, our goodes and poſſeſſions, & that the Heretikes be vſurpers, theeues, ſacriligious men, and robbers?
author: Bristow, Richard, 1538-1581.
title: A briefe treatise of diuers plaine and sure waies to finde out the truth in this doubtfull and dangerous time of heresie Conteyning sundrie worthy motiues vnto the Catholike faith, or considerations t

text: As we haue knowen all theſe things, ſo God be thanked, that by a better Religion, hauing bene better taught, we haue bene no partakers of their wicked deuiſes, but haue put to our helping hands as occaſion hath ſerued, and euer ready to ouerthrowe the auctors and deuiſers thereof.
author: Elizabeth I, Queen of England, 1533-1603.
title: The true copie of a letter from the Queenes Maiestie, to the Lord Maior of London, and his brethren conteyning a most gracious acceptation of the great ioy which her subiectes tooke vpon the apprehens

text: And this her Highnes hath willed to be made knowen vnto you all, with this, that ſhee will not faile with all care, and by all good meanes that appertaine to a Chriſtian prince, to ſeeke the cōſeruation of you all ſo louing and duetifully affected Subiects.
author: Elizabeth I, Queen of England, 1533-1603.
title: The true copie of a letter from the Queenes Maiestie, to the Lord Maior of London, and his brethren conteyning a most gracious acceptation of the great ioy which her subiectes tooke vpon the apprehens

author: Elizabeth I, Queen of England, 1533-1603.

text: Wee thinke meete, that theſe our letters ſhoulde be communicated in ſome generall aſsemblie to our most louing Subiects the Commoners of that Citie.
author: Elizabeth I, Queen of England, 1533-1603.

text: Whoſe mercy is ſo infinite, to ſuch as were oppreſſed: He hath reſtored them to right, and hath their care redreſſed.
author: Elderton, William, d. 1592?
title: The lamentation of follie to the tune of New Rogero.

text: Flatterie is the Forte of Fame, and trueth is troden downe: The innocent do beare the blame, the wicked winne renowne.
author: Elderton, William, d. 1592?
title: The lamentation of follie to the tune of New Rogero.

text: Alas it ſeemed ſtrange, ſuch thraldome in a realme: Which wealthie was to waſt away, by will that was extreame.
author: Elderton, William, d. 1592?
title: The lamentation of follie to the tune of New Rogero.

text: Sith vertue was profeſt, moſt famous franke and frée: Yet men tranſpoſed cleane, more vile and worſe to be.
author: Elderton, William, d. 1592?
title: The lamentation of follie to the tune of New Rogero.

text: Oppreſſion hath beene frée, the poore alas be ſpoyled: Maides and wiues be rauiſhed, the ſimple are beguiled.
author: Elderton, William, d. 1592?
title: The lamentation of follie to the tune of New Rogero.

text: Archbishopp off Canterbury his predesessor / partly for an other exchange off the possessions off the Archbishoprick by a statute established for the same purpose / in the first yeere off Queene Elizabeth before he obteined the Sea.
author: Stubbes, John, 1543-1591, attributed name.
title: The life off the 70. Archbishopp off Canterbury presentlye sittinge Englished, and to be added to the 69. lately sett forth in Latin. This numbre off seuenty is so compleat a number as it is great pit

text: Besides A man may theare see the images off the dead / grauen / comminge out off theare graues to iudgment.
author: Stubbes, John, 1543-1591, attributed name.
title: The life off the 70. Archbishopp off Canterbury presentlye sittinge Englished, and to be added to the 69. lately sett forth in Latin. This numbre off seuenty is so compleat a number as it is great pit

text: He therfore leadinge his liffe so vpprightlye and in differentlye / althoughe by reason off the possessions off his landes diminished / he coulde not benefitt his seruants with any great prefermentes / or rewardes: yet their are very fewe amōgest them on whome / he hath not bestowed sumwhat / that maye succor ther necessities.
author: Stubbes, John, 1543-1591, attributed name.
title: The life off the 70. Archbishopp off Canterbury presentlye sittinge Englished, and to be added to the 69. lately sett forth in Latin. This numbre off seuenty is so compleat a number as it is great pit

text: At which tyme / one off the chiefe ministers off the church / made a sermon and Mathew tharchbishoppe himselfe / was minister off the blessed communion and supper off our Lorde vnto the people / standing in the vpper ende / or corner off the churche.
author: Stubbes, John, 1543-1591, attributed name.
title: The life off the 70. Archbishopp off Canterbury presentlye sittinge Englished, and to be added to the 69. lately sett forth in Latin. This numbre off seuenty is so compleat a number as it is great pit

text: He I saye that should bee a bright light / and sauory salte to all England / prophanely to boast him off such temporall homages / and Lordshipes ouer other and to esteme so glorious the shewe off so many proude Pontificall antecessors / whose onlye names are not cleane yenough for Christian mouthes.
author: Stubbes, John, 1543-1591, attributed name.
title: The life off the 70. Archbishopp off Canterbury presentlye sittinge Englished, and to be added to the 69. lately sett forth in Latin. This numbre off seuenty is so compleat a number as it is great pit

text: The effect is to shewe what a creator off Bishopes he hath been / and howmany he hath consecrated / in his dayes / their vniuersitie / their age / profession / degree off learning / diocese / and naturall contrye / a mater (I warrant) it off great profit.
author: Stubbes, John, 1543-1591, attributed name.
title: The life off the 70. Archbishopp off Canterbury presentlye sittinge Englished, and to be added to the 69. lately sett forth in Latin. This numbre off seuenty is so compleat a number as it is great pit

text: The copie wherout this is tourned / was written by a man off his owne / I thincke his secretarie.
author: Stubbes, John, 1543-1591, attributed name.
title: The life off the 70. Archbishopp off Canterbury presentlye sittinge Englished, and to be added to the 69. lately sett forth in Latin. This numbre off seuenty is so compleat a number as it is great pit

text: Concernynge choſyng of counſailours, I neuer haue redde hard nor knowē, that princis counſaylours and prelates ſhulde be appoynted by rude and ignorant common people, nor that they were perſones mete or of habilitie to diſcerne and choſe mete and ſufficient coūſailours for a prince.

text: And we and they ſhal ſo loke on this cauſe, that we truſt it ſhal be to your confuſion, if accordynge to our former letters ye ſubmitte not your ſelfes.

text: The Apoſtles were deliuered to the power of men to be puniſhed, the Apoſtles deliuered mē to the power of the diuel to be tormented.

title: A consolatorie epistle to the afflicted catholikes, set foorth by Thomas Hide Priest

text: Euenſo malitious ſynners be ioyned with the iuſte, and they be approued good, which endure good amonge the euil.
author: Hide, Thomas, 1524-1597.
title: A consolatorie epistle to the afflicted catholikes, set foorth by Thomas Hide Priest

text: This is ſuch a cauſe, as for the which who ſo hath not the gifte to ſuffer, ought to ſeeke it by praier, and penance.
author: Hide, Thomas, 1524-1597.
title: A consolatorie epistle to the afflicted catholikes, set foorth by Thomas Hide Priest

text: In good times when God was feared, and the churche lawes reuerenced, catholikes puniſhed heretikes, nowe heretikes perſecute catholikes.
author: Hide, Thomas, 1524-1597.
title: A consolatorie epistle to the afflicted catholikes, set foorth by Thomas Hide Priest

text: And what els do they ſaye in ſubſtāce againſte the beleued doctrines of the churche, but that the beleuers be papiſtes, and the doctrines papiſtrie.
author: Hide, Thomas, 1524-1597.
title: A consolatorie epistle to the afflicted catholikes, set foorth by Thomas Hide Priest

text: When good and euil men do the ſame thinges, and ſuffer the ſame paynes, they are not to be diſcerned by their doinges or ſufferinges, but by the cauſes, why they ſo doo, or ſuffer, marke the point.
author: Hide, Thomas, 1524-1597.
title: A consolatorie epistle to the afflicted catholikes, set foorth by Thomas Hide Priest

text: When inferiour authoritie commaundeth what we ſhould not doo, we muſt refuſe that authoritie, and feare the ſuperior power.

title: A consolatorie epistle to the afflicted catholikes, set foorth by Thomas Hide Priest

text: What man that is of any chriſtian ſenſe, or catholike zeale, can heare with patiēt eares Godes anointed prieſt and prince of his people, to be called Antechriſt?

text: Nay and if thou hast so moche witte to remembre / vpon the wordes that thou thy self spakest / I declared what incōuenience mought happen by the flaterynge silence of a cōfessour: wenest thou that I was neuer confessed?
author: Elyot, Thomas, Sir, 1490?-1546.
title: Pasquil the playne

text: Nowe whanne these two felowes come to theyr maister / they wyll tell al that they haue herde of me / it makith no mater.

title: Pasquil the playne

text: If before bataile ioyned, thou beholdest thy side the weiker: and thyne aduersaries more puissaunt and stronger: speke than of policie, wherby thou hopest to optayne the victorie.
author: Elyot, Thomas, Sir, 1490?-1546.
title: Pasquil the playne

text: And whan he spekethe / or doethe any thynge for his pleasure: I studye with wordes to commende it.
author: Elyot, Thomas, Sir, 1490?-1546.
title: Pasquil the playne

text: But yet supposest thou / that grace wyll so lyghtly entre / where false opinion and viciouse affectes be so depely imprinted / excepte they be fyrste some what remoued by good perswasiō? onles thou thinkest, that euery man shall be called of god, as saint Paule was / who was elected.
author: Elyot, Thomas, Sir, 1490?-1546.
title: Pasquil the playne

text: I wolde to god / that thou woldest affirme alway truthe to thy maister / as thou doest nowe to me.
author: Elyot, Thomas, Sir, 1490?-1546.
title: Pasquil the playne

text: I wote not whither thyneye soughte for Harpocrates, but sure I am, that thyn ere sought for Pasquillus.
author: Elyot, Thomas, Sir, 1490?-1546.
title: Pasquil the playne

text: But tell me Harpocrates as thou thinkest, were not speche nowe expedient? or howe mought thy maister be otherwise curid? with silence trowist thou?
author: Elyot, Thomas, Sir, 1490?-1546.
title: Pasquil the playne

text: But betwene two men full of wordes, trouthe shall neuer or late be espied: wherfore I wil no more Gna tho meddel with the, but from hens forth I wil speake to Harpocrates: for if he can perswade me, that his silence is better than my babblynge.
author: Elyot, Thomas, Sir, 1490?-1546.
title: Pasquil the playne

text: Of this ſort are ſundrie of our nation, whoſe blaſphemous writinges come dayly to our handes, to the tryall of our faith and conſtancie, to the farther blinding of the reprobate, and their greater condemnation in the day of the Lord Ieſus Chriſt.

text: Alſo yt the people ſhal praye into the eſt is not proued by ſcripture: and yet they ſaye, that by the tradiciō of the apoſtles it is to be beleued.
author: Smith, Richard, 1500-1563.
title: Of unwryten verytyes

text: But yet yf ſome of the ſayd articlys that be called vnwryttē verities were ſuffered to cōtinue as thinges that be more like to be true, thā otherwyſe: and no neceſſitie of belefe to be deryued ther vpon.
author: Smith, Richard, 1500-1563.
title: Of unwryten verytyes

text: And as to ye ſayd other pretē ced vnwrytē verities, yt is to ſay, yt almē ſhuld reſort to Rome, as to ye moſt high & principal chyrche.
author: Smith, Richard, 1500-1563.
title: Of unwryten verytyes

text: For as long as ther be diſorders in the clergye, it wyl be heard to bryng the people to good ordre.
author: Smith, Richard, 1500-1563.
title: Of unwryten verytyes

text: And yf it were admytted, that ye clergie myght be receaued to afferme that ther be ſoche veryties, beſyde ſcripture, yet they could not proue them.
author: Smith, Richard, 1500-1563.
title: Of unwryten verytyes

text: That it may therfore be lawfully doubted, whether ſoche coūſels were gathered in the holy gooſt or not, & whether they erred in theyr iudgemētes or not, and it is no doubte, but ye in ſome general counſels they haue done ſo in dede.
author: Smith, Richard, 1500-1563.
title: Of unwryten verytyes

text: And as to ye ſayd vnwrytē verytie, that holy creame ſhuld be made after ye maū dye, it perteyneth only to thē that haue auctoritie to iudge whether it be an vnwryten veritie, or not, and to iudge alſo what is the very auctoritye of making of that creame.
author: Smith, Richard, 1500-1563.
title: Of unwryten verytyes

text: For yf they be ſuffered to mayntayne that ther be any verytyes, whych the people are bounde to beleue vpon payne of dampnaciō, beſyde ſcripture, it wyl perſwade partly an inſufficiencye in ſcripture, & ther vpō myght folowe greate daungers many wayes.
author: Smith, Richard, 1500-1563.
title: Of unwryten verytyes

text: For the pretence of ſoch vnwryten verytyes, ne yet of makyng of lawes, to bynde kynges & princes and theyr people: ne yet that bothe powers, that is to ſaye, ſpiritual & temporal, were in the clergye, began not in the clergye yt now is, but in theyr predeceſſours.
author: Smith, Richard, 1500-1563.
title: Of unwryten verytyes

text: For Paule speaketh héereof, saying: To vvhome vvee gaue not place by subiection for an houre, that the truth of the gospel might continue vvith you.
author: Bullinger, Heinrich, 1504-1575.
title: Questions of religion cast abroad in Helvetia by the aduersaries of the same: and aunswered by M. H. Bullinger of Zurick: reduced into .17. common places. Translated into Englishe by Iohn Coxe. 1572

text: And bicause the example of the Apostles, which yée doe vse, sheweth yt they condemned those which taught contrary to Paule, and we haue already proued that yée teach the same, it foloweth that yée also are condemned in them.
author: Bullinger, Heinrich, 1504-1575.
title: Questions of religion cast abroad in Helvetia by the aduersaries of the same: and aunswered by M. H. Bullinger of Zurick: reduced into .17. common places. Translated into Englishe by Iohn Coxe. 1572

text: And therfore, to the foresaide question we answer: that we do not acknowledge nor receiue the Masse, for the institution of God, but flée from it, as being contrary to oure profession, partly for causes already shewed, and partly for such causes as héereafter we shall shewe.
author: Bullinger, Heinrich, 1504-1575.
title: Questions of religion cast abroad in Helvetia by the aduersaries of the same: and aunswered by M. H. Bullinger of Zurick: reduced into .17. common places. Translated into Englishe by Iohn Coxe. 1572

text: But sith the eternall wisedome of God hath giuen the same vnto them, let vs content our selues therewith, onlesse we would séeme to haue more wisdome than god.
author: Bullinger, Heinrich, 1504-1575.
title: Questions of religion cast abroad in Helvetia by the aduersaries of the same: and aunswered by M. H. Bullinger of Zurick: reduced into .17. common places. Translated into Englishe by Iohn Coxe. 1572

text: And againe: Obey those which haue the ouersight of you, and submyt your selues: for they watch for your soules, as they that must giue accountes, that they may do it with ioy.
author: Bullinger, Heinrich, 1504-1575.
title: Questions of religion cast abroad in Helvetia by the aduersaries of the same: and aunswered by M. H. Bullinger of Zurick: reduced into .17. common places. Translated into Englishe by Iohn Coxe. 1572

text: For the Latines interprete this woorde heresie by the name of sectes: and these woords sectes and sectaries are vsually receyued in common spéeche.

text: And vnto faythe he attributeth a certayne effectuall working, bicause that from hir all good works, yea hope and charitie do spring.

text: But to this Question we aunswere thus: Bicause the churche of Chryste is catholike or vniuersall, it can not be bound, tyed, or shutte vp into one certayne place: for how can it otherwyse be called the catholike or vniuersall church?

text: As for al other thinges vaniſhe away: theſe vertues be immortall: al other pleaſures and worldly dignites peryſhe: but as theſe vertues be fer frō al perell / ſo they be euerlaſtyng.

text: Than truly the empere excedeth all other thinges / whan ye ruler therof enclyneth nat to vndiſcrete cruelnes / but to amiable equite & iuſtice / fleynge beaſtly cruelnes / and enſuyng godly kyndnes.

author: S. R. (Simon Robson), d. 1617.

text: When Titans beames had baniſht Lunas light And duskiſh dim which dide the day with darke, Sent foorth from fame report that worthie wight, With trompet ſhrille made heauen and earth to harke, Immortall gods and mortall men did marke The meſſage which with great ſolemnitie, was thus declarde to all of each degree.
author: Blenerhasset, Thomas.
title: A reuelation of the true Minerua The effect of this booke. Who on earth be gods: and by what meanes mortall men may bee made immortall.

text: For true report with golden trumpe doth ſounde her worthie prayſe: But your reproch by rumour doth rebounde in the hie wayes Of all the worlde, ſo you in infamie Muſt liue, and ſhee in royall dignitie: howe can ſhee fade whom vertue made The greateſt godeſſe by degree.
author: Blenerhasset, Thomas.
title: A reuelation of the true Minerua The effect of this booke. Who on earth be gods: and by what meanes mortall men may bee made immortall.

text: Oppreſſion rules with cruell tyrannie, In Spayne is ſpitefull ſuperſtition ſpread: Harde roughnes doth remaine in Germany, Fidelitie from faithleſſe Fraunce was flead: In Italie fancie is ſuprime head: Blinde ignoraunce in Barbary remaine, The Turke doth loue the diuell, and God diſdaine.
author: Blenerhasset, Thomas.
title: A reuelation of the true Minerua The effect of this booke. Who on earth be gods: and by what meanes mortall men may bee made immortall.

text: The preſent gods ſeeing this great turmoile, Made haſte with ſpeede her perſon to defende, Saide Saturne let vs keepe her from the foile, This wicked world ſhee all her force doth bend To ſinke ſuch as by vertue woulde aſcend.
author: Blenerhasset, Thomas.
title: A reuelation of the true Minerua The effect of this booke. Who on earth be gods: and by what meanes mortall men may bee made immortall.

text: A Ladie like my ſelfe at laſt, at laſt my ſelfe haue founde, that ſhee may be renowmde: Fame telles her name with buſie blaſt To all vpon the ground: The ſweetneſſe of her voice Doth make the gods reioyce, Therefore Calliope To little Englands worthie Queene Doth giue her great degree.
author: Blenerhasset, Thomas.
title: A reuelation of the true Minerua The effect of this booke. Who on earth be gods: and by what meanes mortall men may bee made immortall.

text: As men before Saturnus time were rude, Nowe much more brute and ſauage they will bee, If care of conſcience doth not ſinne detrude: You muſt therefore erect diuinitie, And one ordaine of great and good degree, Who muſt poſſeſſe Mineruas former place, So all the worlde true knoweledge will imbrace.
author: Blenerhasset, Thomas.
title: A reuelation of the true Minerua The effect of this booke. Who on earth be gods: and by what meanes mortall men may bee made immortall.

text: A Poore Pilgrime who ſeekes the circle rounde Of all the worlde to finde his heartes deſire, On tope of hie Pernaſſas hill hee found This booke, which al the Muſes did admire, With golden chain on deske of Genepire Faſt lockt it lay vpon Apollos ſeate.
author: Blenerhasset, Thomas.
title: A reuelation of the true Minerua The effect of this booke. Who on earth be gods: and by what meanes mortall men may bee made immortall.

text: Lady of all delight Delight of Ladies all, All the moſt worthie wight Moſt worthie wight they ſhall, Shall they?
author: Blenerhasset, Thomas.
title: A reuelation of the true Minerua The effect of this booke. Who on earth be gods: and by what meanes mortall men may bee made immortall.

text: The tearing tract of time hath waſted and worne out the worthie, The mightie maine now may mourne ſuch loſſe, ſith the ſea hath her glory.
author: Blenerhasset, Thomas.
title: A reuelation of the true Minerua The effect of this booke. Who on earth be gods: and by what meanes mortall men may bee made immortall.

text: It muste nedes then be true, that Charite maketh men do bothe these thinges, to forsake synne, and to embrace vertue.
author: Lupset, Thomas, 1495?-1530.
title: A treatise of charitie

text: But I feare me, you haue more ofte spoken the worde charitie, then you haue studyed to lerne, what thynge shulde be Charitie: and therby ye saye peraduenture of your selfe more then you doo.
author: Lupset, Thomas, 1495?-1530.
title: A treatise of charitie

text: Now then to gette this reste, that therby we may gette charitie, we muste caste aweye the loue of this lyfe: the whiche causeth all the sayde ruffelynge passions, by the whiche our soule standeth in peryll of dethe.
author: Lupset, Thomas, 1495?-1530.
title: A treatise of charitie

text: It is not syster, the numbre of wordes or of lynes, that ma keth a tale or a boke to be called longe or shorte.
author: Lupset, Thomas, 1495?-1530.
title: A treatise of charitie

text: Likewyse loue is the common affecte of fauour: charitie is loue reduced into a due order towardes god and man, as to loue god alone for him self, and to loue man for goddes sake.
author: Lupset, Thomas, 1495?-1530.
title: A treatise of charitie

text: I holde me contented brother, and pray I wyl firste, that I may thynke possible to be thus perfect.
author: Lupset, Thomas, 1495?-1530.
title: A treatise of charitie

text: These be the thinges, that suffre no mynde reste, any of these passions troubleth the mynde continually from one fantasy to an other: so that no quietnes can be had.
author: Lupset, Thomas, 1495?-1530.
title: A treatise of charitie

text: Thirdly I may loue for vayn glo rye, as if I loke by my neyghbour to be worshypped or auaunced to honour.
author: Lupset, Thomas, 1495?-1530.
title: A treatise of charitie

text: Cruely it is to deriue and to take out from our loue in god, an other loue towardes man for god.
author: Lupset, Thomas, 1495?-1530.
title: A treatise of charitie

text: Likewiſe the contagion ſuſpected to remaine in any clothes, either wollen or linnen, cannot very well be auoided by better meanes then by fire and water, and by often waſhing of them in froſts and ſunneſhine with good diſcretion, and burning the clothes that are of ſmall value.
author: A. T., practitioner in physicke.

text: And if he that eateth it be infected, it wil driue it cleane from his hart, and if he be not infected, it will preſerue him within the ſpace of xxiiij houres after the receipt thereof.

text: Mary this I thinke, that like as bloud-letting is not good againſt all diſeaſes, ſoe alſo it is not good in all perſons, but onely in thoſe that will be content to vſe afterward a moderate and conuenient diet.
author: A. T., practitioner in physicke.

text: And now I ceaſe to ſpeake any more hereof, but I will as briefly as I may entreate ſomwhat of the vſe and benefit that doth ariſe & come of Purging, and Bloud-letting, & I would wiſh all thoſe that do practiſe the ſame, to be carefull thereof.

text: There ſhall be preſented vnto thée, the depriuation of all earthly delights, the inſupportable payne and paſſion of death, the ende and laſt Pageant of thy life, the horrour of thy graue, the curſed condition of thy body, allotted to be deuoured of woormes.
author: Luis, de Granada, 1504-1588.
title: The conversion of a sinner faithfully translated out of Italian, by M.K.

text: But omitting all other conſiderations, the ſtate of the happie is an vniuerſall felicitie, wherein all good things are conteined: and contrariwiſe, the condition of the wicked, is the hauen where arriueth all vnhappineſſe, the nourſe of ſorrow, and harbour of diſtreſſe.
author: Luis, de Granada, 1504-1588.
title: The conversion of a sinner faithfully translated out of Italian, by M.K.

text: If all the diuine ſcriptures might be powred out, to ſée what would iſſue thereof, ſcarce any thing would appeare more often to our view then this.

title: The conversion of a sinner faithfully translated out of Italian, by M.K.

text: Wherfore what can be more vndecent and intollerable, then that ſuche a vile vermine ſhould delude a Lorde ſo puiſſaunt, that with a becke or a word can detrude thée into the deapth of hell and damnation.
author: Luis, de Granada, 1504-1588.

text: For therein is accompliſhed this ſaying of Iob, that the ſugred ſoppes of the vngodly, ſhalbe at the laſt deuoured with wormes.

text: Or haſt thou any bill of his hande, whereby hée is hound to beſtow vpon thée ſuch paſſing priuiledges?
author: Luis, de Granada, 1504-1588.
title: The conversion of a sinner faithfully translated out of Italian, by M.K.

text: To alleage that thou art thine owne enemie herein, and that thou doeſt not deſire theſe good things, is moſt vntrue: for a man is by nature a friende to himſelfe, and humaine will hath felicitie for his ſubiect, which is the ende of his deſires.
author: Luis, de Granada, 1504-1588.
title: The conversion of a sinner faithfully translated out of Italian, by M.K.

text: What ſhall that curſed generation imagine then will become of themſelues hearing this? for if, as Iob ſaith, we can ſcarce abide to heare his mildeſt wordes, who can abide thoſe thundring threats of his omnipotencie?
author: Luis, de Granada, 1504-1588.
title: The conversion of a sinner faithfully translated out of Italian, by M.K.

text: Whereby it followeth, that if the life bee miſchéenous, the death is miſerable, except God for ſome ſpeciall purpoſe doth diſpoſe it otherwiſe.
author: Luis, de Granada, 1504-1588.
