text: This vnitie we must by no meanes breake, but first séeke all the waies that possible we can, to make the same safe and sound.
author: Nash, Thomas, 1567-1601, attributed name.
title: A myrror for Martinists, and all other schismatiques, which in these dangerous daies doe breake the godlie vnitie, and disturbe the Christian peace of the Church. Published by T.T.

text: To whom he answereth: in déede we must séeke, but yet onely those things which pertaine to our saluation, and not strange things which are nothing necessarie, but are rather contrarie to the Scriptures, and rule of our faith.
author: Nash, Thomas, 1567-1601, attributed name.
title: A myrror for Martinists, and all other schismatiques, which in these dangerous daies doe breake the godlie vnitie, and disturbe the Christian peace of the Church. Published by T.T.

text: I will set before you those of more deserued fame and learning, and thereby a greater temptation to good men.
author: Nash, Thomas, 1567-1601, attributed name.
title: A myrror for Martinists, and all other schismatiques, which in these dangerous daies doe breake the godlie vnitie, and disturbe the Christian peace of the Church. Published by T.T.

text: Againe, One Lorde, one Faith, one Baptisme, one God the Father of all, which is aboue all, through all, and in all.
author: Nash, Thomas, 1567-1601, attributed name.
title: A myrror for Martinists, and all other schismatiques, which in these dangerous daies doe breake the godlie vnitie, and disturbe the Christian peace of the Church. Published by T.T.

text: The vnitie of the Church therfore by the places alleadged, consisteth in the spirit, in the word of God, in the Sacraments, & in a most néere bond with Christ, who is the head of all the members of the Church.
author: Nash, Thomas, 1567-1601, attributed name.
title: A myrror for Martinists, and all other schismatiques, which in these dangerous daies doe breake the godlie vnitie, and disturbe the Christian peace of the Church. Published by T.T.

text: Such is the state of the church of England at this day, through the diuersitie of opinions, that weaklings are greatly dismaied.
author: Nash, Thomas, 1567-1601, attributed name.
title: A myrror for Martinists, and all other schismatiques, which in these dangerous daies doe breake the godlie vnitie, and disturbe the Christian peace of the Church. Published by T.T.

text: But yet there must be great care had, that it be a procéeding in déed, and not rather a backsliding, an innouation & alteration from good to euill.
author: Nash, Thomas, 1567-1601, attributed name.
title: A myrror for Martinists, and all other schismatiques, which in these dangerous daies doe breake the godlie vnitie, and disturbe the Christian peace of the Church. Published by T.T.

text: And if they finde not the Church according to their conceit, they incontinent forsake the same and make a scisme.
author: Nash, Thomas, 1567-1601, attributed name.
title: A myrror for Martinists, and all other schismatiques, which in these dangerous daies doe breake the godlie vnitie, and disturbe the Christian peace of the Church. Published by T.T.

text: This contagion hath so spread it selfe like a canker through the veines and hearts of the world at this daie, that there is almost no hope of anie recouerie.

title: A myrror for Martinists, and all other schismatiques, which in these dangerous daies doe breake the godlie vnitie, and disturbe the Christian peace of the Church. Published by T.T.

text: For man vnto man, can nought threate ye wote More greuous then death, that horryble lote But yf ye haue death, that Iuſtyce gyue can Drede then your deſertes, and blame ye not man.
author: Gardiner, Stephen, 1483?-1555.
title: Theyr dedes in effecte my lyfe wolde haue Stephen Wynton. Your dedes in effecte that made your lyfe braue / H.S.

text: What ſhulde I regarde, this tranſytorie ſtate Regarde and thynke on, both early and late I muſte a newe lyfe, that euer ſhall laſte Subiecte to no death, no ſyckeneſſe, no waſte.
author: Gardiner, Stephen, 1483?-1555.
title: Theyr dedes in effecte my lyfe wolde haue Stephen Wynton. Your dedes in effecte that made your lyfe braue / H.S.

text: From hence and herein, your comforte and ſtaye Repoſed you haue, whiche nedes muſte decaye If God for this loſſe, do graunt ye dewe gayne God ſhylde ye from death, ſuche lyfe to retayne.
author: Gardiner, Stephen, 1483?-1555.
title: Theyr dedes in effecte my lyfe wolde haue Stephen Wynton. Your dedes in effecte that made your lyfe braue / H.S.

text: THeyr dedes in effecte, my lyfe wolde haue Theyr wordes do pretende, my lyuynge to craue Theyr dedes I drede not, theyr wordes beynge ſuche I drede and regarde, in maner as moche.
author: Gardiner, Stephen, 1483?-1555.
title: Theyr dedes in effecte my lyfe wolde haue Stephen Wynton. Your dedes in effecte that made your lyfe braue / H.S.

text: Than welcome be death, the entrye of lyfe And dewe to the worlde, the ſtage of all ſtryfe Lyfe loſt in this wyſe, releuyth agayne For euer in blyſſe, to lyue without payne.
author: Gardiner, Stephen, 1483?-1555.
title: Theyr dedes in effecte my lyfe wolde haue Stephen Wynton. Your dedes in effecte that made your lyfe braue / H.S.

text: Your lyfe hath ben lewde, whiche ye eſteme lyght Of force to leaue gooddes, no thanke to go quyght Thoughe matters and dedes, nought moue you at all Let God and his threates, your ſtowtenes appall.
author: Gardiner, Stephen, 1483?-1555.
title: Theyr dedes in effecte my lyfe wolde haue Stephen Wynton. Your dedes in effecte that made your lyfe braue / H.S.

text: Amende and repente, your ſtobourne eſtate That truthe hath neare tryed, but almoſte to late A patarne moſte popyſſhe, from fyrſte to the laſte As wylfull, as wyttie, whiche wante worketh waſte.
author: Gardiner, Stephen, 1483?-1555.
title: Theyr dedes in effecte my lyfe wolde haue Stephen Wynton. Your dedes in effecte that made your lyfe braue / H.S.

text: I doubte the welcome of death, to that lyfe Plaſed for Popes pageantes, in ſtage of moche ſtryfe Lyfe loſt in this wyſe, releuyth agayne As he that from blyſſe, returneth to payne.
author: Gardiner, Stephen, 1483?-1555.
title: Theyr dedes in effecte my lyfe wolde haue Stephen Wynton. Your dedes in effecte that made your lyfe braue / H.S.

text: My lyfe is but vyle, I eſteme as lyght Then ſhulde I in gooddes, or lyuynge delyght Whom matters and dedes, nought moueth at all Shulde wynde and vayne wordes, his courage appall.
author: Gardiner, Stephen, 1483?-1555.
title: Theyr dedes in effecte my lyfe wolde haue Stephen Wynton. Your dedes in effecte that made your lyfe braue / H.S.

text: From whence came Otto the first Emperour of that name, and Bruno Bishop of Colayne, and Gerberga the noble wife of the french king Lewes the fourth.

title: A defence of the gouernment established in the Church of Englande for ecclesiasticall matters Contayning an aunswere vnto a treatise called, The learned discourse of eccl. gouernment, otherwise intitu

text: And whie is it rather put with Gouernours, than with distributers of almes, béeing called shewers of mercie: and the name of almes, deriued rather of mercie, than of Gouernors?
author: Bridges, John, d. 1618.
title: A defence of the gouernment established in the Church of Englande for ecclesiasticall matters Contayning an aunswere vnto a treatise called, The learned discourse of eccl. gouernment, otherwise intitu

text: Not onely the exection of Consistorie Gouernors in euerie congregation, must be brought in, but the Princes supremacie must nowe giue place vnto them.
author: Bridges, John, d. 1618.
title: A defence of the gouernment established in the Church of Englande for ecclesiasticall matters Contayning an aunswere vnto a treatise called, The learned discourse of eccl. gouernment, otherwise intitu

text: And if they shoulde all bée measured by this Learned discourse, might not these wordes returne to their Maisters? that neyther they are all of the best learning: except they haue better learning, that they keepe yet in store for an after reckoning.
author: Bridges, John, d. 1618.
title: A defence of the gouernment established in the Church of Englande for ecclesiasticall matters Contayning an aunswere vnto a treatise called, The learned discourse of eccl. gouernment, otherwise intitu

text: Whereby not onely we see, that this argument is the very argument of the Anabaptistes, and therefore not to be vsed of our Bretheren: but also that those places, Romaines 12.. & 1.
author: Bridges, John, d. 1618.
title: A defence of the gouernment established in the Church of Englande for ecclesiasticall matters Contayning an aunswere vnto a treatise called, The learned discourse of eccl. gouernment, otherwise intitu

text: And must this also, as a part of this Learned discourse of Eccl. gouernment, be solemnly registred, for a matter breeding and nourishing superstitious opinions in the simple peoples hearts: which in a well reformed Church, is not to be suffred?
author: Bridges, John, d. 1618.
title: A defence of the gouernment established in the Church of Englande for ecclesiasticall matters Contayning an aunswere vnto a treatise called, The learned discourse of eccl. gouernment, otherwise intitu

text: Consuls at Rome, both chiefe alike together at one time, ouer all the other Senators, their-selues being of the same order and company of Senators.
author: Bridges, John, d. 1618.
title: A defence of the gouernment established in the Church of Englande for ecclesiasticall matters Contayning an aunswere vnto a treatise called, The learned discourse of eccl. gouernment, otherwise intitu

author: Bridges, John, d. 1618.

text: I made solutions full manie a one Of spirits, ferments, salts, yron, and steele, Weening so to make the Philosophers Stone: But finally I lost euery deele, After my bookes yet wrought I weele, Which euermore vntrue I preeued, Which made me oft full sore agreeued.
author: Ripley, George, d. 1490?
title: The compound of alchymy. Or The ancient hidden art of archemie conteining the right perfectest meanes to make the philosophers stone, aurum potabile, with other excellent experiments. Diuided into twe

text: And in likewise without the matter putrifie, It may in no wise truly be alterate, Neither thy Elements may be diuided kindly, Nor the coniunction of them perfectly celebrate: That thy labor therefore be not frustrate, The priuitie of our putrifying well vnderstand, Or euer thou take this worke in hand.
author: Ripley, George, d. 1490?
title: The compound of alchymy. Or The ancient hidden art of archemie conteining the right perfectest meanes to make the philosophers stone, aurum potabile, with other excellent experiments. Diuided into twe

text: If this menstrue by labour exuberate With it may be made Sulphur of nature, If it be well and kindly acuate And circulate into a spirit pure, Then to dissolue thou must be sure, Thy base with it in diuers wise, As thou shalt know by thy practise.
author: Ripley, George, d. 1490?
title: The compound of alchymy. Or The ancient hidden art of archemie conteining the right perfectest meanes to make the philosophers stone, aurum potabile, with other excellent experiments. Diuided into twe

text: And for thy proportion thou must beware, For therein maist thou be beguil'd, Therefore thy work that thou not mare, Let thy bodie be subtilly fyl'de With Mercury as much then so subtil'd, One of the Sunne, two of the Moone, Till altogether like papp be doone.
author: Ripley, George, d. 1490?
title: The compound of alchymy. Or The ancient hidden art of archemie conteining the right perfectest meanes to make the philosophers stone, aurum potabile, with other excellent experiments. Diuided into twe

text: The earthly grosenes therefore first mortified, In moysture blacknes ingendred is; This principle may not be denied, For naturall Philosophers so sayne ywis: Which had, of whitenes thou maist not mis; And into whitenes if thou congeale it once, Then hast thou a stone most precious of all stones.
author: Ripley, George, d. 1490?
title: The compound of alchymy. Or The ancient hidden art of archemie conteining the right perfectest meanes to make the philosophers stone, aurum potabile, with other excellent experiments. Diuided into twe

text: For by such calcination their bodies be shent, Which minisheth the moysture of our stone: Therefore when bodies to powder be brent, Dry as ashes of tree or bone, Of such calxes then will we none; For moysture we multiplie radicall, In calcining minishing none at all.
author: Ripley, George, d. 1490?
title: The compound of alchymy. Or The ancient hidden art of archemie conteining the right perfectest meanes to make the philosophers stone, aurum potabile, with other excellent experiments. Diuided into twe

text: Thou must diuide thy white Elixer into parts two Before thou rubifie, & into glasses two let thē be doone.
author: Ripley, George, d. 1490?
title: The compound of alchymy. Or The ancient hidden art of archemie conteining the right perfectest meanes to make the philosophers stone, aurum potabile, with other excellent experiments. Diuided into twe

text: Thus in this Chapter which is but briefe, I haue thee taught thy true solution: Now to the third gate goe, for this is won.
author: Ripley, George, d. 1490?
title: The compound of alchymy. Or The ancient hidden art of archemie conteining the right perfectest meanes to make the philosophers stone, aurum potabile, with other excellent experiments. Diuided into twe

text: Fire of nature is the third menstruall, That fire is naturall in each thing; But fire occasionate, we call vnnaturall, As heate of ashes, and balnes for putrifying: Without these fires thou maist naught bring To Putrifaction, for to be seperate, Thy matters together proportionate.
author: Ripley, George, d. 1490?
title: The compound of alchymy. Or The ancient hidden art of archemie conteining the right perfectest meanes to make the philosophers stone, aurum potabile, with other excellent experiments. Diuided into twe

text: Alſo that warde is not able to withſtande the force of thyne enemyes, except it be ſomtyme renued wt good warryours.
author: Porcia, Jacopo di, conte, 15th cent.
title: The preceptes of warre, setforth [sic] by Iames the erle of Purlilia, and tra[n]slated into englysh by Peter Betham

text: Whych pollicye wyl ſerue at theſe dayes agaynſt the Almaynes that vſe a greate nombre of gunnes in theyr armyes.
author: Porcia, Jacopo di, conte, 15th cent.
title: The preceptes of warre, setforth [sic] by Iames the erle of Purlilia, and tra[n]slated into englysh by Peter Betham

text: Yf we perceyue the ſtomakes of our enemyes to quayle and waxe faynte, it is good, gredelye to purſue them, that we maye eyther put them to flyght, or elles vtterly ſlee thē before they recouer theyr ſtrength.
author: Porcia, Jacopo di, conte, 15th cent.
title: The preceptes of warre, setforth [sic] by Iames the erle of Purlilia, and tra[n]slated into englysh by Peter Betham

text: For whē his frende aſked of him why in ſo ieoperd ſome a battayle, he went to ſlepe, he gaue hym this anſwere merely.
author: Porcia, Jacopo di, conte, 15th cent.
title: The preceptes of warre, setforth [sic] by Iames the erle of Purlilia, and tra[n]slated into englysh by Peter Betham

text: Alſo let the capitayrs remembre to ſetforth the doinges of hys ſouldiours with hygheſt prayſe, vſynge ſome oration, eftſones gyuing thē immortall thankes for theyr manfull valiauntneſſe in that battayl: declaring al thinges to be done according to theyr loyall duty and allegeaunce.
author: Porcia, Jacopo di, conte, 15th cent.
title: The preceptes of warre, setforth [sic] by Iames the erle of Purlilia, and tra[n]slated into englysh by Peter Betham

text: He that doth not helpe and defend hys capytayne, whan he maye, or leaueth hym whan he is enuironed & ſet abowte wyth enemyes, is worthye to be hanged on a payre of gallowes.
author: Porcia, Jacopo di, conte, 15th cent.
title: The preceptes of warre, setforth [sic] by Iames the erle of Purlilia, and tra[n]slated into englysh by Peter Betham

text: Do thou not deferre ne yet be ſlacke, leſt they recouer them ſelues, and aſhamed of theyr cowardlye flyght tourne agayne and cauſe the to recule, recoueryng the battayle, whyche nowe before was loſte.
author: Porcia, Jacopo di, conte, 15th cent.
title: The preceptes of warre, setforth [sic] by Iames the erle of Purlilia, and tra[n]slated into englysh by Peter Betham

text: Although other iniuryes maye be ſuffered, and to forget them is a token of a noble mynde, yet diſſoyaltye by all meanes is to be reuenged and acquyted.
author: Porcia, Jacopo di, conte, 15th cent.
title: The preceptes of warre, setforth [sic] by Iames the erle of Purlilia, and tra[n]slated into englysh by Peter Betham

text: And therewt comely it is, the captayne not to be defamed wyth lecherye and coueytouſneſſe, which be vyces chefelye to be eſchued & abandoned.
author: Porcia, Jacopo di, conte, 15th cent.
title: The preceptes of warre, setforth [sic] by Iames the erle of Purlilia, and tra[n]slated into englysh by Peter Betham

text: The more may all true harts lament, to see so little care, Of people nowe in these our dayes, that will no time beware.
author: La Marche, Olivier de, ca. 1426-1502.
title: The trauayled pylgrime bringing newes from all partes of the worlde, such like scarce harde of before. Seene and allowed according to the order appointed.

text: Take héede in time, the best way séeke, the more shall be thy gaine, Thy bodie eke in strength shall grow, so lesse will be thy paine.
author: La Marche, Olivier de, ca. 1426-1502.
title: The trauayled pylgrime bringing newes from all partes of the worlde, such like scarce harde of before. Seene and allowed according to the order appointed.

text: And eke such ougly wights therein, such fearfull Champions twaine, And most of all Dame Attropos, hir sight was most my paine, I shewed mine humaine nature then, that thought in pleasures trace, That no misfortune should haue hapt, my courage to displace.
author: La Marche, Olivier de, ca. 1426-1502.
title: The trauayled pylgrime bringing newes from all partes of the worlde, such like scarce harde of before. Seene and allowed according to the order appointed.

text: Make spéede quoth she, and ride apace, and so we did no doute, Till we the sight of the bare fielde, had wholy passed oute: And then I askte Dame Memorie, if I might make report, Of that Combat which I had séene, there tride in such a sort.
author: La Marche, Olivier de, ca. 1426-1502.
title: The trauayled pylgrime bringing newes from all partes of the worlde, such like scarce harde of before. Seene and allowed according to the order appointed.

text: Which makes his entrance to the mind, to fill mans mind with griefe, And therfore Dolor did conclude, that he ought be the chiefe.
author: La Marche, Olivier de, ca. 1426-1502.
title: The trauayled pylgrime bringing newes from all partes of the worlde, such like scarce harde of before. Seene and allowed according to the order appointed.

text: God graunt vnto all faythfull hartes, such race alwayes to runne, That no desyre of worldly welth, their mindes once ouercume: Then be you sure, when vitall thred, by Attropos is rent, With Gods elect in lasting ioyes, no care more to relent.
author: La Marche, Olivier de, ca. 1426-1502.
title: The trauayled pylgrime bringing newes from all partes of the worlde, such like scarce harde of before. Seene and allowed according to the order appointed.

text: The Spider labors still to make, a web to snare the flies, So Sathan he attendant is, with falshoode and with lies, To catch in trap if that he can, and by what meanes to get, The simple soule into his power, he daily layes his net.
author: La Marche, Olivier de, ca. 1426-1502.
title: The trauayled pylgrime bringing newes from all partes of the worlde, such like scarce harde of before. Seene and allowed according to the order appointed.

text: Thus leauing off from troublous thought, I gan againe to minde The iourney, which I tooke in hande, and how I was assignde, Not once to stay till I had bene in euery land and coste, Wherby that I such newes might bring, as well to least as moste.
author: La Marche, Olivier de, ca. 1426-1502.
title: The trauayled pylgrime bringing newes from all partes of the worlde, such like scarce harde of before. Seene and allowed according to the order appointed.

text: When flesh by Dolefulnesse is brought, to weake Debilitie Then straight Defiance lye betwixt, the marie ioyntes and knée: Euer striuing still in man, except freshe bloud abound, Decreasing all the vitall powers, & Death straight giues the wound.
author: La Marche, Olivier de, ca. 1426-1502.
title: The trauayled pylgrime bringing newes from all partes of the worlde, such like scarce harde of before. Seene and allowed according to the order appointed.

text: Afterwarde take halfe the nombre of perches of the longer ſyde, the whiche is. x. for the bredth.
author: Benese, Richard, d. 1546.
title: The boke of measurying of lande as well of woodland as plowland, pasture in the feelde: to compt the true nombre of acres of the same. Newly corrected, compiled by Sir Richarde de Benese.

text: Afterwarde laye the right & the left ſydes togyther, and they make. xxii. perches in the whole ſume.
author: Benese, Richard, d. 1546.
title: The boke of measurying of lande as well of woodland as plowland, pasture in the feelde: to compt the true nombre of acres of the same. Newly corrected, compiled by Sir Richarde de Benese.

text: Lykewyſe if ye haue half perches, or quarter perches, or els halfe perches & quarter perches both in ye length, and alſo in ye bredthe of the meaſure Then ye muſte alwayes ſumme euerye one of them by them ſelfe in the length, that ſtande in that bredth.
author: Benese, Richard, d. 1546.
title: The boke of measurying of lande as well of woodland as plowland, pasture in the feelde: to compt the true nombre of acres of the same. Newly corrected, compiled by Sir Richarde de Benese.

text: Then, ye ſhal compte the halfe perches by them ſelfe, and the quarter perches by them ſelfe, and ſume them in the contrarie ſyde, as in the example.
author: Benese, Richard, d. 1546.
title: The boke of measurying of lande as well of woodland as plowland, pasture in the feelde: to compt the true nombre of acres of the same. Newly corrected, compiled by Sir Richarde de Benese.

text: And the whole ſume of the aſcēce, the which i. C. lx. for the length, then multyplye.
author: Benese, Richard, d. 1546.
title: The boke of measurying of lande as well of woodland as plowland, pasture in the feelde: to compt the true nombre of acres of the same. Newly corrected, compiled by Sir Richarde de Benese.

text: Therfore ye ſhall not vſe that maner of comptynge by caſtynge the whole nombre of all the ſydes into. iiii. equall partes, and by takynge one parte of them for the length, & one other for the breadth bycauſe it is falſe.
author: Benese, Richard, d. 1546.
title: The boke of measurying of lande as well of woodland as plowland, pasture in the feelde: to compt the true nombre of acres of the same. Newly corrected, compiled by Sir Richarde de Benese.

text: Afterwarde ye ſhall meaſure frō the midle poynt within the figure, to the vtter ſyde of the cyrcuyte, and take the nō bre of perches of that meaſure for ye bredth, as in this exāple.

text: Thus doubtfull of minde, and at defiance with destinie, as a fauourer of Epicurus, I saide: What place is there left vnto diuine prouidence, séeing that all things fall out and happen to all men otherwise than they deserue, considering that their worthinesse would be well rewarded?

text: Séeing therefore man is a liuing soule, and a most excellent creature: I saie that such as by Fortune haue lost their haire, and are become bald, must and ought to haue preferment aboue the rest.

text: WE forbid the making of any solemne processions, as well in respect of the death of our late cousin the Prince of Condie, as in respect of the iorney of S. Bartilmewe, and of all other dooings that may renewe the remembrance of troubles.
author: France. Sovereign (1574-1589 : Henry III)
title: The edict or proclamation set forthe by the Frenche Kinge vpon the pacifying of the troubles in Fraunce, with the articles of the same pacification. Read and published in the presence of the sayd King

text: LIKEWIZE wee denounce that the leuying and bringing forth of the Swissers, and namely of the Erles of New castle and Valangin, and of others of the Cantons whatsoeuer they were, was not done but for our seruis.
author: France. Sovereign (1574-1589 : Henry III)
title: The edict or proclamation set forthe by the Frenche Kinge vpon the pacifying of the troubles in Fraunce, with the articles of the same pacification. Read and published in the presence of the sayd King

text: WE ordayne, that the Catholique and Romane religion shall be set vp and stablished agayne, in all places and parts of this our Realme, & of the contryes vnder our gouernance, vvhere the excercise therof hath bin lefte of, That it may be freely and quietly excercised vvithout any trouble or lette.
author: France. Sovereign (1574-1589 : Henry III)
title: The edict or proclamation set forthe by the Frenche Kinge vpon the pacifying of the troubles in Fraunce, with the articles of the same pacification. Read and published in the presence of the sayd King

text: Likewise also euery mā shall enioye the arrerages of rents whiche haue not bene taken by vs or by our commaundement & graunt, or by order of Iustice, or by commaundment of the cheefe Rulers of either part.
author: France. Sovereign (1574-1589 : Henry III)

text: In vvitnesse vvhereof vvee haue signed these presents vvith our ovvne hand, and cavvsed oure seale too bee set and put thereto, that it may bee a firme and stable thing for euer.
author: France. Sovereign (1574-1589 : Henry III)
title: The edict or proclamation set forthe by the Frenche Kinge vpon the pacifying of the troubles in Fraunce, with the articles of the same pacification. Read and published in the presence of the sayd King

text: HENRY by the grace of God King of France & Pollande, To all that are present and to come, greeting.

title: The edict or proclamation set forthe by the Frenche Kinge vpon the pacifying of the troubles in Fraunce, with the articles of the same pacification. Read and published in the presence of the sayd King

text: Neuerthelesse, the last willes and Testaments of souldyers, that haue bin made during the present and former troubles, as well on the one part as on the other, shall stand in full force and strength according too the order of Lawe.
author: France. Sovereign (1574-1589 : Henry III)

text: O good lorde, how many thynges ſhall ye fynde in all olde bokes here and there moſte fautily redde?
author: Valeriano, Pierio, 1477-1560.
title: A treatise vvriten by Iohan Valerian a greatte clerke of Italie, which is intitled in latin Pro sacerdotum barbis translated in to Englysshe

text: Tylle at the laſte one, that was ſomewhat bolder than the other, began to ſtroke one of the ſenatours beardes: and he wolde nat ſuffre hym, but ſtrake hym with a rodde.
author: Valeriano, Pierio, 1477-1560.
title: A treatise vvriten by Iohan Valerian a greatte clerke of Italie, which is intitled in latin Pro sacerdotum barbis translated in to Englysshe

text: Artemidorus ſaythe, that the fathers are worthy to be honored, whan their chyldren be ſene with manly beardes.
author: Valeriano, Pierio, 1477-1560.
title: A treatise vvriten by Iohan Valerian a greatte clerke of Italie, which is intitled in latin Pro sacerdotum barbis translated in to Englysshe

text: For within a daye after, or two at the moſte, when they miniſtre ageyne, they contaminate the bleſſed ſacrament with heares, and cōmytte the ſame offence, for whiche they accuſed them that weare berades.
author: Valeriano, Pierio, 1477-1560.
title: A treatise vvriten by Iohan Valerian a greatte clerke of Italie, which is intitled in latin Pro sacerdotum barbis translated in to Englysshe

text: Do ye not ſee, if ye ſtryue ageynſt beardes, there be ſo many good men that weare berdes, that your buſynes ſhall be laughed to ſcorne with euery man?
author: Valeriano, Pierio, 1477-1560.
title: A treatise vvriten by Iohan Valerian a greatte clerke of Italie, which is intitled in latin Pro sacerdotum barbis translated in to Englysshe

text: But nowe of late, we haue not onely lefte the name of good maners, but alſo the veri right patheway of the ſame.
author: Valeriano, Pierio, 1477-1560.
title: A treatise vvriten by Iohan Valerian a greatte clerke of Italie, which is intitled in latin Pro sacerdotum barbis translated in to Englysshe

text: And alſo ye ſhal fynde wrytten in manye auctours theſe wordes: Theyr chekes were cladde with yonge wolly heare.
author: Valeriano, Pierio, 1477-1560.
title: A treatise vvriten by Iohan Valerian a greatte clerke of Italie, which is intitled in latin Pro sacerdotum barbis translated in to Englysshe

text: For what other thing by theyr interpretation, maketh they hym, that weareth a bearde, but a proude and an yuell man, that lyueth not after the lawes? and he is wycked, that deſerueth to be banyſſhed out of the churche of Chriſte.
author: Valeriano, Pierio, 1477-1560.
title: A treatise vvriten by Iohan Valerian a greatte clerke of Italie, which is intitled in latin Pro sacerdotum barbis translated in to Englysshe

text: But I woll bydde them fare well, and as men vnworthy of honeſt companye, to be ſent away ſomewhyther, where they may remayne vnknowen, and lye and inioye theyr fonde appetite.
author: Valeriano, Pierio, 1477-1560.
title: A treatise vvriten by Iohan Valerian a greatte clerke of Italie, which is intitled in latin Pro sacerdotum barbis translated in to Englysshe

text: For by it all yll adfectes breke forth from the herte, as bawdry, aduoultrye, thefte, leſynges, backebytyngꝭ, & ſuche lyke / theſe thynges defyle a man.
title: Hereafter folowe x. certayne places of scrypture, by whome it is proued that the doctrynes and tradycyons of men ought to be auoyded

text: So this is the Elogye of the pope, preſtes, and monkes, whiche is gyuen to them by Paule.
title: Hereafter folowe x. certayne places of scrypture, by whome it is proued that the doctrynes and tradycyons of men ought to be auoyded

text: Now yf chryſte wyll not yt the conſcyence be bounde to any place, ſurely than of ryght the conſcyence oughte to be free fro meates, drynkes, clothes, tradycyons, and other outwarde thynges.
title: Hereafter folowe x. certayne places of scrypture, by whome it is proued that the doctrynes and tradycyons of men ought to be auoyded

text: For it is ordayned by theyr Decrees, that certayne dayes men ſhulde abſtayne from fleſſhe, egges, butter, cheſe, mylke, & other creatures of god.
title: Hereafter folowe x. certayne places of scrypture, by whome it is proued that the doctrynes and tradycyons of men ought to be auoyded

text: And they haue alſo for them ſelfes peculyer garmentes faſcyoned fer from other mēnes, agayne all whiche thynges Paule boldly fyghteth.
title: Hereafter folowe x. certayne places of scrypture, by whome it is proued that the doctrynes and tradycyons of men ought to be auoyded

text: Where agayne thou mayſt ſe the tradycyons of men to be applyed to Satan euyn by god thorow the ſayeng of Paule, as through goddes Inſtument.
title: Hereafter folowe x. certayne places of scrypture, by whome it is proued that the doctrynes and tradycyons of men ought to be auoyded

text: It ſhall make no matter with howe many vowes a man promyſe theſe doctrynes for the more ſtrayte vowe and othe, that in this behalfe ſhall be made, ye more ſoone ſhulde it be broken of & let at large.
title: Hereafter folowe x. certayne places of scrypture, by whome it is proued that the doctrynes and tradycyons of men ought to be auoyded

text: For yf a man wolde forbede the eatynge of thoſe meates to morowe, or.ii. dayes folowynge, ſhulde not this place ſerue hym well, al though he were not named a manyche?
title: Hereafter folowe x. certayne places of scrypture, by whome it is proued that the doctrynes and tradycyons of men ought to be auoyded

text: For as ſoone as the herte begynneth to applye to mēnes tradycyons it wexeth ſtraunge to the trueth, and nothynge regardyth it.
title: Hereafter folowe x. certayne places of scrypture, by whome it is proued that the doctrynes and tradycyons of men ought to be auoyded

text: Restore to life my wicked soule, which else is like to die: So shall my voice vnto thy name, sing praise eternally.
author: Breton, Nicholas, 1545?-1626?
title: The passions of the spirit

text: His faultlesse members nayled on the crosse, His holy head was crowned all with thornes, His garments giuen by lots to gaine our losse, His power derided all with scoffes and skornes, His body wounded and his spirit vexed: To thinke on this, what soule is not perplexed?
author: Breton, Nicholas, 1545?-1626?
title: The passions of the spirit

text: To hate a loue must argue lothsome nature, To wrong a friend must proue too foule a deede, To kill thy selfe will shew a curssed creature, To slay the soule no more damnation neede.
author: Breton, Nicholas, 1545?-1626?
title: The passions of the spirit

text: Forgiue thy people all their crime, whose aid on thee doth still depēd And with thy hand in this our time Our noble Queene O lord defend: And that shee may hir foes deface, powre vpon hir thy heauēly grace.
author: Breton, Nicholas, 1545?-1626?
title: The passions of the spirit

text: Where words desolu'd to sighes, sighes into teares, And euery teare to torments of the minde, The mindes distresse, into those deadly feares, That finde more death then death it selfe can finde.
author: Breton, Nicholas, 1545?-1626?
title: The passions of the spirit

text: No: could my soule in comfort once conceiue him, I hope his mercy would not let mee leaue him.
author: Breton, Nicholas, 1545?-1626?
title: The passions of the spirit

text: Thy blessed will I haue despised, vpon a stubborne minde: And to the sway of worldly things my selfe I haue enclinde. forgetting heauē & heuēly powers where God & saints doth dwell: My life had like to tread the path, that leads the way to hell.
author: Breton, Nicholas, 1545?-1626?
title: The passions of the spirit

text: But now my god & loadstar bright I will no more doe so: To think vpon my former life, my heart doth bleed for woe.
author: Breton, Nicholas, 1545?-1626?
title: The passions of the spirit

text: I saw him faultlesse, yet I did offend him: I saw him wronged and yet did not excuse him: I saw his foes, yet sought not to defend him: I had his blessings, yet I did abuse him.
author: Breton, Nicholas, 1545?-1626?
title: The passions of the spirit

text: Wherefore I counſell all good Chriſtians to be watchfull, that theſe thinges come not ſodainly vppon them, and ſo I will ende this Chapter with the wordes of Dauid.
author: Grapheuis, Rodulphus.
title: Prædictio astrologica. The great and vvonderfull prognostication, for the yeare of our Lord 1598. Written by Rodulphus Grapheus Doctor of Phisick in the Towne of Deuenter. Translated out of Dutch into

text: THis yeare it ſhalbe wonderfull and ſtrange, Beginning on the 10. of March to come, Wherein both Sun & Moon ſhalbe eclipſt, The Sun but once, the Moon in double fold: What great effects theſe 3.
author: Grapheuis, Rodulphus.
title: Prædictio astrologica. The great and vvonderfull prognostication, for the yeare of our Lord 1598. Written by Rodulphus Grapheus Doctor of Phisick in the Towne of Deuenter. Translated out of Dutch into

text: That which full ſtout did ſtand ſhal haue a fall, He that was proude in all his actions, And among beaſts accounted fierce and ſtrong, Shall become weake in that he takes in hand, And too much luſt ſhall make him impotent.
author: Grapheuis, Rodulphus.
title: Prædictio astrologica. The great and vvonderfull prognostication, for the yeare of our Lord 1598. Written by Rodulphus Grapheus Doctor of Phisick in the Towne of Deuenter. Translated out of Dutch into

text: Emperours of Turkey, that are of Ottomans race, and then it ſhall decay and be wholly ouerthrowne, which if it happen all Chriſtendome hath cauſe to reioyce.
author: Grapheuis, Rodulphus.
title: Prædictio astrologica. The great and vvonderfull prognostication, for the yeare of our Lord 1598. Written by Rodulphus Grapheus Doctor of Phisick in the Towne of Deuenter. Translated out of Dutch into

text: We haue this yeare likewiſe diuers coniunctions and aſpects of Planets, which ſignifie much warres, troubles, mutinies, bloodſheddinges, and ſecret practiſes in the low Countries, and thoſe that lie Weſt ſouthweſt from it.
author: Grapheuis, Rodulphus.
title: Prædictio astrologica. The great and vvonderfull prognostication, for the yeare of our Lord 1598. Written by Rodulphus Grapheus Doctor of Phisick in the Towne of Deuenter. Translated out of Dutch into

text: You ſhall likewiſe heare of great ſtrife betwéene men and their wiues, whereby controuerſie will ariſe, ſo that many weddinges ſhall be holden, where there wil be no muſicke, and where the Lorde or rulers of the land ſhall be betrayed.
author: Grapheuis, Rodulphus.
title: Prædictio astrologica. The great and vvonderfull prognostication, for the yeare of our Lord 1598. Written by Rodulphus Grapheus Doctor of Phisick in the Towne of Deuenter. Translated out of Dutch into

text: The firſt and laſt dayes of this preſent Month Mars and Mercurius are the gouernors, Whereby ſtrange thinges ſhall then be heard and ſeene, With vprores and rebellions manifolde: The common people thereby ſhall it rew, Mercurius many ſubtill ſleights ſhall vſe, But he and his in fine ſhall dearely buy it.
author: Grapheuis, Rodulphus.
title: Prædictio astrologica. The great and vvonderfull prognostication, for the yeare of our Lord 1598. Written by Rodulphus Grapheus Doctor of Phisick in the Towne of Deuenter. Translated out of Dutch into

text: There wil be no want of fruites, but rather want of amendment in men, for that wickednes dayly increaſeth more and more, and we giue our minds rather to beaſtly cruelties, then loue and Chriſtian humanity.
author: Grapheuis, Rodulphus.
title: Prædictio astrologica. The great and vvonderfull prognostication, for the yeare of our Lord 1598. Written by Rodulphus Grapheus Doctor of Phisick in the Towne of Deuenter. Translated out of Dutch into

text: I find alſo in the prouinciall figure, that Iupiter is eleuated aboue Venus, which ſignifieth that womens nature is alwayes deſirous of pleaſure, for they are the mother of our generation: They ſhall alſo bee fortunate in childbearing, and are worthy of honour in all places.
author: Grapheuis, Rodulphus.
title: Prædictio astrologica. The great and vvonderfull prognostication, for the yeare of our Lord 1598. Written by Rodulphus Grapheus Doctor of Phisick in the Towne of Deuenter. Translated out of Dutch into

author: Taverner, Richard, 1505?-1575.

text: Wherfore it is to be feared, leste God wyll visite them, not by heapynge vpon them hys benefytes and graces whych they refuse & neglecte, but by pourynge vpon them hys iuste yre and vengeaunce accordynge to theyr desertes.
author: Taverner, Richard, 1505?-1575.

text: For wyth Christe by true fayth arte thou quyckened agayne (sayeth saynt Paule) from death of synne to lyfe of grace, and in hope translated frō corporall and euer lastynge death, to the euerlastynge lyfe of glorye in heauen: where nowe thy conuersation shulde be and thy harte and desyre set.
author: Taverner, Richard, 1505?-1575.

text: What so euer is sought to the soule helth the same is al togither conteyned and accomplished in holy scripture.
author: Taverner, Richard, 1505?-1575.

text: The Sonne shalbe torned into darckenes and the Mone into bloude, before that greate and notable daye of the Lord come.
author: Taverner, Richard, 1505?-1575.
title: The Epistles and Gospelles with a brief postil vpon the same from after Easter tyll Aduent, which is the somer parte set forth for the singuler co[m]moditie of all good Christen men and namely of pres

text: And ye nowe therfore haue sorowe: but I wyll se you agayne, and youre hartes shall reioyse, and youre ioye shall no man take from you.
author: Taverner, Richard, 1505?-1575.
title: The Epistles and Gospelles with a brief postil vpon the same from after Easter tyll Aduent, which is the somer parte set forth for the singuler co[m]moditie of all good Christen men and namely of pres

text: And here is to be noted that Christ woll not haue hys preachers cu riouse vpon ydle questions or vayne philosophie.
author: Taverner, Richard, 1505?-1575.

text: But I wole shewe you the treuth why I muste departe, partly bycause ye maye vnderstand what maner kyngdome my kingdome is, and partly what ye ought to loke for in it.
author: Taverner, Richard, 1505?-1575.

text: What ioye I pray you is this? vndoutedly it is no worldely or corporall leapynge or daunsing and reioising, but it is a spirituall ioye wherof saint Paule maketh mention wher he saith.
author: Taverner, Richard, 1505?-1575.

text: And albeit the pleaſant encounter of mine eys, ſeaming more liberal on your behalf, with a familiaritie more thē ordinarie to al men, may perſuade a certein differēce I haue put betwen the frendſhip of you & reſpect of any other, with deſyer to embrace you aboue any one creature.
author: Bandello, Matteo, 1485-1561.

text: Roderico amaſed no leſſe with the tragicall farewell of his frende, then moued with iuſte anger againſte the vnſéemely tyranny of Geniuera, commaunded certeine of his companie to reſtore the traunce of Diego, and with the reſte addreſſed hym to the mercileſſe gentlewoman, whome he threatned in this ſorte.
author: Bandello, Matteo, 1485-1561.

text: But if diſdayne ſhall quyt him vvith diſpyght And yeld him loth, for long deſired grace Then ſtabbing glayue the deſperat breſt muſt ſmyte Or frantycke vvyſe runne out a ſauage race, Thus if of gladd or ſad he happ the gayne Both haue this end, in loue nought is but vayne.
author: Bandello, Matteo, 1485-1561.

text: Alas good madam: the only hope of my life & cōpforte of my carefull harte, how long ſhall I hange in the doubteful ballance of my preſente death, or lyfe? what date alas haue you appointed to giue ende to my deſperate ſorowes, yf my pennance not ſufficiente for thoffence I haue committed?
author: Bandello, Matteo, 1485-1561.
title: Certaine tragicall discourses written out of Frenche and Latin, by Geffraie Fenton, no lesse profitable then pleasaunt, and of like necessitye to al degrees that take pleasure in antiquityes or forrei

text: But Fentons frame hath vvouen an other vvebbe His paynfull penn hath died a ſtraunger hevve He tels vvhen vvitt is in his lovveſt ebbe And vvarns the Shunne the bayne that coms by vievve VVhich ſo doth chaunge the ſence of euery vvight That from a man to beaſt it tournes him quitt.
author: Bandello, Matteo, 1485-1561.
title: Certaine tragicall discourses written out of Frenche and Latin, by Geffraie Fenton, no lesse profitable then pleasaunt, and of like necessitye to al degrees that take pleasure in antiquityes or forrei

text: Howe often alas, haue I made you priuye to thinwarde affection of my mynde, by the outwarde regardes & glaunces of my exterior partes?
author: Bandello, Matteo, 1485-1561.
title: Certaine tragicall discourses written out of Frenche and Latin, by Geffraie Fenton, no lesse profitable then pleasaunt, and of like necessitye to al degrees that take pleasure in antiquityes or forrei

text: My folly forcde a fall of all I hadd And frendes forſoke me in my greateſt need My rentes retird vvith route of roiſters trade And fancy fedd me vvith the foode of euill ſpede I ſoughte to ſovve the ſeedes of ſtayed lyfe vvhen lo I cropt the frutes of greater ſtryfe.
author: Bandello, Matteo, 1485-1561.
title: Certaine tragicall discourses written out of Frenche and Latin, by Geffraie Fenton, no lesse profitable then pleasaunt, and of like necessitye to al degrees that take pleasure in antiquityes or forrei

text: Ne vvas my loue deuoide of lyke annoye Syth ſhe vvith equall grieff paid tribute to my paine, She vveard her youth in dule in ſteade of ioye The vievve of my miſhapps bredd vvo in euery vayne Her pleaſant tyme paſſd in continuall teares VVhoſe ſooddes aye bathd her greene and mayden yeres.
author: Bandello, Matteo, 1485-1561.
title: Certaine tragicall discourses written out of Frenche and Latin, by Geffraie Fenton, no lesse profitable then pleasaunt, and of like necessitye to al degrees that take pleasure in antiquityes or forrei

text: And wherſoeuer any litle commoditie falleth out in the commō weale, there ſwarmeth together whole legions to gather of worldlynges, there they are.
author: Drant, Thomas, b. 1601 or 2.

text: This money is their ſacrifice for all their ſinnes, the Monarche of the world, the maſter of miſrule, the abater of diſcipline, ye ſmother of wrincled countenaunces.
author: Drant, Thomas, b. 1601 or 2.

text: Thou art like the Iewes whom Eſay ſpeaketh of xxviij. chap. Who cryed out, That they had ſmittē truce with death, & made a couenant with their graue.
author: Drant, Thomas, b. 1601 or 2.
title: A fruitfull and necessary sermon, specially concernyng almes geuing, preached the Twisday [sic] in Easter weeke The yere of our Lord. 1572. at S. Maries Spittle. By Thomas Drant, bachelor in diuinitie

text: If any man be welthy, the Scripture will ſay that hée may waſhe his wayes with butter, And that oyle doth drop out of his rockes.
author: Drant, Thomas, b. 1601 or 2.
title: A fruitfull and necessary sermon, specially concernyng almes geuing, preached the Twisday [sic] in Easter weeke The yere of our Lord. 1572. at S. Maries Spittle. By Thomas Drant, bachelor in diuinitie

text: Though frendly warnynges folyes now appears: The day drawes on, the houre is hard at hand That you ſhall curſe eche cauſe that ſtoppt your ears: And made you kick to heare your vices ſcand.
author: Drant, Thomas, b. 1601 or 2.
title: A fruitfull and necessary sermon, specially concernyng almes geuing, preached the Twisday [sic] in Easter weeke The yere of our Lord. 1572. at S. Maries Spittle. By Thomas Drant, bachelor in diuinitie

text: But if any of yours chaunce to kill one, whether that then through the priuiledge of your badge, and marke hée is not vntouchable, Theſe & many other the lyke queſtions if I might ſpeake vnto you as to my neighbour, good Lordes and noble men, I would demaunde of you.
author: Drant, Thomas, b. 1601 or 2.
title: A fruitfull and necessary sermon, specially concernyng almes geuing, preached the Twisday [sic] in Easter weeke The yere of our Lord. 1572. at S. Maries Spittle. By Thomas Drant, bachelor in diuinitie

text: But you, you decke your ſelues, you pricke your ſelues, you pruen your ſelues, you ſpangle your ſelues, you pouder your ſelues.
author: Drant, Thomas, b. 1601 or 2.

text: The Clergy as it nowe is reſembled moſt aptly (my thought) the nature of Foxes, who thought they ſéeme to ſléepe before company, yet they will ſpoyle and praye when no body looketh on & ſurely they ſleepe as ſinne is ſayd to ſléepe in Geneſis.
author: Drant, Thomas, b. 1601 or 2.

text: This text that I doe meane to entreate of is onely for almes, and for openyng of your bowels, and geuyng relief vnto the poore.

text: And therein heartens vp his seruile powers, VVho flattred by their leaders iocound show, Stuffe vp his lust: as minutes fill vp howres.
author: Shakespeare, William, 1564-1616.
title: Lucrece

text: This deede will make thee only lou'd for feare, But happie Monarchs still are feard for loue: VVith fowle offendors thou perforce must beare, VVhen they in thee the like offences proue; If but for feare of this, thy will remoue.
author: Shakespeare, William, 1564-1616.
title: Lucrece

text: The father saies, shee's mine, ô mine shee is Replies her husband, do not take away My sorrowes interest, let no mourner say He weepes for her, for shee was onely mine, And onelie must be wayl'd by COLATINE.
author: Shakespeare, William, 1564-1616.
title: Lucrece

text: For in the dreadfull dead of darke midnight, VVith snining Fauchion in my chamber came A creeping creature with a flaming light, And softly cried, awake thou Romaine Dame, And entertaine my loue, else lasting shame On thee and thine this night I will inflict, If thou my loues desire do contradict.
author: Shakespeare, William, 1564-1616.
title: Lucrece

text: O shame to knighthood, and to shining Armes, O foule dishonor to my houshoulds graue: O impious act including all foule harmes.
author: Shakespeare, William, 1564-1616.
title: Lucrece

text: VVhen shall he thinke to find a stranger iust, VVhen he himselfe, himselfe confounds, betraies To sclandrous tongues & wretched hateful daies?
author: Shakespeare, William, 1564-1616.
title: Lucrece

text: Shee sayes her subiects with fowle insurrection, Haue batterd downe her consecrated wall, And by their mortall fault brought in subiection Her immortalitie, and made her thrall, To liuing death and payne perpetuall.
author: Shakespeare, William, 1564-1616.
title: Lucrece

text: VVhen patternd by thy fault fowle sin may say, He learnd to sin, and thou didst teach the way.
author: Shakespeare, William, 1564-1616.
title: Lucrece

text: So vnder his insulting Fauchion lies Harmelesse LVCRETIA marking what he tels, VVith trembling feare:as fowl hear Faulcōs bels.
author: Shakespeare, William, 1564-1616.
title: Lucrece

text: That nighte when all the Fleete had greatest hope to haue had their desire, and to haue enioyed that Carricke whome they had garded with greate pollicy.
author: Raleigh, Walter, Sir, 1552?-1618.
title: The sea-mans triumph Declaring the honorable actions of such gentlemen captaines and sailers, as were at the takinge of the great carrick, lately brought to Dartmouth, with her burthen and commodities

text: VVherefore we had not neede to be slacke in praying to the God of all power, wisedome, and strength, that it will please him to encrease the nomber of faithfull and obedient subiects, continue the raigne of our most Soueraigne Lady, and consounde all her foes.
author: Raleigh, Walter, Sir, 1552?-1618.
title: The sea-mans triumph Declaring the honorable actions of such gentlemen captaines and sailers, as were at the takinge of the great carrick, lately brought to Dartmouth, with her burthen and commodities

text: Other newes there is none, but generall good tidinges of all our men of warre, that spent the Sommer abroade, who haue prospered well: whose actions deseruinge commendations, when I shall certainely know, I will further aduertise you: Till when I humbly recommend my selfe vnto your worships seruice.
author: Raleigh, Walter, Sir, 1552?-1618.
title: The sea-mans triumph Declaring the honorable actions of such gentlemen captaines and sailers, as were at the takinge of the great carrick, lately brought to Dartmouth, with her burthen and commodities

text: The whole Fleet bare againe with Floweres and comming neere the Illand might perceiue the Spaniards, how they laboured, to saue the best they had aborde, hauing not ceased all that night from hard trauaill and carryinge a shore what they might.
author: Raleigh, Walter, Sir, 1552?-1618.
title: The sea-mans triumph Declaring the honorable actions of such gentlemen captaines and sailers, as were at the takinge of the great carrick, lately brought to Dartmouth, with her burthen and commodities

text: These enuious villaines, seeing no remidye but to fall into their handes, that would haue taken great care of her, Fyred the Caricke before any of our Fleete could lay her abord, and almost all forsooke her.
author: Raleigh, Walter, Sir, 1552?-1618.
title: The sea-mans triumph Declaring the honorable actions of such gentlemen captaines and sailers, as were at the takinge of the great carrick, lately brought to Dartmouth, with her burthen and commodities

text: The nexte that came to her rescue was the valiant Sir Iohn Burrowe, who attempting with great valour to boorde her, was putt off againe, and receiued a shott which had like to haue endaungered himselfe.
author: Raleigh, Walter, Sir, 1552?-1618.
title: The sea-mans triumph Declaring the honorable actions of such gentlemen captaines and sailers, as were at the takinge of the great carrick, lately brought to Dartmouth, with her burthen and commodities

text: The third was the golden Dragon of London, whereof was Captaine Maister Newport, whoe most brauely gaue the attempte, but was likewise put off, the Carricke beeinge so huge, that those Shippes did but little good.
author: Raleigh, Walter, Sir, 1552?-1618.
title: The sea-mans triumph Declaring the honorable actions of such gentlemen captaines and sailers, as were at the takinge of the great carrick, lately brought to Dartmouth, with her burthen and commodities

text: As I haue herein done my best to signifie the same vnto you and others, and could well wishe it were published, to the view of the worlde, to the ende, their names who haue hardly aduentured for it: may reape the honour they haue deserued, to the encouragemente of others.
author: Raleigh, Walter, Sir, 1552?-1618.
title: The sea-mans triumph Declaring the honorable actions of such gentlemen captaines and sailers, as were at the takinge of the great carrick, lately brought to Dartmouth, with her burthen and commodities

text: The Foresight and the rest of the Fleete, beeing farre off, hadd likewise discried her, and bare with the reste.
author: Raleigh, Walter, Sir, 1552?-1618.

text: Oh that we might ſee now a litle with S. John that holy Citie, new Jeruſalē, deſcending frō heauen, prepared of god as a bride trimmed for her huſbande.
author: Day, Richard, b. 1552, attributed name.
title: Christian prayers and meditations in English French, Italian, Spanish, Greeke, and Latine.

text: As for me, I was like a deafe man and heard not, & as one that is dombe, which doth not open his mouth.
author: Day, Richard, b. 1552, attributed name.
title: Christian prayers and meditations in English French, Italian, Spanish, Greeke, and Latine.

text: Kinges with their armies did flie, they did flee, and the ornament of an houſe deuided the ſpoyle.
author: Day, Richard, b. 1552, attributed name.
title: Christian prayers and meditations in English French, Italian, Spanish, Greeke, and Latine.

text: Now, he (deare father) we learne by thy ſpirite, was aſcended and taken vp in his very body into heauen, whether Steuen loked vp and ſawe thy Chriſt ſtanding on thy right hand: to whom he prayed: Oh Lorde Ieſu receiue my ſpirite.
author: Day, Richard, b. 1552, attributed name.
title: Christian prayers and meditations in English French, Italian, Spanish, Greeke, and Latine.

text: Alſo how much more we ought to care for the ſoule that it may ſee wel, then for the body.
author: Day, Richard, b. 1552, attributed name.
title: Christian prayers and meditations in English French, Italian, Spanish, Greeke, and Latine.

text: Where the Prince is without vnderſtanding, there is great oppreſſion and wrong: but if he hateth coueteouſnes, he ſhall long raigne.
author: Day, Richard, b. 1552, attributed name.
title: Christian prayers and meditations in English French, Italian, Spanish, Greeke, and Latine.

text: The king is as an Angell of God in hearing of the good and bad, therefore the Lorde God is with hym.
author: Day, Richard, b. 1552, attributed name.
title: Christian prayers and meditations in English French, Italian, Spanish, Greeke, and Latine.

text: Lift vp your heades (O ye gates) and be ye lift vp you euerlaſting doores, and the king of glory ſhal enter in.
author: Day, Richard, b. 1552, attributed name.
title: Christian prayers and meditations in English French, Italian, Spanish, Greeke, and Latine.

text: The king is wiſe according to the wiſedome of an Angell of God, to vnderſtand all thinges thac are in earth.
author: Day, Richard, b. 1552, attributed name.
title: Christian prayers and meditations in English French, Italian, Spanish, Greeke, and Latine.

text: And therin he fareth like a mā / to whō a bridgrome had deliuered a goodlye golde ringe wt a riche rubie therin / to deliuer to his bryde for a token.
author: Frith, John, 1503-1533.

text: Thys cuppe or chalice ys the new testament: That ys / thys cuppe or chalice which I deliuer you doth sygnifye the newe testamēt.
author: Frith, John, 1503-1533.

text: The antecedēt or first ꝑte of the reason is ꝓued by the wordes of christe wc saith that the fleshe ꝓfiteth nothinge at all / meaning that yt doth not ꝓfite as they vnderstode him: that is to saie / yt profiteth nothinge to be eaten carnallie wt their teth & bellye / as they vnderstode him.
author: Frith, John, 1503-1533.

text: And yt ys named to be don the same daye thorough the celebracyon of the sacrament (thorough kepynge the memoryall of the thyng once don̄) which ys not don that daye / but was don longe agoon.
author: Frith, John, 1503-1533.
title: A boke made by Iohn Frith prisoner in the tower of London answeringe vnto M mores lettur which he wrote agenst the first litle treatyse that Iohn̄ Frith made concerninge the sacramente of the body and

text: Yf they had thought ether that it could not be there or that yt was not there in dede / they wold not for all the good in this worlde haue wryten as they haue done.
author: Frith, John, 1503-1533.
title: A boke made by Iohn Frith prisoner in the tower of London answeringe vnto M mores lettur which he wrote agenst the first litle treatyse that Iohn̄ Frith made concerninge the sacramente of the body and

text: Nowe yf thys be true / thē ys your reason not worth a rishe / for christes naturall bodie ys not in the worde wc is p̄ched / as all men knowe.
author: Frith, John, 1503-1533.
title: A boke made by Iohn Frith prisoner in the tower of London answeringe vnto M mores lettur which he wrote agenst the first litle treatyse that Iohn̄ Frith made concerninge the sacramente of the body and

text: For thorough the beleue that thys bodye ys there / mē fall downe and worshipe yt / And thynking to pleasse god / do dāpnable synne agaynst hī This I saye / ys the cause that I so ernestly wryte agaynste yt / to auoyde the Idolatrye that ys cō mitted thorough yt.
author: Frith, John, 1503-1533.
title: A boke made by Iohn Frith prisoner in the tower of London answeringe vnto M mores lettur which he wrote agenst the first litle treatyse that Iohn̄ Frith made concerninge the sacramente of the body and

text: Notwtstonding I wolde not that any shulde counte that I make my saynge (whiche is the negatiue) any artycle of the faythe.
author: Frith, John, 1503-1533.
title: A boke made by Iohn Frith prisoner in the tower of London answeringe vnto M mores lettur which he wrote agenst the first litle treatyse that Iohn̄ Frith made concerninge the sacramente of the body and

text: And therfore yf he speake not of the sacrament / then haue you concluded that the sacrament ys not hys naturall bodye: the contrarie wherof you wold haue mē beleue.
author: Frith, John, 1503-1533.

text: Let him eate ſodden fleſh at dinner, and at ſupper alſo, if he be of a very hote temperature, or els hee ſhall vſe roſted at ſupper, in little quantitie, or in ſtead of that, ſome reaſonable quantitie of Reiſons, the which doe corroborate the entrals.
author: Lowe, Peter, ca. 1550-ca. 1612.
title: An easie, certaine, and perfect method, to cure and preuent the Spanish sicknes Wherby the learned and skilfull chirurgian may heale a great many other diseases. Compiled by Peter Lowe, Arellian: . .

text: Likewiſe they which haue the skin fleane of their ſecret parts, take not ſo eaſilie the maladie as others, becauſe beeing alwaies vncouered, it is not ſo tender and delicate, and therefore not ſo apt to receiue infection.
author: Lowe, Peter, ca. 1550-ca. 1612.
title: An easie, certaine, and perfect method, to cure and preuent the Spanish sicknes Wherby the learned and skilfull chirurgian may heale a great many other diseases. Compiled by Peter Lowe, Arellian: . .

text: Theſe things happen by not knowing the nature of the maladie, and remedies, not the varietie of the bodies, and the nature of the partie infected.
author: Lowe, Peter, ca. 1550-ca. 1612.
title: An easie, certaine, and perfect method, to cure and preuent the Spanish sicknes Wherby the learned and skilfull chirurgian may heale a great many other diseases. Compiled by Peter Lowe, Arellian: . .

text: To a pint of the decoction add halfe an ounce of Sene, 2, dragmes of Hermodact, and a little Lycoris, after the full ebullition add an ounce of ſirop of Roſes laxatiue.
author: Lowe, Peter, ca. 1550-ca. 1612.
title: An easie, certaine, and perfect method, to cure and preuent the Spanish sicknes Wherby the learned and skilfull chirurgian may heale a great many other diseases. Compiled by Peter Lowe, Arellian: . .

text: That which is of the beſt ſort is of a meane greatnes, recent, dry, & vncorrupted; which beeing put in the fire, the ſubſtance doth appeare gummie, the collour yellow, with a meane palenes within, the barck cleauing hard to the tree.
author: Lowe, Peter, ca. 1550-ca. 1612.
title: An easie, certaine, and perfect method, to cure and preuent the Spanish sicknes Wherby the learned and skilfull chirurgian may heale a great many other diseases. Compiled by Peter Lowe, Arellian: . .

text: Then muſt the body be prepared by vniuerſall remedies, as yee haue heard in the former Treatiſe, becauſe the bodie being full of humors, the vſing of hote medicaments, ſuch as are the Cathereticks, make eaſily new fluxions on the part affected.
author: Lowe, Peter, ca. 1550-ca. 1612.
title: An easie, certaine, and perfect method, to cure and preuent the Spanish sicknes Wherby the learned and skilfull chirurgian may heale a great many other diseases. Compiled by Peter Lowe, Arellian: . .

text: Take a little of Orpiment, the ſhells of Eggs burned, the ſhells of Muſcles put into very ſmall powder, and mingle it with roſat Meſues, Cerat Galien, or a little of Oyle of ſweet Almonds.
author: Lowe, Peter, ca. 1550-ca. 1612.
title: An easie, certaine, and perfect method, to cure and preuent the Spanish sicknes Wherby the learned and skilfull chirurgian may heale a great many other diseases. Compiled by Peter Lowe, Arellian: . .

text: But firſt the body and humors muſt be prepared with conuenient remedies, as hereafter you ſhall heare, to the end the euacuation may be the eaſier & ſurer.
author: Lowe, Peter, ca. 1550-ca. 1612.
title: An easie, certaine, and perfect method, to cure and preuent the Spanish sicknes Wherby the learned and skilfull chirurgian may heale a great many other diseases. Compiled by Peter Lowe, Arellian: . .

text: Thus by the vſage of theſe remedies, with a iuſt forme of diet, the ſicke ſhall be healed perfectly.
author: Lowe, Peter, ca. 1550-ca. 1612.
title: An easie, certaine, and perfect method, to cure and preuent the Spanish sicknes Wherby the learned and skilfull chirurgian may heale a great many other diseases. Compiled by Peter Lowe, Arellian: . .

text: And so, vnder couler, of space, and beware To taunt at gods prechers, as muche as they dare Sayeng, such passe not, by here saye to go And preach in ther pulpittes, that thus some saye so.
author: Kethe, William, d. 1608?
title: Of misrules contending, with gods worde by name And then, of ones iudgment, that heard of the same.

text: But now if in conscience, speake frely I maye In mynde I digresse not, from that whyche some saye If mysrule mayntayned be, and seke to ascend In this casse I doute muche, but mark well the ende.
author: Kethe, William, d. 1608?
title: Of misrules contending, with gods worde by name And then, of ones iudgment, that heard of the same.

text: But now to my purpose, agayne for to come This misrule, through madnes, at last frynds had some Of whome he gat comforte, as it maye well seme His boldnes well wayed, who would not so deme.
author: Kethe, William, d. 1608?
title: Of misrules contending, with gods worde by name And then, of ones iudgment, that heard of the same.

text: That gods worde muche lothing, could it not abyde But stepped fourth boldly, and misrule defied Wyshing from misrule, all men to refrayne As from a thing noysome, to vile, and to vayne.
author: Kethe, William, d. 1608?
title: Of misrules contending, with gods worde by name And then, of ones iudgment, that heard of the same.

text: But be it, that some saye, by here say a misse And saye not (through here say) the truth as it is Doth it therfore folow, for that thinge fourth brought That al thinges whyche some say, therfore shuld be nought.
author: Kethe, William, d. 1608?
title: Of misrules contending, with gods worde by name And then, of ones iudgment, that heard of the same.

text: What law is so strayt made, they feare not to breake What threat can suche tounges stoppe, they feare not to speake What doctrine can dryue them, to know what they be What myschief may moue them, that onely they se.
author: Kethe, William, d. 1608?
title: Of misrules contending, with gods worde by name And then, of ones iudgment, that heard of the same.

text: In Sodom and Gomor, suche lyke stryffe began Betwene this madde mysrule, and gods worde: but than Could god longe abide it? when he in his fume With sulphire and brimston, mysrule dyd consume.
author: Kethe, William, d. 1608?
title: Of misrules contending, with gods worde by name And then, of ones iudgment, that heard of the same.

text: His owne Iewish people, as ofte as they ranne A maddyng with mysrule, wyth plages God beganne To lerne vs that mysrule, he alwayes did hate And yet (alas) se you? how he plaith chek mate.
author: Kethe, William, d. 1608?

text: As we ſee in Adā, in Cain, and in many others, who when they were fallen from God, they ſought not to God to bee reconciled againe, but God ſought vnto them: yea, and when they hyd themſelues, yet God found them out.

text: The infant ouercōmeth his mother with crying, the child his father with wéeping, & the ſeruant his maſter by entreaty, & wilt not yu be intreated O Lord?

text: God is mercifull, God is mercifull, as though God were made all of mercie, and that ther were no iuſtice in him at al: and thus the wicked make Gods mercie an occaſion to ſinne, which thinge the Prophete Nahum in the firſt of his Propheſie doeth ſharply reproue.
author: Dent, Arthur, d. 1607.
title: A sermon of repentaunce a very godly and profitable sermon preached at Lee in Essex / by Arthur Dent ...

text: Therefore my deare brethren, I beſéech you by the mecies of God in the bowels of Ieſus Chriſt, that none of all theſe common lets may ſtay you from ſpéedy, and vnfeigned Repentance.

title: A sermon of repentaunce a very godly and profitable sermon preached at Lee in Essex / by Arthur Dent ...

text: Oh that they would call to mind theyr open & ſecret ſins, & me thinketh it ſhould make their heart bléed within their belly to thinke vpon them.

text: Hée reproueth the Iewes, becauſe they coulde diſcerne the face of the Skye, but could not diſcerne the ſignes of the times.

text: Our life for the ſhortneſſe and inconſtancie of it in the ſcripture is compared to graſſe, to a vapour to ſmoke, and to a Weauers ſhuttle which glideth away ſwiftly.

text: Here then we haue a glaſſe to beholde our ſelues in, whethereuer we haue Repented or no. For if wee find not this change and alteration in vs, we haue not repented, and ſo conſequently remaine vnder Damnation.
